Instead the class sat there with the question hanging in the air like the smell of disinfectant from the hallway. Gavin stared at the sparse corkboard by the window, where only two faded posters hung, and tried to think. He remembered last fall, when he'd claimed the cafeteria ran out of pizza by Wednesday, and Maya had counted for a whole week and shown it lasted until Thursday. He'd been wrong then, too, and it had stung, but not as much as being wrong without knowing would have.

"Wait," he said slowly. "It's not just an opinion. It's a claim. Like, it could be checked. Nobody has checked it yet, but we could." Priya tilted her head. "How?" she asked. "Follow everybody home?" Someone laughed. "A survey," Gavin said. "We ask every student how they get to school and count it up. Then we'd know if most of them walk or not." The word felt good in his mouth, solid, like a handle on a door he could actually open.

Mr. Okafor suggested they postpone the debate until they had data, and the class agreed to run the survey at lunch on Thursday. On Thursday, Gavin stood at the cafeteria door with a clipboard, pencil shaking slightly from too much excitement and not enough breakfast. The first twenty kids mostly said "bus," which surprised him. By the time the third lunch period started, his tally sheet was a mess of slashes and smudged graphite, but a pattern was climbing out of it anyway, one he hadn't predicted and Priya hadn't either.

They counted the sheets in Mr. Okafor's room after school, the radiator ticking, the hallway outside gone quiet. Priya totaled the walkers; Gavin totaled everyone else. He looked at her total, then at his own, then out the window at the empty car line loop, still painted yellow. "So I was wrong," he said, "but I was right that we could find out." Priya grinned and spun the clipboard toward him. "Count them again," she said. "I want to see your face when you get to the end."

The zit had appeared on Sunday, right on the end of Emmett's nose, and school pictures were on Wednesday morning. He leaned against the car window while his mom drove, tilting the visor mirror to study it again, as if it might have shrunk since breakfast. It had not. His little sister used to get chocolate on her face and it wiped off with a napkin. This thing was different, and it seemed unfair that his own face would betray him two days before the photographer.

"Mom, can we stop somewhere? Like a pharmacy?"

She glanced over. "For what, honey?"

"Nothing. Face stuff." He felt his ears go hot. "Dad appointed me to pick up his razors anyway," he added, which was technically true, since Dad had said "grab me some razors if you're out" last week. Mom pulled into the parking lot of the drugstore by the hardware shop.

Emmett found the razor aisle first, then drifted to the wall of face washes, which was bigger than he expected. He was scanning shelves when a girl from his grade, Priya, appeared beside him, holding two bottles and turning them over to read the backs.

"Picture day?" she asked. "Me too. I woke up with three of them on my chin." She held up a bottle. "This one says it removes excess oil. My brother says pimples show up because of puberty. Hormones make the oil glands in your skin produce more oil, and it's called sebum, and it clogs your pores."

"Oil glands?" Emmett said. "I thought it was like dirt or something."

"That's what I thought. But it starts inside." She compared labels again. "So washing a million times wouldn't even fix it, because the stuff is coming from under the skin." She put one bottle back and kept the stronger one.

Emmett picked up a wash labeled for oily skin and read the back. The instructions were explicit: use twice daily, avoid eyes, rinse thoroughly. Twice daily. He counted backward. Two days until pictures meant four washes, if he started tonight. One wash right now in the store bathroom, one before bed, two more tomorrow and Tuesday. It wasn't much of a plan, but it was a plan, and having one made his shoulders loosen.

He paid with his own money, and in the car he read the bottle the whole way home, checking the ingredients like they were a code he might crack.

"Did you get your dad's razors?" Mom asked as they turned onto their street.

"Razors," Emmett said. "Right." He'd forgotten them completely. He ran back inside the store, grabbed the razors, and caught up with his mom at the register, the face wash in one hand and the razors in the other, four washes left before Wednesday.

The lights went out at 7:40, right in the middle of Alexandra's homework, and the whole house sank into a black so complete she couldn't even find her own elbow. "The power's out," her little brother Marcus announced from the hallway, as if she might not have noticed.

Alexandra fished the flashlight from the kitchen drawer and did some thinking while Marcus bumped into the coffee table behind her. The streetlights outside were dark too, which meant it wasn't just their house. And on the walk home from school, after the storm, she had seen a wire lying across the sidewalk two blocks over. It had looked harmless, dull and quiet, not sparking or humming like wires in movies. But her science teacher had once said something Alexandra had never forgotten: a fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported. Mr. Okafor had made them all repeat it twice, which had seemed ridiculous at the time and now seemed like the smartest thing anyone had ever done.

"Marcus, do not eat that cheese," she said, shining the flashlight on him. He froze with the block halfway to his mouth. "That's for dinner. It's the most nutritious thing we have until the fridge situation stabilizes." The situation, as far as she could tell, was that the temperature inside would fluctuate every time he opened the door to graze, and the cheese would not survive his snacking until morning.

Her phone was at nine percent, so she typed fast: "Mom. Power out on our street. I think it's the downed wire on Elm, two blocks from school. I saw it on the way home. I did NOT touch it, I stayed way back. Please call it in to the power company, my battery is almost dead." Send. The battery dropped to eight percent, then seven, as if to add commentary.

Twenty minutes later the porch lit up, the refrigerator hummed like a released prisoner, and headlights swept the window. Marcus cheered. Alexandra's phone buzzed once before it died: "Reported. Proud of you. Also I'm bringing pizza, keep your paws off the cheese." Alexandra laughed and hid the cheese behind the milk anyway.

Michael stood at the counter of Delgado's Corner Store with four dollars and a math test folded in his back pocket, and he had a problem. The problem was that Mr. Pruitt had promised a pizza party for the whole class if anyone scored a hundred on Friday's test, and Michael was the only one even close. The other problem was the machine by the door.

It was an old claw machine, and today it held a single rubber ball with a coordinate grid printed on it, along with a few random prizes nobody wanted. Michael had already spent two dollars trying to grab that ball. The claw's grip seemed to evaporate every time it lifted, like his luck was steaming away into the air. If he could win the ball, he'd have the one study tool he actually wanted, because the ball showed equations and their lines, and lines were exactly the thing he couldn't picture.

"Four dollars," said Rosa, who worked the register and was in his sister Ana's grade. "You going to buy gum or feed that machine again?"

"Neither yet," Michael said. He unfolded the practice sheet Mr. Pruitt had given him. At the top, Ana had scrawled a battleship game from last night, where she'd sworn his shot at (3, 5) was a miss because he'd counted up three and over five instead of across first. They'd argued until their dad made them wash dishes.

Michael tapped the paper. If he solved for x, he'd get a number. Then he could put that number in the first slot of a pair and pick any number for the second slot, and plot the point. He tried it with 2x plus 1 equals 7. He subtracted the 1 from both sides in his head, then divided, and got x equals 3. So the pair started with 3, then across first, like Ana kept insisting. He drew a quick grid on the back of his receipt, marked (3, 5) by counting three across and five up, and marked (3, 0) too, and there they sat in a line going straight up and down, like a fence post.

"The first number is across," he said out loud. "The second one is up or down."

"So?" said Rosa.

"So the ball is the same thing." Through the scratched glass, every printed line on that rubber ball slanted upward at the same steady angle, and each label started with the x value. If he imagined the claw dropping at a spot three across from the left wall and five up from the bottom, he could aim it like a plotted point instead of guessing.

He fed in his last quarter, counted three across, five up, and pressed the button. The claw swung, dropped, and closed on the ball. It lifted. It held.

Rosa leaned over the counter. "Okay, that was not luck."

The claw carried the ball toward the chute, then stopped directly above it and opened its grip, one inch short of the drop. Michael stared. Then he grabbed the receipt, folded it into a tight wedge, reached through the prize flap, and nudged the ball the last inch until it tumbled into his hand.

"Friday," he told Rosa, holding it up. "Class pizza. Three across, five up."

Grandma Wei arrived on Thursday, and by Friday night Isla had a problem: what to wear to her cousin Marisol's wedding shower on Saturday. Grandma had barely unpacked before she started pulling clothes out of Isla's closet and sorting them into two piles, one for yes and one for no.

"Not the white dress," Grandma said, holding up Isla's favorite one like it was a wet sock.

"It's a wedding thing," Isla said. "Marisol's whole theme is white. The invitations are white. The cake is white. The bride even wears white."

Grandma set the dress on the no pile and smoothed it flat, as if to preserve its feelings. "White is for mourning at funerals," she said. "In traditional Chinese culture, that is what we wear. For the dead." Then she pointed at Isla's rust-colored skirt. "Wear this."

Isla stared at her. She had never heard anything like this. Her brain started running its usual algorithm for arguments with Grandma: state facts, provide evidence, lose anyway.

Dad came through with the lasagna, and Isla got her chance. "Dad, tell Grandma white is a wedding color."

Dad put down the dish and rubbed his neck. "Both are true," he said. "Lots of Western brides wear white. And in Grandma's tradition, white is worn for mourning. Different people, same color, opposite meanings." He gave the no pile a guilty glance. "At your Aunt Po's funeral, everyone wore white. Marisol's wedding, the bride will too. Nobody's wrong."

Isla chewed on that through half a plate of lasagna. Same color. Two meanings. That meant the shower was going to be a room full of people doing opposite things at the same time, and only some of them would know it. She imagined Marisol's grandmother from Mexico, her neighbors, her own grandma, all handing gifts and thinking completely different thoughts about identical white napkins.

So she tested it. "Grandma, what if everyone at the party wears white except me? Won't I look like I'm at the wrong event?"

"Then you will look like the only person there with respect," Grandma said.

"That's a rebellious plan," Isla said. "Wearing not-white to a white party."

"Rebellious," Grandma agreed, spearing a meatball.

Isla tried one more angle. "Grandma, Marisol asked me to hand out the favors. White boxes with white ribbons. If I wear the rust skirt, the pictures will look strange."

Grandma put down her fork. For a moment Isla thought the algorithm had finally found a winning input. Then Grandma said, "The boxes are white?"

"Every single one."

Grandma looked at the window for a while. "Then the boxes are for mourning," she said, "and Marisol must pick new boxes, or I must pick new eyes." She picked up her fork again and went back to the lasagna. "Hand me the bread, and on Saturday you wear the rust."

Alexis laced his skates in the bench area of Riverside Ice Arena and watched his best friend Dante glide past the tryout line with his usual speed. That was the strange part. Dante was the fastest skater in sixth grade, but this morning he had wobbled twice during warm-ups, and when Coach Reyes blew the whistle, Dante's stop was so abrupt that he nearly fell over backward. Alexis filed that away and took his own turn around the cones.

The tryouts were for the school hockey team, and thirty kids had shown up to participate. Alexis wanted a forward spot, but so did Marcus Tran, who had been talking all week about how he was going to take it. Marcus was fast, too. During the second drill, Alexis noticed something. Marcus kept yawning on the bench. When the puck came to him, he reacted late, half a second behind, like a video with bad lag.

Between drills, Alexis sat next to him. "You look like you're skating through glue," Alexis said.

"I was up till two playing Starfall Six," Marcus admitted. "I only slept six hours. I figured I'd be fine."

Alexis had spent a week researching sleep for a science project, mostly so he could win arguments about bedtime. "Kids our age are supposed to get nine to twelve hours a night," he said. "Even teenagers only get to drop down to eight to ten. Six isn't on the chart for anybody."

"Whatever," Marcus said, and skated off, wobbling on the first turn.

Alexis thought about it while he waited for the scrimmage. He had a theory, one he couldn't see directly: the problem wasn't skating skill, it was an invisible cause, missing sleep, slowing everyone who had it. He could test it. His own plan had been to stay up nervous and wake at six, but instead he had gone to bed at nine thirty, and his legs felt springy on every crossover. When the scrimmage started, he cut left, took the pass, and scored on a rebound while Marcus watched the play arrive a beat too late.

At the end, Coach Reyes posted the list on the rink door. Alexis made forwards. Dante, who had crashed into the boards twice, made alternates. Marcus's name was not on the paper at all.

On the walk out, Dante pulled his hood up. "My cousin said there's a supplement for this. He's basically an entrepreneur, he sells protein powder to eighth graders out of his locker."

"Forget the powder," Alexis said. "Try nine hours."

Dante groaned. "That's so much sleeping."

Alexis pointed at the scoreboard clock, which still glowed above the empty ice. "You've got tryouts again in March. That's like ninety nights. You could test it properly."

Dante squinted at the clock, did some visible math, and said, "Fine. But if I turn into a grandpa who goes to bed at eight thirty, you're carrying my bag."

Alexis swung his own bag over his shoulder and said, "Deal," and the doors hissed shut behind them.

Kayla read her story aloud at the kitchen table, alone, because yesterday she had read it aloud to the class and watched Marcus fall asleep with his eyes open. Not closed. Open. That took a kind of commitment.

She counted something on the draft. Every sentence she'd written was long. She'd written them long on purpose, because long sentences seemed like more sentence for the money. Her first one had fourteen words, the next one had fifteen, the one after that had thirteen. They marched. They marched like a line of identical bricks, and apparently a line of identical bricks could put Marcus to sleep in under a minute.

The dilemma was this: cut them down, or mix them up. She tried cutting the weak adjectives first, the ones her teacher had circled in red, the verys and reallys and nicelies. That helped a little. The sentences got cleaner but they still marched, thirteen, twelve, thirteen, like a metronome nobody had asked for.

So she tried the other thing. She broke one long sentence in half and left the piece of it standing there on its own. "Nobody answered." Three words. Then a long sentence after it, then another short one. She read the new version out loud in the empty kitchen, slowly, the way she'd read to the class, and she could hear something change. Her voice had somewhere to go now. It sped up, slowed down, sped up again, like she was driving a bike over hills instead of a parking lot.

"It has rhythm," she said to the refrigerator. The refrigerator did not disagree.

She read it one more time to calibrate, timing herself with the microwave clock, and the whole thing felt about a minute shorter and a hundred percent less like a lullaby. It seemed logical, anyway, that Marcus's open-eyed sleep had been caused by the march of same-length sentences, and that a person needed a few short ones to break up the long ones, like rest stops. She underlined the short sentences in blue so she could see the pattern down the page: long, long, short, long, short, long. A heartbeat, sort of. Not a march.

At school the next day she raised her hand before her nerve could change its mind. She read the first paragraph, got to "Nobody answered," and looked up. Marcus was sitting straighter. He was actually blinking.

"You're not asleep," Kayla said.

"I'm deciding whether to be," said Marcus. "Keep going."

Samantha taped the folded program to her bedroom mirror so she would see it while she practiced. The order of songs ran down the page, and at the bottom, in her music teacher's handwriting, was the note she kept rereading: "After the last song, exit stage left, row by row." She hummed the second verse of "Oh, Shenandoah," stopped, and looked at the note again.

The problem was the word "left." In the mirror behind her, her bedroom door appeared on the right, but Samantha knew it was really on the left, because a mirror flips things. The audience, she thought, would be like a mirror. They would face her. So when they looked at her, her left side would be on their right. If stage left meant the left side as the audience saw it, she would walk toward the piano. If it meant her own left, she would walk toward the drums. Two options, and no way to check the answer from her bedroom.

She needed a test. At school the next day, she found Marcus, who had been in last year's concert. "When Mr. Okafor said exit stage left, which way did you actually go?" Marcus pointed toward the gym's far side, the side away from the piano. Samantha stood where a singer would stand, faced the empty bleachers, and checked which hand was on that side. Her left. She worked it out on the spot: stage left and stage right are the performers' left and right as they stand facing the audience.

The night of the concert, the gym lights radiated heat down onto the rows of singers, and Samantha felt the last song approaching, imminent and unstoppable. When the final note ended, Mr. Okafor raised his hand toward the far wing. Row by row, the singers filed off. Priya, beside Samantha, started to turn toward the piano. Samantha caught her sleeve. "Stage left is our left," she whispered, "not the audience's." Priya turned, and they stepped off together into the dark wing, where Marcus was waiting with two bottles of water.

Asher sat in the back row of his new classroom while the teacher talked about the election posters on the wall. "Some of these are propaganda," she said, "posters made to persuade you, not to inform you." Asher copied the word into his notebook, though his mind kept drifting to the moving truck parked outside his old house three states away. His whole life was in those boxes, and tomorrow he would have to face them.

He remembered the last night in the old house, when his sister Priya had dug through a mountain of boxes hunting for her bedsheets. "Nobody labeled anything," she had groaned, pulling out a frying pan, a lamp, and a box of comic books. Asher had stood in the doorway watching her work by flashlight, and an idea had started to digest slowly in his head. The boxes had no writing on them, just brown opaque flaps, all looking the same, so every single one had to be opened and searched. There had to be a better way.

Now, after his first day at the new school, he walked through the empty rooms of the new house. His parents wouldn't arrive with the truck until morning, but the first boxes, the ones they had shipped ahead, were stacked in the garage. Asher found a marker in his backpack and got to work. On each box he wrote two things: the room it belonged in, and what was inside. "Kitchen, pots and pans." "Priya's room, bedsheets." When the truck came, his uncle would only have to read a box once and carry it straight to the right place, instead of dropping everything in the living room like last time.

The next morning, the truck rumbled into the driveway. Asher handed boxes off the lift one by one, pointing with the marker. "Bathroom, up the stairs." "My room, second door." Priya grabbed a box, read the label, and grinned. "Bedsheets," she said. "You're a genius." By lunch, most of the boxes had already found their rooms, and Asher carried the last one, marked "My room, comic books," up the stairs two at a time.

Benjamin's laptop was so dilapidated that it made a sound like a dying kazoo whenever he opened more than three tabs, but it still ran a spreadsheet, which was all he needed. The problem was this: his cousin Marcus had sworn, in the family group chat, that TJ Ruiz was a better hitter than Sam Okafor, and Benjamin had exactly one weekend to prove him wrong. Batting average said Marcus was right, and Benjamin did not enjoy that.

He started copying numbers into the spreadsheet, row after row, while eating chips over the keyboard. His mother paused at the doorway and remarked that the hygiene of a desk used as a cafeteria was not something she wanted to quantify, then left him to it. He was still sulking over the averages when he remembered Saturday at his uncle Ray's sports bar, the TV turned to a baseball classic, his uncle swirling his drink.

"Some smarty-pants wrote a book called Moneyball," Uncle Ray had said. "Michael Lewis, 2003. It was about how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." Then he had gone back to his wings, as if he hadn't just handed over a weapon.

Benjamin sat up so fast the chair squeaked. On-base percentage. Not hits. Times a player reached base, walks included. He found the columns for walks, typed the formula, and dragged it down the whole sheet, watching new numbers appear like something rising to the surface of a lake.

When he re-sorted the players by the new column, Sam Okafor climbed from eleventh to third, and TJ Ruiz sank like a stone with a family. Sam walked constantly; it didn't look exciting, so nobody talked about it, but there he was on base, inning after inning, being quietly useful. Marcus was ranking players with half the picture. Benjamin spent another hour checking, re-checking, and making the chart prettier than it needed to be, because charts that looked official won arguments.

He pasted the chart into the group chat and waited, hands folded behind his head. Three dots appeared. Then Marcus replied: "ok but I was still right about the nachos." Benjamin typed back, "Send me the nacho data and we'll see," and hit send before he could reconsider his life choices.

Hazel had forty dollars and a plan: new basketball shoes, the ones with the springy sole, if they went on sale before Saturday's tryouts. The mall food court smelled like pretzels, and above it all a video wall played the shoe ad on loop. "Everybody's switching," a deep voice said, while a hundred blurry feet stamped past the camera. A famous point guard Hazel kind of admired looked straight at her and said, "I don't lace up anything else." Then the screen flashed the words REVOLUTIONARY and UNSTOPPABLE in gold.

She stopped walking. Something about that ad was like the wartime posters she'd been digging through for her library project. She'd started with posters from the 1940s, stern faces and pointing fingers, and then found something better. In a dusty reference book she read that the Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda. She'd written the sentence on an index card, but she hadn't really believed people needed lessons in spotting tricks. Now, standing under a thirty-foot shoe ad, she thought maybe they did.

She tested it like a game. First ad: "Everyone's switching." Her social studies teacher would say that was a bandwagon appeal, the same move as a poster showing a whole town buying war bonds. Second: REVOLUTIONARY and UNSTOPPABLE, words so vague they meant nothing, just loaded words, the book's term for language built to push feelings instead of facts. Third: the point guard. Would he really wear those shoes if the company didn't pay him? Celebrity testimonial, she scribbled on her hand with a pen from her pocket. Three tricks in one minute. She despised feeling handled, like her forty dollars had a target painted on it.

Inside the shoe store she picked up the box. The springy sole felt the same as the plain pair on the next shelf, which cost eighteen dollars less. An ambiguous sign said SALE, but the tiny print said "selected styles," and none of the selected styles were her size. "Can I try both?" she asked the clerk, a teenager named Priya who was balancing a stack of boxes one-handed while helping an older man find wide sizes.

Priya set the boxes down. "Smart question. Half the spring is the price tag, honestly." The older man chuckled. Hazel ran the length of the aisle in each pair. The cheaper ones gripped better on the slick floor; she could feel her cuts quicker. It wasn't proof, exactly, one run down one aisle, but it was evidence.

She bought the cheaper shoes, and with the leftover money she bought a pretzel and slid half of it across the table to a boy from her school, a refugee named Amir who'd arrived in the fall and usually sat alone with nothing from the food court. "For tryouts?" he asked, pointing at the box. "For tryouts," she said, and laced them up right there, double-knotted.

"Everybody's switching," she muttered at the video wall on her way out, and walked past it in her new shoes.

Ellie had been on the couch for three days, and she was tired of soup. She propped herself up on the armrest and watched the vapor rise from her mug of lemon tea, curling and vanishing near the ceiling. Her throat still felt scratchy, and her nose was red from tissue after tissue. The math competition at school was on Friday, and she wanted more than anything to be back for it.

When Mom came home from the pharmacy, Ellie sat up with an abrupt bounce. "Did you get the medicine? The kind that kills germs?"

"Everything the doctor said to get," Mom said, holding up a bag of cough syrup, tissues, and popsicles.

"Not that. Antibiotics," Ellie said. "Lily's little brother had a sore throat, and he took antibiotics and got better fast. If I take them, I could be back at school by Friday."

Mom set down the bag. "That's for the doctor to decide. We have a video call with her in ten minutes."

When the call started, Ellie asked right away. "Can you prescribe antibiotics? I need to get better fast. I have a competition."

The doctor shook her head, not unkindly. "Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they have no effect on viruses, so they wouldn't help you. A cold or the flu is a virus. Antibiotics just don't work on it."

Ellie frowned at the screen. "Then how do I get better?"

"Rest, fluids, time. Your body does the work."

So Ellie made a plan to conserve her energy. She spent Thursday on the couch doing practice problems in her head, drinking tea, and sleeping whenever her eyes got heavy. She noticed that the more she rested, the less her throat hurt, and by Friday morning her fever was gone and her nose had almost stopped running.

At school, she slid into her seat just as the competition papers were handed out. Lily leaned over. "You made it."

"Rest and fluids," Ellie whispered, "and a lot of nothing." She picked up her pencil and read the first problem.

The gym smelled like popcorn and rubber soles, and Alexandre had a problem: his cousin Theo, the best shooter on the Ravens, had gone cold for three games, and today Coach Ramirez was watching from the bleachers, deciding who would start in the tournament. Alexandre kept a small notebook with every shot Theo took, home and away, because the local paper only printed one number and he wanted to know how it was built.

By halftime Theo had made 4 of 10, and the scoreboard screen flashed his season average: 40 percent. In the third quarter he got hot, swishing five straight, and the average ticked up to 50. The announcer's voice boomed over the squeak of sneakers. "Theo Cardoso, up ten percentage points today, folks." Two rows down, a radio reporter said into her microphone, "That same jump is a 25 percent increase for the young guard."

Alexandre stopped chewing his popcorn. Ten and twenty-five, about the same shot? He wrote both numbers and stared at them, then leaned toward the reporter. "How can it be ten and also twenty-five?" She smiled but kept talking into her recorder, so he turned to his notebook instead. He counted the season totals again, slow and careful, the way he counted everything. Both phrases pointed the same direction, from 40 to 50. Maybe they were two doors into the same room. He wanted to disclose the trick to somebody before the buzzer.

Next to him, Marcus was scribbling a sign that said MARCUS SAW IT FIRST, because his older brother worked the scoreboard clock and Marcus wanted the whole gym to know. "Check this," Alexandre said, showing him the notebook. "Ten percentage points, or a 25 percent increase. Same change, different words." Marcus squinted, then grinned. "So when the paper says Theo improved 25 percent, he only made one more shot out of ten?"

"Exactly," Alexandre said. Coach Ramirez wrote something in a small book and underlined it twice, his face neutral as a locked door, though his prescription for winning was famous: defense first, always. Theo caught a pass at the top of the key, rose, and released.

The net snapped clean, and Marcus held his sign over his head.

The door banged open before Marcus could knock twice. It was Tasha, Dev's older sister, and she didn't say hi. "Take your shoes off and don't touch the kitchen," she snapped, then stomped upstairs. Marcus stood in the doorway holding his model rocket kit until Dev pulled him inside.

"She's like that," Dev said, spreading the kit across the living room carpet. "Always mad about something. Last week she yelled at me for breathing too loud." Marcus nodded, but something felt off. Tasha had helped him build a launch pad just last month, laughing the whole time. People didn't flip like a light switch for no reason, he thought, unless they were just that kind of person. He decided to test it. "Hey Dev, is anything going on with her?"

Dev shrugged. "How should I know? She's just rude."

They glued fins and taped the nose cone. Through the ceiling came footsteps, back and forth, back and forth, then a phone buzzing, then a long silence. Marcus kept one ear on it while his hands worked. He was beginning to build a second idea in his head: maybe Tasha's mood had a hidden cause, something he couldn't see, the way you can't see the wind but you can watch the flag.

At the tense moment, the footsteps stopped right above them, and a voice said, very quietly, "I'm sorry, Grandma. I'll come Saturday." Marcus froze with the glue tube in his hand. Dev looked up too.

Tasha came down a few minutes later, eyes red. "Sorry I barked at you guys. I just got a call. Grandma's in the hospital." She looked at the rocket spread across the floor. "That's a good one. Spontaneous combustion in the engine, right? That's what makes it go?" Marcus said yes, that was basically the motive power, fuel burning all at once. She almost smiled and went to make them popcorn.

Later, Dev's cousin Renard showed up and started complaining that a kid at school had slammed a door in his face that morning. "Total jerk," Renard said.

"Maybe," said Marcus. "Or maybe something happened to him you don't know about." He told them what he'd read in his brother's psychology book, holding it up to the light. "Psychologist Lee Ross named it the fundamental attribution error in 1977. We blame people's personality and skip their situation. Kind of like ants colonizing a whole picnic because one crumb fell, we spread the blame everywhere." Renard frowned, thinking. Then he picked up the spare nose cone and asked, "So when does this thing fly?"

Nolan got to Desh's house first, so he had the best view of the disaster. The science club's robot, built over three weekends for the county fair, sat dead in the middle of the garage, and the four members who arrived after him were already shouting.

"It's the battery," Marcus insisted. "I tested it Friday. It drains way too fast, like something is consuming all the power in ten minutes."

"You're wrong," Amelia said. "I watched the wheels on Saturday. The left one jerks. It's a motor problem."

Desh shook his head. "The wiring is the problem. I checked the circuits, and the backup sensor cable is pinched."

Nolan had been out of town and had seen nothing but a group chat full of arguing. Then Priya, the fifth member, was absent, sick with the flu. At her mother's suggestion, Nolan called her, and she asked him to read her text out loud to the group. He held up his phone.

"I only ever worked on the sensor that detects toxic gas," Nolan read. "I know that part works. I tested it with vinegar fumes Sunday. But I never saw the whole robot running. Someone else has to tell me about the rest."

Everyone went quiet. Nolan looked around the garage at four people who had each seen exactly one piece of the machine, and the shape of the argument suddenly made sense to him. He remembered a story his grandfather told him, from ancient India, about blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant and then describe the animal completely differently. The one holding the trunk imagines a snake; the one at the leg insists it is a tree.

"It's the parable of the blind men and the elephant," he said. "That's us. We've each only touched one part."

Desh grinned slowly. "So nobody's wrong. Everybody's just holding a different piece." They ran the robot whole, with all systems on, and watched together. It lurched left because of the motor, and the motor strained because the pinched cable made the sensor draw too much power, which drained the battery and set off the toxic-gas alarm by the vinegar residue Priya had left inside.

"So Marcus's battery, Desh's cable, Amelia's wheel, and Priya's sensor were all real," Nolan said, unscrewing the pinched cable cover. "Just one at a time."

Twenty minutes later the robot rolled straight across the driveway, and Amelia whooped so loud that Desh's neighbor looked over the fence. Marcus filmed it on his phone to send to Priya, and at the end he added, "Your nose works. The whole elephant works."

Mackenzie had read The Lighthouse of Hallow Bay three times, but for her book club report she needed something more than a summary. She carried the novel, a stack of yellow sticky notes, and a pencil to the reading nook by the window, where the afternoon light fell in a warm stripe across the cushion. She had decided on a small ritual: every time the blue door of the old boathouse appeared in the story, she would mark the page and write one sentence about what was happening there.

The first blue door showed up in chapter two, when the main character, Ivy, pressed her ear against it and dreamed of the father who had disappeared at sea. Mackenzie wrote "hope of his return" on the note and pressed it onto the page. In chapter five, Ivy hid behind the same door while her cousin searched for her, and in chapter nine, the door stood open, letting in the wind while the family argued inside. Mackenzie sat back and looked at her row of notes like a string of flags.

At the kitchen table that evening, her older brother Dev leaned over her shoulder. "What's with all the yellow paper?"

"Every time the blue door shows up, I mark it," Mackenzie said. "I'm trying to see if it means something different each time."

Dev nodded. "Recurring image like that is called a motif," he said, and went back to his sandwich.

In the nook the next morning, Mackenzie formulated a test. If the door really changed meaning, then the last time it appeared should be almost the opposite of the first. She found the final mention in chapter twenty: Ivy painting the door gray herself, the day she finally stopped waiting for news of her father. Mackenzie read the page twice, then peeled off her first sticky note and laid it beside the last one. Hope of his return, one said. Letting him go, said the other. Same door, same hinges, same blue paint, but by the end it meant something entirely different. She checked the middle notes and saw the pattern in order, hiding place, shelter, then farewell.

That afternoon Dev found her taping the sticky notes in a long line down the hallway, chapter by chapter, like train cars.

"You know that's going to leave marks on the wall," he said.

Mackenzie stood at the far end and looked down the row. "Look at it from here," she said. "It goes from blue to gray."

Eleanor set her fork down beside her meatloaf and stared at the newspaper folded next to her plate, because the draft for her current events report was due by email at eight o'clock tonight, and it was already six forty-five. The article she had chosen ranked quarterbacks by something called passer rating, and the numbers made no sense to her at all. One quarterback had 104.2. Another had 158.3, and the caption under his photo called it perfect.

"Why would a perfect score be a weird number like that?" she asked her brother Marcus, who was stacking green beans on his knife like he was building a wall.

Marcus shrugged. "It's just what it is. Football stuff." He wanted to finish dinner fast so he could colonize the whole living room couch before their cousin arrived, spreading his blanket and controller across every cushion like territory he claimed by sitting on it first.

"A hundred would be perfect," Eleanor insisted. "Like on a test. If the scale starts at zero and ends somewhere, perfect should end at one hundred." She flipped the paper over and ran her finger down the ranking column again, counting the quarterbacks listed there. Twelve names, twelve different numbers, all squeezed down from games she had never watched. Somewhere behind each number were completions and yards and touchdowns and interceptions, and all of it had been crushed together into a single figure, the way her school averaged test scores into one grade. But the top number still bothered her, hanging there like a picture she couldn't get to hang perpendicular to the floor.

"Maybe it's not out of a hundred," Marcus said through a mouthful of beans. "Maybe the whole scale is different."

Eleanor grabbed her mother's phone from the counter and typed "passer rating maximum" into the search box. She read, scrolled, and read again. "It says the passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number," she announced, "on a scale from zero to a maximum of 158.3." She set the phone down. "So a perfect rating isn't a hundred. It's a strange number, and it's the top of the whole scale."

Marcus had stopped stacking beans. "So that guy with 158.3 is literally the best you can be?"

"By the rating, yeah." Eleanor was already rewriting the first line of her report in her head. She had planned to argue that the rankings were unfair because her favorite team's quarterback sat seventh, but now she understood that his number was built from everything he had done all season, folded together. Seventh wasn't a judgment of him as a person. It was arithmetic. She picked her fork back up and speared a green bean off Marcus's abandoned wall.

At 7:58 she hit send, then carried her plate to the sink. Marcus had claimed the couch, blanket and all, and was waving the remote at her.

"Want to watch the highlights?" he asked. "That perfect guy plays tonight."

Eleanor dried her hands on the towel. "Show me the numbers at the end," she said, and sat down on the last free cushion.

Samuel's cleats were still damp from the morning dew when Coach Marisol dragged a thick rope out of the equipment shed and dropped it across the center circle. "Tug-of-war," she announced. "Championship Saturday has one at halftime, and we are going to win it."

Devon, who lived upstairs from Samuel in the apartment building where their families were tenants, threw both fists in the air. "I've been waiting all season for this!"

They pulled in pairs first, then four against four, then all eight. Samuel gripped the rope in the eight-on-eight round and noticed something strange. When it had been just him against Devon, his arms burned and his legs shook. Now, with the whole team heaving together, his pull felt easier. Lazy, almost. He glanced down the line. Marco was definitely leaning back less than before. When Coach blew her whistle and called the pull "sloppy," Marco's face went pink.

That night Samuel couldn't let it go. He pulled a strand of spaghetti from his dinner and tugged it, thinking. He could infer something from what he'd seen: the more people on the rope, the smaller each person's pull seemed to get. But was that real, or was he imagining it? The only way to find out was a test.

At Tuesday practice he begged Coach Marisol for the spring scale she used for fitness testing. She hooked it to the rope and the fence post. Devon pulled alone and the scale read ninety pounds. Then four boys pulled together, and Samuel did the math in his notebook. Devon's share of the four-man pull was smaller than his solo pull. Same for Marco. Same for everyone. The pattern held.

"You sound like my grandfather," Coach said, laughing. "In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller."

"Ringelmann," Samuel repeated, writing it down. "So what do we do about it?"

Coach rubbed her chin. "That, scientist, is your problem."

On Saturday, the stadium smelled like popcorn and cut grass, and the stands were louder than any game all season. At halftime, Samuel gathered his team in the end zone. "Every pull is your pull," he told them. "Nobody's hiding on this rope." He pointed at the opposing team's biggest puller, a tower of a kid. "He's not the rope. He's just one guy."

The whistle blew. Samuel planted his feet, kept his arms straight, and pulled as hard as if he were alone in his backyard. Down the line he heard Devon growling like a guard dog, and the rope came, inch by glorious inch, until the red flag crossed the chalk line. Devon tackled Samuel into the grass, and the whole team piled on, shouting, "Ringelmann!" at the sky.

Maya's dog, Biscuit, flattened himself under the coffee table the second the thunder cracked, and Peyton watched him shake. "He's scared," Maya said, not looking up from her phone. "It's happening right now, the storm. He's freaked out by the actual thunder."

Peyton nodded slowly. Maya had been quiet all afternoon, checking the weather app, then the soccer app, then the weather again. Her cleats sat by the door, already double-knotted, though the tryout was still four days away. "You keep doing that," Peyton said, pointing at the phone. "Is there thunder in there?"

"No. It's the tryout list. They posted the roster numbers and mine is eleven, which is fine, but what if they move me to defense, what if I trip in the first drill, what if Coach Reyes already decided." Maya set the phone face down, then picked it up again. Peyton thought about Biscuit under the table. He was shaking at the thunder that was actually booming outside. Maya was shaking at thunder that had not happened yet and might never happen at all. "So Biscuit is scared of the storm," Peyton said, testing the idea out loud, "and you're not scared, exactly, because nothing's happening right now. It's more like you're worried about what might happen Friday. My mom says that's anxiety. Fear is the reaction to a threat happening now, and anxiety is worry about a threat that might happen in the future."

Maya stopped scrolling. "So Biscuit has fear and I have anxiety."

"Basically."

"Great. The dog is more competent than me."

"He's hiding under a table," Peyton said. "You're sitting on a couch eating all my chips."

"That's my coping mechanism. Chips consume my stress." Maya held up the nearly empty bag as proof, and Peyton laughed and grabbed the last chip, calling a truce over the crumbs.

Maya stood, put the phone in a drawer, and closed it. "Okay. If it's about a might, not a happening, then I can practice instead of worrying. Want to go outside before the next rumble?"

They laced up their cleats on the back step. Maya had just struck the ball against the fence twice when the drawer, muffled, began to buzz.

Raphael sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open to the tryout roster, refreshing it every thirty seconds like an organism that had learned one trick and could not stop performing it. His sister Dara leaned over his shoulder, though she was supposed to be researching her debate topic, which was whether the school should sell smoothies in the cafeteria, a cause she had championed for two weeks with rising passion.

The list appeared at 4:02. Raphael's name was not on it.

"I don't get it," he said. "I beat half those kids in the sprints."

Dara, who wanted his laptop the moment he stopped needing it, scrolled the page for him. "Look at the birthdays they posted. Weird."

He looked. Of the fifteen names, eleven had birthdays from January to June. Three were in fall. One, a kid named Osei, was in November. Not a single December birthday but his own, anywhere.

"You're the youngest kid in your whole grade, basically," Dara said. "You've told me that forty times."

Raphael started to argue, then stopped. It wasn't just his grade. The cutoff for school was January first, which meant kids born in that first month were almost a year older than kids born in December. Same tryouts, same drills, months and months of extra growing. He grabbed a scrap of paper and wrote the birthdays in two columns, old half and young half, and stared at the lopsided result. Then he searched "birth month sports team selection" and found it had a name.

"Relative age effect," he read aloud.

"What's that?"

"Players born early in the selection year get picked more than ones born late. It's a real thing. People study it."

Dara was quiet for a moment, which for her was eloquent. "So you got cut partly because of your birthday?"

"Partly." He closed the laptop before she could reach for it. "There's a winter league with January tryouts. New year, new cutoff. I'll be the old one for once."

"That's your plan? Wait four months and get older?"

"I'm going to train the whole time," he said, and began clearing the table, moving fast, already perspiring.

Ellie divided the garden behind the barn into two square plots, drew a map on cardboard, and tried to classify the seeds into neat groups: roots, leaves, things that climbed. Her younger brother, Marcus, wanted the climbing ones, the beans, because he liked the way the pump handle rose and fell like a piston when Grandpa filled the trough, and he figured beans working their way up a string would be just as satisfying to watch.

"You can have the beans," Ellie said, "if you help water." Marcus agreed, but he preferred watering his own way, which was a light sprinkle from the green can every single morning, the way he sprinkled the dog in July. Ellie watered her plot differently. Twice a week, she let the hose run slowly until the ground was soaked deep down, and on the other mornings she did nothing at all.

For weeks both plots looked the same, and Marcus was smug about it. Then came the hot week. By Thursday his bean leaves hung limp at noon and stayed limp into the evening. Ellie's tomatoes drooped a little in the heat, but they lifted again by supper. On Saturday, before either of them watered anything, Ellie dug carefully at the edge of each plot with her trowel. In Marcus's soil she found the bean roots, thin and white, spread out just under the surface where the ground was already dry and cracked. In her own plot she had to dig twice as deep before she found roots, heading downward where the soil was still dark and damp.

"Look," she said, and Marcus crouched beside her, poking his finger into the hole. "Mine stayed up top because I only ever gave them a little drink. Yours went down hunting for water." He wiped his hands on his jeans and frowned at his wilting beans, then at the hose. "So if I soak them good, will they grow deeper roots and quit fainting every day?"

"Only one way to find out," Ellie said, and she handed him the hose. Marcus turned the nozzle to a slow trickle and held it steady at the base of the first bean plant while a predatory ground beetle, the kind that patrols for cutworms, crossed the wet dirt ahead of the spray. Ellie marked the spot with a popsicle stick so they would know exactly where the change had begun, and they sat in the shade of the barn to wait for the water to sink all the way down.

The group chat pinged at 9:14, right while Zack was supposed to be asleep. It was Maya: "someone posted my old blog in the school forum. with screenshots. my OLD blog."

Zack sat up in the dark, phone glowing under his blanket. "i thought you deleted it in fourth grade," he typed.

"i did. like, a hundred times. it's still THERE."

Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again. Dev wrote, "deleted stuff can't just come back. unless somebody saved it."

Zack's stomach did a slow flip. Because he had a blog too, from back when he thought he was going to be a famous inventor, full of posts about his "unbreakable alloy spoon" project, which had actually snapped in half on day two. He had also, once, put up a photo of himself in front of his house. With the house number visible.

"hold on," he typed. He opened his laptop, keeping the screen tilted away from the door in case his dad checked on him. He searched his old blog's address, then tried something Maya had mentioned in the chat, something called the Wayback Machine. Since 1996, he read, the Internet Archive had been saving copies of public web pages, and anyone could look at old versions of many websites.

His heart was hammering by the time the page loaded. Slowly, line by line, his old blog rebuilt itself on the screen. There he was at nine years old, grinning in front of the house, number and all. There was his post about how the strength of his spoon would "fluctuate depending on the temperature of the soup." Maya commented on it. Total strangers could have commented on it. Total strangers could have read it, saved it, shared it.

He screenshotted nothing. He just sat there.

"Zack you still there?" Maya asked.

He typed with cold fingers: "found my blog too. the photo of my house is still up. and i found a page from my school's old site with the field trip schedule. anybody could have known where our whole grade was that day."

Dev wrote, "so deleting doesn't actually delete."

"not if it was ever public," Zack sent. He started a new list of things to fix, starting with telling his dad in the morning. Then Maya's name popped up at the top of the chat, and beside it, a stranger's account had just joined the group.

Evan had been building the same cardboard vessel at the park picnic table for three Saturdays, a sailboat with a mast he had cut so it stood perfectly perpendicular to the deck, and today Marcus was not sitting across from him. Marcus was all the way over by the duck pond, throwing pebbles, because yesterday Evan had told everyone in the cafeteria that Marcus still slept with a stuffed rabbit named Captain Fluff. Marcus had found out at lunch, and now here they were at opposite ends of the park on a Saturday morning.

Evan walked to the pond with the note he had written on notebook paper. He read it out loud instead of handing it over, because Marcus would not take anything from him. "Dear Marcus, I'm sorry if you were upset about what I said."

Marcus picked up another pebble and did not throw it. "That's a non-apology," he said. "You're sorry if I was upset. Like it's my fault for being upset."

Evan looked at the paper. He read the line again in his head. The "if" was the problem. He had written sorry about Marcus's feelings, not sorry about the thing he himself had said. He had said it out loud in the cafeteria on purpose, to get a laugh, and everyone had laughed, and Marcus had sat there with his tray.

"I have to do it over," Evan said. He went back to the picnic table, took out his pencil, and folded the old note into the boat's hull. He wrote a new one and walked back. "Dear Marcus. I'm sorry I told everyone about Captain Fluff. It was your private thing and I used it to make people laugh. That was wrong. I won't say anything about your stuff again. Do you want to finish the boat? I can't get the sail to stay up."

Marcus turned the pebble over in his hand. The wind came off the pond and smelled like mud and duckweed. "The sail keeps falling because the mast is too skinny for the hole," he said. "You need to wedge something in there. A rolled-up piece of paper."

"The old note," Evan said. He unfolded it, rolled it tight, and pushed it into the base of the mast while Marcus held the deck steady. The sail stood.

They carried the boat to the pond's edge and set it in the water. It heeled over, righted itself, and drifted out toward the ducks. "Still floats," Marcus said. "Even with a non-apology inside it."

At dinner Joseph pushed his lasagna around the plate and finally said it. "Grandpa, your fertilizer story doesn't prove anything." Grandpa set down his fork. Last summer he had told the story a dozen times: he'd sprinkled some blue powder on his tomato plant, and by August the plant had grown taller than the fence. "One plant, one summer, one story," Joseph said. "The company claims it works, and their claim is supposed to be backed by tested evidence. But how would we even test it ourselves?" His little sister, Mina, grinned around a mouthful of garlic bread, and his mother raised one eyebrow in a way that felt faintly sinister, like she already knew the answer and was waiting to see if he did.

The kitchen smelled of oregano and burnt cheese. Rain streaked the window, and the porch light refracted through the drops so that every bead glowed orange. Joseph stared at that glittering pattern while the problem turned over in his mind. He needed to know if the blue powder caused the growth, but a hundred things could make a plant tall: sun, water, luck. Then the idea arrived, so suddenly he knocked over his water glass.

"Two pots," he said, grabbing napkins while Mina shrieked about her poem notebook, the one with a stanza about tomatoes on the first page, which was now soaked. "Same soil, same seeds, same window, same water. Everything the same, except one pot gets the powder and one doesn't. Grandpa told me that's what scientists call the control group. It gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested. So if the powdered pot grows taller, the difference has to come from the powder and nothing else."

Grandpa chuckled. "Six weeks, then. Winner picks the movie."

"Deal," Joseph said, and shook on it, blue powder already waiting in his pocket.

Rebecca sat on her bed with the family group chat open, typing and deleting the same message for the fourth time. Priya hadn't spoken to her in six days, not since Rebecca told the whole lunch table about Priya's disastrous audition for the spring musical. Priya had walked out of the cafeteria, and now her replies had gone from paragraphs to nothing at all. Rebecca finally sent, "Can we talk?" to the chat, along with, "Not to you guys. Just needed to say it out loud somewhere."

Her older brother Marcus answered first. "Then why post it here?" he typed, adding a shrugging emoji. Her mom sent a thumbs up, which was her way of saying she was listening. Rebecca stared at the screen. The real problem wasn't talking. The real problem was that she wasn't even sure what she wanted anymore. She wasn't angry at Priya for icing her out, not really. But the thought of sitting with her at lunch again, of everything going back to normal, made her stomach tighten. She typed, "I think I've forgiven her but I don't want to be best friends again yet. Is that even allowed?" Then, before anyone could answer, she searched the phrase on her phone, because she wanted to know before she had to hear an opinion.

The psychology page she found made her sit up straight. There were two different things, and they had two different names. She read it twice, then texted the chat a screenshot. "Look. Forgiving and reconciling," she wrote. Marcus replied within seconds. "So you can do the first one without the second one." Rebecca typed, "Yeah. Forgiving just means letting go of resentment. Reconciling means rebuilding the relationship. So the friendship doesn't have to go back to exactly how it was." Her mom sent a single message: "Both are yours to decide."

On Saturday, Rebecca walked to Priya's house and stood on the porch holding two hot chocolates, which was a feasible plan only because she lived three blocks away. Priya opened the door, saw the cups, and sighed. "I'm still mad," she said. "That's fine," Rebecca said. "Me too, a little. But I'm done being resentful about it. Can we just sit on the steps?" Priya considered the larger cup, the one with extra whipped cream, and stepped outside.

Jade crouched over an old picture frame in the backyard, arranging pebbles, bottle caps, and broken tiles into a mosaic for the neighborhood art contest. Her little brother Leo sat on the porch steps eating a pickle and offering advice nobody asked for.

"Put the big blue cap in the middle," he said. "Middle is best. Middle is the boss."

Jade tried it. The blue bottle cap went dead center, surrounded by a tidy ring of white pebbles, like a donut staring at her. She frowned. It looked like something from a plumbing catalogue, all neat and dull, not like the lagoon she'd imagined. She slid the cap left, then right, then almost center again. Still boring. Still a donut.

"Your art has the personality of a sock," Leo announced.

"Your face has the personality of a pickle." But he had a point, and she knew it. She flipped through her mom's old photography book on the grass, hunting for ideas, and stopped at a page with pictures marked up in pencil. Someone had drawn lines over the photographs, two straight lines one way and two perpendicular, cutting each picture into nine boxes like a tic-tac-toe board. The interesting subjects sat along those lines, or right where the lines crossed, never in the exact middle. The book called it the rule of thirds.

Jade grabbed a stick and drew the same grid in the dirt beside her frame, imagining the lines stretched across her mosaic. If the lines crossed in the four corners of the center square, then the blue cap belonged on one of those crossing points. She moved the cap up and to the left until it sat just off center, on a crossing, then rebuilt the pebbles around it so they swirled toward the cap instead of circling it like a fence.

She stood back and squinted. The whole thing suddenly had a direction, like water flowing somewhere. It wasn't a donut anymore. It was a lagoon.

"Whoa," said Leo, pickle paused halfway to his mouth. "It's looking at me sideways."

Jade took a photo on her mom's old phone to preserve the design in case a squirrel attacked, then carried the frame to the shade so the glue wouldn't dry too fast in the sun. Leo followed, dragging his pickle.

"Teach me the tic-tac-toe trick," he demanded.

"First, throw away that pickle. It smells like regret."

Leo sniffed it, shrugged, and took another bite.

The Hendersons' living room was packed by the second quarter, and the windows had gone humid from all the shouting and the popcorn. Carter had the best seat, the beanbag by the TV, because he had arrived first. That was the whole reason he was there: Coach Henderson ran a halftime trivia contest every year, and the winner got the giant chocolate basketball that sat on the mantel, untouched, waiting.

"At halftime," Coach Henderson announced during a timeout, "the question is about basketball itself. One question. First right answer wins. And no phones." She tapped the chocolate ball like a gong.

Carter wanted that ball so badly his teeth ached. The problem was that he had no idea what the question would be. Beside him, Mr. Alvarez's cousin Dev, who was fourteen and loud, was already claiming the prize. "Basketball facts are my whole life," Dev said.

The timeout ended, but Carter wasn't watching the players anymore. He was staring at the hoop on the screen. Why was it called a basket? A hoop wasn't a basket. A basket was a thing you carried peaches in. His grandfather had peach baskets in the garage, and Carter had hauled them every August at the orchard. If somebody had named the game, he thought, they must have named it after the first thing they used as a goal. Not a hoop. Something that actually held the ball.

"Hey, Coach," he called across the room, "who made up basketball in the first place?"

She smiled a coach smile, the kind that gives away nothing. "Halftime, Carter. Three minutes."

Two minutes later a storm knocked the power out, and the whole room groaned in the dark. Somebody found the emergency lamp and the little generator in the garage, and Mr. Alvarez yanked the cord until it coughed to life. The TV stayed dead, but the lamp lit the room, and Coach Henderson clapped her hands. "Halftime is halftime. Here's the question. Basketball was invented by a man named James Naismith. Where and when, and what did he use for goals?"

"Peach baskets!" Carter shouted before he could stop himself. "That's why it's called a basket!" The words were out, and now he had to back them up, fast, before Dev could contradict him with something confident and wrong. Carter closed his eyes and pictured the game being brand new, a gym, winter. "December 1891," he said. "A YMCA training school. In Springfield, Massachusetts."

The room went quiet except for the generator humming in the garage. Coach Henderson slowly lifted the chocolate basketball off the mantel and weighed it in her hands.

"Nobody," she said, "has ever gotten all of that."

She tossed it underhand toward the beanbag, and Carter caught it against his chest with both arms.

When Nora arrived at Priya's house, she nearly stuck out her hand for a shake, but Priya's grandmother pressed her palms together and nodded instead, so Nora copied her, palms together, and the grandmother smiled. Nora had brought a gift, a box of chocolates, and she handed it over with her left hand because her right was holding her coat. The grandmother took it, but her eyebrows did something small and strange, and she passed the box to her other hand before setting it down.

At dinner, the table was crowded with dishes Nora had never eaten before, rice and chicken and something spicy that made her nose run. She noticed something while reaching for the serving spoon. Priya, Priya's father, even little cousin Danial, all of them ate with their right hands only. Every time Danial's left hand crept toward the plate, his mother tapped the table beside it until he moved it back. Nora quietly revised her theory that the grandmother's eyebrows had been about the chocolates. It was about the hand.

She decided to test it. When the rice dish came around, she lifted it with her right hand and offered it to Priya's father, even though her reach felt awkward and elastic across the crowded table. He took it with his right hand too, and this time the eyebrows stayed calm.

"In Malaysia we use the right hand for eating and for giving and receiving things," Priya said, leaning close. "It's a sign of respect."

Nora kept her left hand in her lap after that. When the tea came, she received the cup with her right hand, and when she passed the bread, she used her right hand again, even when it meant setting down her spoon first. The grandmother watched her across the table, then ladled an extra spoonful of chicken onto Nora's plate and said something to Priya in a language Nora didn't understand.

"She says you eat like a proper Malaysian," Priya translated.

Nora grinned and picked up her spoon with her right hand.

At dinner Tyler pushed his peas around his plate while his little sister talked about Maya's bracelet stand at the fair. Maya had sold out on Saturday, at four dollars a bracelet, and now everyone wanted some.

"Everybody keeps asking her for more," Emma said, "but she's out of beads."

Tyler remembered the fair, the smell of kettle corn drifting past Maya's table, the way she'd stacked her bracelets in rows, brittle little shells of painted macaroni that clicked when you touched them. He'd watched a woman buy three at once without even asking the price. He'd wanted one himself, but four dollars was more than his allowance could stretch to after the settlement he'd made with his dad over the broken garage window, two weeks of chores for the repair.

"That's why nobody had them," Tyler said suddenly. "She didn't have very many, and everyone wanted one. So she could charge a lot."

"So?" Emma rolled her eyes.

"So watch what happens now." He grabbed a napkin and drew a table on it, the way he categorized things for science class, sellers down one side and prices across the top. "Maya made a pile of money at four dollars. If you could make bracelets, wouldn't you start?"

By Thursday he had his answer. Three new stands had popped up on his street alone. Mrs. Okafor had a folding table at the end of her driveway, and the twins from two doors down were stringing beads on their porch every afternoon.

"They're all three dollars," Emma reported that night, chewing a mouthful of spaghetti. "And Mrs. Okafor said she'd do two-fifty if you buy two."

Tyler set down his fork. High price, and now more sellers than he could count, all offering bracelets because four dollars had made it worth their while. He thought about the napkin chart, still folded in his pocket, and about waiting too long at the fair.

"So are you going to buy one?" Emma asked. "They're cheap now."

"Yeah," Tyler said, pushing back his chair. "Let's go before everybody in town opens a stand."

The gym at the Maple Street Community Center felt like the inside of a rain cloud. Leo dribbled down the court, and sweat rolled off his elbows before he even reached the foul line. "Come on, one more quarter!" Coach Rivera shouted, but half the Rockets were bent over with their hands on their knees, gasping like fish.

Leo had played in a tournament last month on a day that hit ninety-six degrees, and it had been brutal but somehow easier than this. Today the thermometer said eighty-eight, yet everyone was dragging. He mentioned it to Marcus during a water break. "Maybe we're just tired," Marcus said. "I hibernated all weekend playing video games. My legs are noodles." Leo shook his head. "Last game was hotter. This doesn't add up."

Then he noticed the window. The air outside was thick and hazy, and the glass had a film of moisture on it, even though nobody had touched it. He grabbed his water bottle, poured a little on his forearm, and blew on it. Almost nothing happened. The drop just sat there, shiny and stubborn, refusing to dry. In the drier tournament gym, his soaked jersey had dried stiff in twenty minutes. He tried an experiment on his other arm with a paper towel, fanning it. His damp arm felt cooler than the one with the plain water drop. "Marcus! Come feel my arm. Both of them."

Marcus pressed a finger to each forearm. "Whoa. That one's colder. Why?" Leo grinned. "Sweat's supposed to dry off us to cool us down, right? Today it just sits there and doesn't go anywhere." He jogged to the bench and told Coach. "So in humid weather we overheat more easily, even when it's not that hot out. Can we sub more often?" Coach squinted at him. "That's actually a credible theory. Fine. Rotating every four minutes."

The rotations worked. Fresh legs flooded the court every few minutes, and the Rockets clawed back from eight points down. With ten seconds left, Leo stole the ball at midcourt, drove past two defenders, and laid it up off the glass. The net didn't even ripple. "That," Marcus panted, throwing an arm around him, "is the sweatiest win of my whole life."

Declan stood at Grandma's stove with a heavy pan and a bag of sugar, because tonight he was making the dessert and it had to be authentic caramel sauce, the kind his grandpa talked about from his childhood. Grandma had gone to pick up Aunt Rosa, so Declan had the kitchen to himself. He poured a layer of sugar into the dry pan and turned the heat to medium, watching the pale grains at the edges begin to melt.

His little sister Priya wandered in, drawn by the smell of the Sunday roast crisping in the oven. "That's browning just like the crust on the roast," she said, pointing at the pan. "Same thing, right?"

Declan thought about that. The roast was meat, and meat had no sugar to speak of, so how could plain sugar browning and meat crusting be the same reaction? He scraped the melting sugar with a wooden spoon and watched it turn amber. "This is caramelization," he said. "It's browning that happens when sugar alone is heated. The crust on the roast can't be this, because the Maillard reaction is different. That one also needs amino acids, and meat has those."

"So test it," Priya said, in the annoying way of little sisters who are sometimes right.

He spooned a little of the amber caramel onto a plate, then took a pinch of flour and a splash of milk, mixed them with sugar in a small bowl, and set the bowl beside the pan. He was reaching for a spoon when the pan hissed and a thread of smoke rose from the caramel. He jerked it off the burner too fast, and half of it seized into a hard, pale lump. Perfect dessert, ruined, and everyone due back in twenty minutes.

Priya leaned over the small bowl, sniffed it, and frowned. "Declan. Why is your roast all sweet?"

He spun around. Grandma's roast, the one with the famous crust, glistened under a thin glaze, and sitting beside the oven was Grandma's secret jar with a spoon in it. "That's her sugar glaze," he said slowly. "So the crust is caramelization and the Maillard thing, together." He grabbed the seized lump of caramel, broke it into pieces, and dropped them into a pot of cream to melt again. "Don't tell Grandma we found the jar."

"Too late," said Grandma from the doorway, holding up the jar. "Now stir, both of you."

The phone had been dead since the last gas station, and Dad was still refusing to ask for directions. "Grandpa said the cabin is right on the lake, near a town called Eagle Point," he said, drumming the wheel. "I want to find it before dark. I promised him we'd fish at sunrise."

Bentley unfolded the big paper map across his knees, and it crinkled like an enormous candy wrapper. Across the top and down the side ran rows of numbers, and thin lines crossed the map into a grid. Next to Eagle Point he found a tiny pair of numbers in the index at the back: latitude 44 degrees and 12 minutes north, longitude 87 degrees and 30 minutes west. He stared at the word "minutes" for a long moment. "That can't be how long it takes to get there," he said. "It's not time." But then what was it?

He tested an idea. If the whole state sat between the 44 and 45 lines, and the town's number said 44 degrees and 12 minutes, then the 12 must be a way of measuring distance between the big lines, not minutes on a clock. He held the map up to the light and counted the small tick marks between the printed lines. There were sixty of them. So each degree had to be divided into sixty of these "minutes," and sure enough, some of the finer labels were broken down even further, into seconds. "Sixty seconds in a minute," he said slowly. "It's like the clock, but for space." Dad glanced over. "You figuring that out all by yourself?"

Bentley was secretly proud, and a little envious of kids who got to learn this in a classroom instead of in a hot car. He slid his finger along the 44 degree line, then up from the 87 degree line, and where his fingers crossed, there it was: a small dot labeled Eagle Point, tucked against a blue blot of lake. "Turn left at the next highway, then about twenty miles north," he announced. Dad raised his eyebrows. "That's your verdict?" "That's my verdict," Bentley said. "Unless you want to knock on a stranger's door and ask a random anonymous person in the middle of nowhere."

Dad laughed and took the left turn. The road climbed through pines, and Bentley tracked their progress with his finger the whole way, checking the line numbers at every crossroad. Then the trees broke open and the lake flashed silver in the late sun, with a small cabin at the near shore and a rowboat pulled up on the sand. Dad honked the horn twice, and Bentley folded the map into a neat square and held it up like a trophy as the gravel crunched under the tires. "Grandpa," Dad called through the open window, "we used a map, and my navigator got us here."

Emilia sat at the kitchen table with three ruined greeting cards in front of her. Each one had cracked along the fold, the thick card splitting into bumpy white lines that crossed her careful drawings of tulips. She was making a birthday card for her grandmother, and it had to be perfect, so she pressed a fourth card flat and folded it anyway, watching the paper splinter down the crease.

"There has to be a reason," she said to her cat, Biscuit, who was asleep on the chair beside her. She looked closely at the cracked cards. The folds were straight, but the surface was rough and broken, as if the card had been forced. She thought about the thin paper she folded into paper airplanes, which never cracked. Maybe the thick card was too stiff to bend cleanly on its own.

She tested a small piece of scrap card first. She took a blunt spoon from the kitchen drawer and drew it firmly along a ruler's edge, pressing a shallow line into the card. Then she folded along that line, and the card bent straight and clean, with no crack at all. She blinked at it, then tried a second scrap without the pressed line, and it split like the others. It was not luck. She had been negligent about one small step, and the small step was everything.

The next card transformed under her hands. She scored a line with the spoon before folding, and the spine of the card came out smooth and sharp. On the front she drew tulips, then a border of little stars. Biscuit woke up, yawned, and put one paw on the envelope, as if signing it too.

"You can deliver it with me," Emilia said. She slid the card inside, and the white paper whispered against the edges. On the envelope she wrote her grandmother's name and, underneath, in small letters, "Folded with a spoon."

Anna stood on Platform 4, gripping a sign she had made in marker: WELCOME GRANDPA JOE. The 3:15 from the city hissed in, and among the crowd she spotted his gray cap bobbing like a buoy. He waved with both hands. "One whole week," he announced, hugging her. "And I want to ride every train line this station has, even the slow one nobody likes." Anna grinned, but a worry buzzed at the back of her mind. Last year, when Grandma Rosa visited, Anna had meant to write down her stories and never got around to it. Grandma Rosa couldn't travel anymore, and those stories about her childhood felt like water slipping through fingers. She didn't want that to happen twice.

The week flew by. They rode the slow line to the harbor, and Grandpa Joe told her about the rat he had kept as a boy, a pet rodent named Whiskers who stole buttons. "Was that voluntary, keeping him, or did Whiskers just refuse to leave?" Anna asked, laughing. Grandpa Joe shrugged. "He moved in on his own. Like he chose me." On Friday, the last night, Anna studied him across the dinner table and tried to assess how many stories were still in there. Hundreds, maybe. How could she keep them?

Then she remembered the poster in the library window. A man had been recording his mother in a little booth. The poster had said the recordings go somewhere important, that people interview family members and, with permission, the recordings are saved at the Library of Congress. Anna had walked past it twice. Now she stopped walking. She grabbed her tablet.

"Grandpa, sit here and tell me about Whiskers again," she said, pressing record. "Why?" "There's a project called StoryCorps," she said. "People record interviews with their family, and with permission the recordings get saved at the Library of Congress. Like your stories could live there forever." Grandpa Joe went quiet. "Forever in a library," he murmured. "Then ask me anything, starting from the beginning." He leaned toward the microphone and said, "I was eight years old, and the button was missing from my coat."

The whole premise of the food bank, Dylan discovered, was not just giving food away but giving it away in the right order. He had enrolled as a volunteer that morning because his scout troop needed service hours, and Ms. Reyes had put him on the canned vegetable shelf. He worked fast, sliding the new donations from the big box right into the front of the shelf where his hand fit easiest. When he finished, the row looked full and neat, labels all facing out.

Ms. Reyes walked past, stopped, and frowned at his shelf. "Redo it, please. New cans go in back."

"But the front's the easy spot," Dylan said.

"The easy spot is for the old cans," she said. "First in, first out."

Dylan pulled the new cans out again and stared at the shelf, thinking. So whatever went in first had to come out first, which meant the old cans sat in front where the next volunteer would grab them. He tested it by checking the dates on a few labels. Sure enough, the cans already at the front expired sooner than the ones in his box. It was like a line at a water park: first person in line, first person down the slide. He slid the new cans behind the old ones, all the way to the back, and pushed the old cans forward until the dates ran in order.

By noon his arms ached, but the shelf had a system now, and he liked systems. When the afternoon crew came in, a girl named Priya started stacking a fresh box right into the front of his row. "Back," Dylan said, pointing. "Older stuff goes out first so less expires on the shelf."

"You figured that out yourself?" she asked.

"Sort of. I got it wrong first."

She laughed and carried her box around to the far side. "Race you on the soup aisle."

The pizza place on Fifth Street had a screen as wide as the whole back wall, and tonight it showed the World Cup qualifier while everybody waited for their food. Camille's uncle Rafael leaned across the table toward her grandfather. "First World Cup, Brazil took it. Everyone knows that."

"Uruguay," Grandpa said. He had been a train conductor for thirty years, and he still spoke like he was announcing a departure. "Uruguay won the first one."
