"Argentina, then," said Camille's cousin Mateo, because he had an Argentina jersey and he wanted Argentina to have won everything. "If Uruguay was even in it." Camille noticed that Mateo's argument changed shape whenever it needed to. Brazil, then Argentina, then whoever, as long as it kept the argument going until everyone gave up. That was the pattern, and she wanted to catch it in the open.

By the door stood the old trivia machine, the kind that ate quarters. Camille had watched a man at the counter win a free milkshake on it an hour ago, so she knew it worked and she knew it asked sports questions. If the machine was right, it could settle the table. She dug two quarters out of her jacket, slid them into the slot, and chose the sports category. The machine offered a wall mural that portrayed a 1930s stadium, old leather ball and all, above the words HISTORY OF FOOTBALL, so she picked that one.

The question came up: who won the first FIFA World Cup, held in Uruguay in 1930? The four answers glowed. She pressed Uruguay, and the screen answered in green, then added the detail: Uruguay beat Argentina 4 to 2 in the final. Four goals to two, which Mateo would notice was the equivalent of a two-goal lead the whole second half. She carried the machine's printed ticket back to the table and set it next to his plate.

"Uruguay," she said. "Nineteen thirty. Four to two over Argentina in the final."

Mateo picked up the ticket, read it twice, and put it face down. "Okay," he said, "but who's paying for dessert now?"

The group chat was called "Mud Dogs Rule," and it had been quiet all week until Tuesday night, when Marisol posted a screenshot of two baseball players with a single question: "Who's better?"

Harper sat cross-legged on her bed with her tablet balanced on one knee. She tapped into the stats page and started comparing. The first player was David Justice, the second was Derek Jeter. For 1995, Justice had the higher batting average. She checked twice, because Marisol's older brother had once told her that websites make mistakes. For 1996, Justice had the higher average again. Two years, two wins. She typed, "Justice. Easy," and dropped the tablet beside her.

A minute later Marisol sent a laughing emoji and then a link. "Look at the combined number for both years together." Harper picked the tablet back up. She found the row, read it, and read it again. For the two years combined, Jeter's average was the higher one. She stared at the screen while her ceiling fan ticked around and around above her.

"That's bizarre," she typed slowly. "Justice beats him both years and loses when you add the years up?" Marisol replied that her brother called it Simpson's paradox, and that it had a name because it happened in more places than baseball. Harper decided to test it herself. She pulled up her own basketball free throws from the rec league app, where she kept every practice logged. She sorted the sessions into two groups, took the percentages for each group, then the percentage for all of them together, and worked the numbers with a pencil on the back of her homework. Her percentages moved the same way when she combined groups, which meant the thing on the baseball site wasn't a typo. It was something numbers could just do.

She scrolled up through the chat and noticed something else. Dex, who never missed a chance to argue, hadn't posted at all. She sent him a private message: "You're quiet. You already knew about this, didn't you?"

His reply came as a long text. "OK yes. I found it last summer and I was going to use it to win an argument with you about whether our Mud Dogs season was really as bad as the league standings said. Our average runs per game over the whole season look fine, but that's because of two blowout games. I didn't want to say that out loud because everyone would say I was making excuses." Harper read it twice. She thought about the standings pinned to the gym door, one number standing for all those afternoons, and about how the team's snacks had started to deteriorate into just Dex bringing squashed granola bars, as if morale were a kind of food going stale.

She typed back, "Bring better granola tomorrow and I'll tell the chat the paradox myself." Then she pasted the link into the group chat with the message: "Justice had the higher average in 1995 and in 1996. Jeter had the higher average for the two years combined. Numbers can do that."

Dex answered in four seconds: "Treaty accepted. The granola will be fresh."

Brielle stood in the wings of the music classroom, clutching her flute, and watched Marcus pace. He was two performers ahead of her, and his hands were shaking so hard that his sheet music rattled like a window in a storm.

"You okay?" she whispered.

"My voice is going to crack," Marcus said. He swallowed hard. "My mouth is so dry, and my heart is going like a million miles an hour." He held out one hand so she could see the tremble for herself.

Brielle had felt exactly the same thing at last month's audition, and it had nearly wrecked her. That afternoon she had gone home and scrutinized the notes she'd copied from a science magazine in the library, reading every line twice. The article said stage fright is the body's fight-or-flight response. Adrenaline, it explained, can cause a racing heart, a dry mouth, a shaky voice, and trembling hands. So her body wasn't breaking. It was doing what any organism does when it senses danger, even danger as harmless as forty kids with folding chairs. The weird part, the part she'd wondered about for days, was that her body couldn't actually tell the difference between a bear and a concert.

So she had tested an idea. At the audition, right before her turn, she had taken slow breaths and told herself, out loud in a tiny whisper, "Nothing here is attacking me. This is just a room." Her heart had still pounded, but her hands had gone steady enough to play.

She turned to Marcus now. "Try this," she said, and handed him her water bottle. "Sip. Then breathe with me, slow. And tell your body it's fight-or-flight stuff, that's all it is."

Marcus looked hesitant, but he sipped, and then they breathed together behind the curtain, in through the nose, out through the mouth, four slow times. Ms. Reyes called his name. He walked out, and Brielle watched his shoulders drop as he set his music on the stand.

His first note came out wobbly. His second one didn't. By the chorus he was singing full and clear, and when he finished, he grinned straight at the wings.

Then Ms. Reyes said, "Brielle, you're up."

Brielle walked to the front, lifted her flute, and whispered, "Just a room."

Sawyer refreshed the marketplace page for the third time that morning, and the Frost Dragon egg was still priced at four thousand gold. Last month it had been two thousand. He slumped in his chair, staring at the listing while his snow fox, Pip, curled up in the corner of the screen and began to hibernate, the way the game's pets always did when their owner ignored them too long.

Four thousand gold was impossible. He had been saving for weeks, selling bread from his bakery stall, because bread was a carbohydrate that every player's energy bar needed and it always sold. But at this rate, the dragon egg would stay out of reach forever. He scrolled through the listings and counted them. Only three eggs for sale in the whole market. Three weeks ago, when the price was two thousand, there had been nine.

He sat back. Fewer eggs, higher price. More bread, lower price, because bread was everywhere. Something invisible was pushing the numbers, like a hidden hand. He wanted to see if he was right, so he opened a notebook and started a chart: item, number of listings, price. Then his dad called from the hallway that they were driving to the hardware store.

At the gas station, while Dad filled the tank, a kid about Sawyer's age pointed at the sign. "Why did it go up since last week? It was cheaper." The station attendant, wiping his hands on a rag, shrugged. "Crude oil. The cost of crude oil is usually the biggest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so when crude oil goes up, the pump price goes up too." The kid's dad nodded like this was ordinary news, and Sawyer stood there with his hand on the door of the car, thinking. A price could move because of something far away that you never saw. Crude oil for gasoline. Scarcity for dragon eggs. Maybe the same rule, wearing different clothes.

Back home, he tested his idea. He spent his gold on a cheap fertile soil seed instead of the egg, planted it in his garden plot, and waited three days while more players hatched dragon events. By Saturday, the marketplace showed eleven Frost Dragon eggs, and the price had slid to one thousand eight hundred. Sawyer bought one. In his notebook, under the chart, he wrote "scarce = up, plentiful = down" and drew an arrow. Then he set the egg beside the sleeping Pip, tapped it once, and whispered, "Okay, buddy, wake up. You're about to have company."

Grandma had been at the house since Monday, and by Wednesday Laurence had given up saying whole sentences to her at the park. She would shout across the picnic table by the duck pond, loud enough that a man walking his dog turned to look, and Grandma would still tilt her head and say, "What's that, dear? Speak up." Laurence couldn't understand it, because Grandma heard the ice cream truck's jingle from three blocks away, and she caught every word the deep-voiced park ranger said when he warned everyone about the geese. It was only Laurence's own voice that vanished.

Sitting on the bench, Laurence turned the puzzle over. Grandma had said her hearing was "mostly there, just blurry." Blurry sound. She thought about how the pond's shallow edge bent the light so the stones looked displaced, the way a straw in a glass seemed to refract into two pieces. Maybe sound could get blurry too, and maybe not all sound the same way. The ranger's low voice had come through fine. The ice cream truck, the wind in the reeds, the men playing chess, all low, all clear. Her own voice, and the shrieking little kids near the swings, all high, all lost. She felt a flicker of skepticism about her own idea, because it seemed too simple, but simple was worth testing.

She slid closer to Grandma and dropped her voice into the low register she used for reading the villain's part in class plays. "Grandma. The ducks stole my sandwich." She kept it quiet, quieter than a normal sentence, almost a mumble.

Grandma laughed out loud. "Both of them? Those fundamental criminals of the pond, always after the bread."

"You heard me?" Laurence said, still low. "I barely said it out loud."

"Loud enough, dear. It just wasn't all fuzzy." Grandma shook her head. "The doctor told me years ago, high-pitched sounds go first. I thought he meant bells and whistles. I didn't know my own granddaughter would count."

For the rest of the week, Laurence practiced her low voice until it felt like a coat she could put on. On Friday at the park, she leaned toward Grandma and rumbled, "The ice cream man is coming. My treat."

Grandma was already holding out her hand for coins.

On her third day at Millbrook Middle School, Scarlett got a seat by the window and a lab partner named Dee who kept a bag of gummy worms in her pencil case. "Emergency rations," Dee said solemnly. "Science is hungry work." Scarlett laughed for the first time in a week. After school she walked home to the new house, where the moving boxes still leaned against the walls like tired visitors.

Her mother had told her something at dinner, almost in passing. "I filed the permanent change of address with the Postal Service, so our First-Class Mail gets forwarded to this house for twelve months." Scarlett had chewed on that all evening. If mail could find her here, then Zoe's letters could too. But Zoe hadn't written yet, and Scarlett had no way to know whether the system actually worked or whether her letters would vanish somewhere between Ohio and here. She had a premise: if forwarding was real, a letter sent to the old address should come back to this one. All she needed was a test.

She wrote a note to herself, sealed it in an envelope, and addressed it to the old house in Dayton. "Dear Scarlett," it began, "if you are reading this, the mail is smarter than you thought." At the post office she asked the clerk to confirm it was First-Class Mail, because that mattered, and the clerk nodded and stamped it. Every afternoon for a week she checked the mailbox, finding only a pizza menu and something for her mother. "Be resilient," Dee told her at school. "Also, gummy worm? It helps."

On the ninth day the envelope appeared in the new mailbox, slightly bent, her own handwriting staring up at her. Scarlett whooped so loudly a neighbor's dog barked. That night she wrote Zoe a real letter, explaining the twelve months, telling her to write to the old address, and adding, "P.S. My new friend thinks mail is food for scientists. She is mostly wrong." She sealed it, and in the morning she ran the whole way to the post office, envelope flapping.

Jace had planted his tomato, pepper and squash seedlings on the first warm Saturday of April, certain that warm meant safe. "You're my tenants now," he told the little green rows, patting the soil around them, "and I'm the landlord who waters you." For two weeks they grew, and he thought the hard part was over.

Then the radio said thirty-four degrees tomorrow night, and Jace stood in the backyard frowning at the sky. Warm days had fooled him. He tried to remember what his grandfather had said last summer while picking peppers: "Can't put these out till after the last spring frost. Freezing kills them." Frost. That was the hidden thing, the cold that came at night when nobody was watching.

He wasn't sure the cold would really reach his plants, so he tested it. He covered every bed with old sheets and buckets, except one squash seedling that he left open on purpose, the far corner of the yard away from the house wall. If that one drooped by morning, he would know for certain it was the cold and not something else, like the neighbor's cat or too much water.

Morning came gray and glittering. Under the sheets the tomatoes stood stiff and fine, leaves untouched. The uncovered squash lay flat, its edges blackened and thin as wet paper. Jace knelt beside it, sorry he had needed proof at all. "That wasn't trivial," he said quietly. "That was your whole life." He decided to revise his plan completely: no more planting until frost season was truly over, and he would keep a journal by the window to track each cold snap.

He buried the squash by the fence, then heard the back gate. His little sister Mira stood holding her blanket. "Is it safe now?" she asked. Jace draped his biggest sheet over the pepper bed one more time and nodded. "Safe," he said. "Come on, let's count buds."

Lydia sat in the emergency room with her left wrist propped on a pillow, remembering the last time she had sat in this exact chair, two summers ago, holding the exact same wrist. Back then the doctor had called it an acute fracture, which meant it was a fresh break, and she had worn a cast for six weeks. She remembered the day they took it off.

"It looks wrong," she had said, staring at her left arm next to her right one. The left arm was skinny and pale, like it belonged to a younger kid. "Why is it so much smaller?"

Her older brother Theo had leaned in, squinting. "Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink," he said. "That's why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off." He had read it somewhere, and Lydia had tested it right there in the exam room, squeezing a tennis ball with each hand. The right hand bounced the ball hard off the wall. The left hand barely held on.

Now, waiting for the X-ray results, Lydia ran her thumb along her right forearm, which was currently her good arm but would soon be her only arm. "Hey, Theo," she said. He looked up from the magazine he was pretending to read so she wouldn't be scared. "I'm going to simulate the next six weeks. Every day, I'll make my left hand do things on purpose. Open doors. Carry my backpack. Brush my teeth." She pointed at the arm that had stayed strong because it never got a turn being lazy. "Last time was an anomaly. This time I'll be ready before the cast even comes off."

The doctor came back with the X-ray and said what Lydia already guessed: broken, cast, six weeks. Theo helped her write LEFT ARM: WANTED FOR HARD LABOR on the plaster before the ink could smear.

"So," Lydia said, wiggling the fingers that stuck out of the cast, "who's bringing me the tennis ball?"

Zoe's grandmother had claimed the long stone ledge by the duck pond for her diyas, and she had brought forty of them, packed in a dented biscuit tin. The park was filling up with families for the Diwali celebration, and Zoe's job, assigned the moment they arrived, was to line the little clay lamps along the ledge before dark.

The problem appeared immediately. Her little brother Rohan, who Zoe had privately classified as a one-boy wrecking crew, kept walking the ledge like a balance beam, kicking diyas into the grass. She'd lined up twelve. Now there were nine standing and three in the pond, where a duck was inspecting one with genuine scientific interest.

Zoe crouched and thought. She couldn't watch Rohan and arrange lamps at the same time, and Mom was busy unfolding chairs near the pavilion. So she tested an idea. She moved the diyas from the top of the ledge to the ground beside it, leaving the flat surface empty. When Rohan came sprinting back for his next tightrope walk, he found a bare ledge, lost interest in about four seconds, and ran off toward the playground. It worked. The rule she'd guessed at, that her brother wanted the height and not the lamps, turned out to be true. It felt almost like a paradox: fewer diyas in the obvious place meant more diyas safe.

She was setting them back on the ledge when her grandmother returned with a box of matches and a thermos of chai. "Good, good," Grandma said, patting the row of small oil lamps. "Diyas, all ready for the five days of Diwali. Mr. Patel from the temple called me eccentric for bringing so many, but I told him, better too much light than too little."

"That's not eccentric," Zoe said. "That's just planning."

Grandma laughed so hard she nearly dropped the matches, then struck one and touched the flame to the first wick.

Maya woke to a strange brightness and found the window filled with white. School was closed, the radio said, and her little brother Theo came bouncing into her room in his dinosaur pajamas before she could even find her socks.

The backyard had turned into a flat white plateau, level and smooth, except where the picnic table poked through like a buried boat. Theo wanted to build a snowman right away, but Maya stopped at the porch steps and pulled on her dark wool mitten. Last week she had read one sentence in a library book, and now she wanted to check whether it was true. "Watch," she said. "I'm going to catch them."

She held her mitten out flat and let the snowfall settle on it. The first flakes melted almost instantly, but when she turned her hand toward the shaded side of the porch, where the air was colder, they held their shape. She bent close. Six arms. She brushed them off and caught more. Six arms again, arranged like tiny stars. Theo leaned over her shoulder, breathing fog onto her wrist, until she made him wait on the steps. "You're melting them," she said.

They caught eleven flakes in all, and Maya counted every one. A lacy one had six branching arms. A stubby one, barely bigger than a crumb, still had six. One looked like a tiny plate with six notched edges. "They're all six," Theo said. "Why?" Maya thought about the book's one sentence, which she now believed completely. "Water links up six-sided when it freezes," she said. "So the flakes come out with six sides. Six arms. Every single time." She looked up at the millions of flakes still falling, each one of them six-sided, and felt like she had a secret about the whole sky.

Later they built the snowman on the white plateau of the yard, and Theo insisted on giving it a red scarf because, he said, red was Dad's favorite color and would symbolize him being home early on snow days. When they went inside, their mugs of cocoa were waiting, and Mom warned them not to sniff the bottle of glass cleaner she was using on the window, because it was toxic. Maya drank her cocoa slowly. Before the flakes on her mitten vanished, she had scooped one last big lacy one onto a black notebook cover and carried it to the freezer, where it waited, six perfect arms intact, on the shelf next to the peas. "I'll show Ms. Alvarez on Monday," she said, and closed the freezer door.

Muhammad stood in the living room holding a candle like it was a prestigious trophy, even though it was just dripping wax on a saucer. The power had cut out an hour ago, and his big sister Zainab was stretched on the couch reading by her phone light. Muhammad's stomach growled so loudly that they both heard it.

"Snack time," he announced, and marched to the refrigerator. He opened the door, stared into the dark cold shelves, saw nothing he wanted, and shut it. Two minutes later he opened it again. And again. On the fourth try, Zainab appeared beside him holding her candle.

"Muhammad, stop. The fridge only keeps food safely cold for about four hours in a power cut, if the door stays closed. Every time you open it, you're spending that time." Muhammad blinked at her, then at the fridge, doing the math in his head. He had opened it five times. "So we decide first, then open it once?" he said slowly. "Exactly once," Zainab said. "Like a game show. One pick, no changing your answer."

Muhammad felt his conscience poke him about all those openings, so he made it right. He sat by the candle and wrote a note by hand, which felt hilariously old-fashioned: "Dear Fridge, I have chosen the leftover biryani and one mango juice. I will not peek. Signed, Muhammad." Zainab read it over his shoulder and laughed so hard she nearly snorted out the candle flame. They folded the letter, tucked it under the fridge magnet for proof, and retired to the couch to wait out the dark like brave explorers.

When the clock showed the hour they'd agreed on, Muhammad leapt up, announced "One pick!", flung the door open, grabbed the biryani container and juice in a single sweep, and shut the door with a triumphant bang. "Nailed it," he said, raising the juice like a trophy. Zainab handed him a fork. "Game show champion," she said. "Now eat before the candle retires."

Joseph had never walked so fast with a leash in his hand. Duke, the brown-and-white mutt from the shelter, trotted beside him with his ears up, and Joseph kept glancing down to make sure the dog was still there. "Two blocks to home," he told him, and Duke's tail swung like a piston pumping at top speed. A delivery truck rumbled past with its engine clattering, and Duke bolted, yanking the leash right out of Joseph's fingers.

Joseph tore after him, but the dog vanished behind the Hendersons' hedge and did not come out the other side. He ran his hands through the branches, ducked under, checked the drainage ditch. Nothing. He was about to presume the worst, that Duke was gone for good, when Mrs. Okafor called from her porch, "Your dog's in my garage! He knocked over my flowerpots and he's cowering behind the lawnmower." She added that he was harmless, not some venomous beast, though he was shaking like one.

Joseph knelt in the dim garage and coaxed Duke out with half the granola bar in his pocket. His hands were still trembling when Mrs. Okafor asked how the shelter would even know the dog was his. "That's the chip," Joseph said. "The microchip." He told her it was about the size of a grain of rice, and it held an ID number. A scanner read the number and pulled up the owner's contact details. That was how the shelter had found Duke's first family, and how, when they couldn't keep him, they had known to call Joseph's mom the moment a spot opened up.

Mrs. Okafor leaned close to Duke's shoulder. "A grain of rice? In there?" "Yep," Joseph said, clipping the leash back on, twice as tight this time. "They scanned him at the shelter and his whole file came up in minutes." He scratched Duke's ears and stood. "Come on, boy. Home's that way, and I'm not letting go again."

The camp bus smelled like granola bars and bug spray, and Carson had the window seat, which felt like winning something. Across the aisle, a boy named Dev held up his phone to illustrate the problem: a photo of his older cousin at Camp Windrow last summer, arms glowing an angry, luminous pink. "Put sunscreen on at seven in the morning," Dev said, "and by dinner he looked like a lobster. Explain that."

Carson leaned over the seat. He liked problems you couldn't see the answer to right away, the hidden kind. "Was he outside all day?"

"At the lake," Dev said. "From lunch till five. Swimming, mostly."

The bus rattled over a pothole, and Carson thought hard. Sunscreen went on once, but the sun kept going all afternoon. If the sunscreen washed off in the lake, or just wore off over hours, then one morning application couldn't last a whole day. That would explain the lobster photo without needing anything mysterious. "I think it's a schedule thing," Carson said. "You have to redo it. Like an algorithm. Apply, wait, apply again."

"How long is the wait?"

"That's the part I don't know," Carson admitted, which bothered him the whole rest of the ride. When they pulled into camp, a tall counselor with a whistle and a clipboard climbed aboard and announced that lake time started after lunch, cabins first. In the cabin, one boy named Marcus, who turned out to be that exact cousin from the photo, now a junior counselor himself, dug through his duffel and pulled out a battered tube of sunscreen. "Rule from the doctor," Marcus said, tossing it to the nearest bunk. "Reapply about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating. Learned that the hard way."

Carson felt the whole thing click into place like a puzzle snapping shut. Every two hours. Right after swimming. That was the missing line of the algorithm, and the lobster photo was the proof.

At the lake, Carson set a timer on Dev's phone and they swam until the whistle blew. When the buzzer went off, they clambered onto the dock, dripping, and slathered on another coat while the other campers stared. "What are you doing?" a girl asked.

"Following the two-hour rule," Carson said, holding out the tube. "Want in?"

The twist came at dinner. Dev's phone buzzed with a text from his mother, and his face fell. "It's my cousin. The other one. She's at a different camp." He turned the screen around: a photo of a girl, shoulders bright pink, holding up a sad thumbs-up. "She put it on this morning and forgot."

"Send her the rule," Carson said, already reaching for the phone. "Every two hours. Right after swimming. She can start tonight."

Dev typed it out, then looked up and grinned. "Camp doctor in training, huh?"

"Camp bus detective," Carson said, and hit send.

Avery discovered the problem before breakfast, when she went out to shovel the front steps in yesterday's snow pants. Dad had scattered rock salt across the porch on Tuesday, and the icy patches under it had not shrunk one bit. The salt just sat there, like glittery gravel doing absolutely nothing.

Weird, she thought. She checked the thermometer nailed by the door. It read minus 12 degrees Celsius, which her brother, Milo, said was about 10 degrees Fahrenheit, colder than the inside of a freezer. "Ha," Milo said from the doorway, still in pajamas. "Even the salt gave up and went back to bed."

"Salt doesn't have a bed," Avery said, but she was already drafting a plan. She scooped a spoonful of the leftover salt, carried it to the kitchen, and wrote a note to keep track, because science deserved paperwork.

EXPERIMENT, the note said. Fact I know: salt melts ice. Fact I see: our salt is NOT melting anything. Question: is it too cold for salt? Guess: yes. Test: bring the ice inside where it's warm and see if the same salt starts working.

She chipped a chunk of ice off the porch railing, dropped it into a bowl with the old salt, and set it on the table. While she waited, she drew an intricate diagram of the porch in the margins, complete of a drawing of Milo as a snowman, since he refused to come outside.

In twenty minutes the ice in the bowl had gone slushy, with the salt sitting in little holes it had melted. Same salt, same ice, different temperature. So it had to be the cold. Somewhere between the warm kitchen and the minus 12 porch, the salt crossed a line where it quit working. Later, checking a weather site, she found the number: ordinary rock salt stopped working well below about minus 10 degrees Celsius, which was 14 degrees Fahrenheit. Colder than that, and you were just decorating your steps.

The hill behind the school was calling, so Avery left the note on the table, propped against the salt box where Dad would find it: "Don't waste the salt, it's too cold. It stops working below about minus 10 Celsius, or 14 Fahrenheit. The formula for a good snow day is zero school plus one sled."

She pulled her sled up the hill twice, and on the third run Milo waved from the bottom and shouted, "Hey, scientist! Race you home for hot chocolate!"

The line for the Solar Hours concert wrapped twice around the arena, and Addison had been in it since 6:40 a.m., which she considered a meticulous use of a Saturday. Her plan was simple: fifty-dollar tickets went on sale at ten, and she had fifty-two dollars, the extra two for a bottle of water. The problem was that everyone in line wanted the same thing, and there were only so many tickets. She could see the scarcity without being told; she just had to count the people ahead of her and hope the math worked out.

By 9:15 the man in the neon vest came down the line with a sign, and Addison read it twice. Front section tickets now eighty dollars, it said, because demand was heavy. Eighty dollars was more than fifty, and Addison watched the effect ripple through the line in front of her. A boy three spots ahead put his money back in his pocket and left. Two girls behind him studied the sign, argued in low voices, and left too. Addison held her fifty-two dollars and did not leave, because the regular seats were still fifty, and fewer people buying the expensive ones meant the line moved faster.

She tested her idea at the hot dog cart near the gate. All morning the cart sold lemonade for four dollars, and only a few people bought it, even though the day was hot enough to make the pavement shimmer. Then the vendor, wanting to empty his cart before the show, called out that lemonade was now two dollars. Half the line turned around. Kids who had walked past it twice came back, and the vendor ran out in fifteen minutes, his ice buckets scraped clean. Addison bought one, mostly for research, and drank it slowly in the shade.

Her brother Theo texted her a message while she waited for the doors: "Did you get tickets? Mom says scalpers are selling front row for 200 outside." Addison typed back: "Not buying. When the price went up to 80, half the line walked away. When lemonade dropped to 2, it sold out in 15 min." Theo replied with a single thumbs up, which she felt understated her achievement.

Inside, a girl with green streaks in her hair overheard Addison explaining the ticket math to a friend. "Oh, that's the law of demand," the girl said. "Price up, people buy less. Price down, they buy more."

Addison nodded as if she had known the name all along, and lifted her two-dollar lemonade in a small toast to the empty cart.

The bus dropped them at the science center at ten sharp, and Hudson had a plan folded in his back pocket. Last year, on this same trip, he had skipped the hardest clue on the scavenger hunt sheet to save time, and Marcus had won by two points. He'd been frugal with his minutes, and it had cost him everything. This year he told himself he would slow down and read every sign, even the boring ones.

"Prism room first," said Priya, tugging his sleeve. That was her want, and she made no secret of it: the exhibit where beams refract into rainbows, because she'd promised her little brother a photo of it. Hudson went along, mostly because the first clue wasn't far away, and partly because after last year he'd decided that racing ahead alone hadn't made him any smarter.

The fire-safety wing held an old hand-pumped engine, brass fittings gone soft with age, and beside it hung a painting of a white dog covered in black spots. "Why is there a dog?" Marcus asked, holding his clue sheet. "It's not even technology." The sheet asked the same thing: Why did firehouses keep spotted dogs?

Hudson studied the engine instead of the dog. Two long poles crossed at the front, and leather harnesses hung where horses would have stood. There were no horses in the painting, but there was a road, and the dog was painted running, always running, ahead of everything. He thought about the horses, invisible in every picture, and about how loud and crowded streets used to be. A slow idea formed. "They ran ahead," he said. "Like a scout."

Priya wasn't listening. She had found something behind the engine, a wooden model street with a tiny carriage and a lever. When Hudson pulled the lever, a small spotted dog slid out on a wire and crowds of tiny metal people scattered to the sides. He pulled it twice more, watching the same pattern each time. "The dog clears the road," Hudson said. "That's the whole job."

Marcus leaned over the model, unconvinced. "So firehouses kept them because they got along with the horses and ran ahead of the carriages?" Hudson nodded, then pointed to the harnesses, then to the dog's position in the painting, out in front, ears back. Marcus wrote it down slowly, the way he never wrote anything, and for once he looked less sure of winning than curious.

The final clue led to the gift shop, where Hudson counted his seven dollars and found nothing but postcards in his price range. Priya bought a glass prism that refract­ed the shop lights across the ceiling, and she held it up for Marcus's camera, laughing, while the shop attendant rang it up. "You only lost by two points because you skipped the dog last year," Marcus said, reading his old sheet from his pocket. Hudson stared at him. There had been a dog clue last year too, a different painting, and he had walked right past it. "Want to split the postcard?" Marcus asked, sliding one across the counter toward him.

Wyatt crouched over the camp stove, turning the bacon with a fork, while his little sister Nora arranged napkins on the picnic table for the third time. She had announced at breakfast that she was in charge of table decoration, and she intended to take the job seriously. "Move your elbow," she said. "You're blocking the centerpiece." The centerpiece was a pinecone on a rock.

Dad stood nearby rinsing a coffeepot at the water jug. The bacon had been going fine until Wyatt dropped in a new strip and the grease in the pan caught, a soft orange flame licking up the side. Wyatt's hand shot toward the water jug, but Dad got there first. He didn't splash. He turned the burner off, then slid a lid across the top of the pan, and the fire went out like someone had pinched it.

"What?" Wyatt stared at the lid. "Why not water?"

"Water on a grease fire turns to steam in a flash and throws the burning oil everywhere," Dad said. "Turn off the heat, cover it, and the fire smothers." He lifted the lid a peek to check, then set it back down. "Ask Grandpa about the kitchen curtain when he was my age."

Wyatt turned that over while the pan cooled. He tried to picture it: liquid water flashing into vapor, dragging drops of burning oil with it. It seemed backwards that water, which he thought of as the fire fighter's best friend, could make a grease fire worse. He decided the most probable explanation was that Dad was right and his own instincts were wrong, and that he'd better remember the exact order of things: heat off first, then lid.

Two nights later it was Wyatt's turn again, this time frying potatoes in oil while Nora elaborated on her centerpiece by adding two acorn caps and a twist of foil. Dad had hiked down to the lake with Mom. Wyatt turned away for one second to grab the salt, and when he looked back the oil had flared, flames curling over the pan's edge and Nora screaming his name.

His whole body wanted the water bottle on the table. Instead he made himself think of the curtain story, and the picture he'd built in his head: water flashing into vapor, oil flung in a burning ring. He snapped the burner knob off, grabbed the lid, and slid it over the pan. The flames died under the metal. Nora stood frozen with the water bottle in her hand, arm half raised, and Wyatt held up his palm.

"Not that," he said. "Cover it, don't drown it." He lifted the lid a crack, saw only dark oil and potatoes, and slid it back on. "Give me a minute, and then you can put the napkins out."

Auntie Ru's car would pull into the driveway at six o'clock sharp, and Katherine still hadn't figured out what to do about the greeting. Her cousin Tama was coming all the way from New Zealand, and Mom had said, "He'll expect a hongi, so be ready." Ready for what? The word sat in Katherine's head like an opaque window she couldn't see through, and dinner was two hours away.

"Maybe it's a handshake," said her little brother Ben, who wanted nothing more than to be in charge of handing Tama his welcome gift, because handing people gifts meant being the center of attention for at least ten seconds. He had already claimed the job at breakfast. "Everybody does handshakes."

Katherine didn't think so. Mom had pressed her noses together in the air, twice, practicing in front of the hall mirror like a secret code. So it involved faces. Katherine tried it on Ben, leaning in forehead-first, and Ben dissolved into giggles and fell off the couch. Definitely faces, she decided, and probably not a kiss, because Mom never kissed anyone at the door except Grandpa.

At the table that night, which had been stretched with the good tablecloth and all three extra chairs, Katherine watched like a scientist. Tama arrived at 6:02 with a paper-wrapped parcel of chocolate fish for Grandma, and everyone murmured approval, because in this house you never arrived without something, whereas at her friend Priya's house you were scolded for bringing gifts, as if you doubted the host's generosity. Strange, Katherine thought. Same object, opposite meaning, like a coin with two faces.

Then it happened. Tama stood in front of her, tall and smiling, and leaned in. Katherine matched him. Their noses and foreheads touched, warm and brief, and stayed pressed together for one held breath. When they drew apart, Tama's eyes were bright, and Grandma made a small satisfied sound from her chair.

"What does it mean?" Katherine whispered as they sat down, because Ben was already unwrapping the chocolate fish without asking, elbows planted on the table, and Mom was clearing her throat at him in the family's universal signal for elbows off, which Tama noticed and seemed to file away like a rule for later.

"It's called a hongi," Tama said. "Sharing the breath of life."

Katherine looked at him across the breadbasket and wondered whether everyone he knew at home walked around carrying a piece of everyone else's breath inside them. "So we're kind of family now," she said.

"We were already," said Tama, and passed her the potatoes before Ben could reach them.

The snow came down so thick overnight that school was canceled before Noah even finished his cereal, which meant the whole backyard was his. He pulled on boots, zipped his coat to his chin, and burst out the sliding door into a world that was white, quiet, and completely untracked. Ten degrees, his weather app said, but next to it was a smaller number that made him stop halfway down the steps: it felt like two below zero.

"Wind chill," his older sister Priya called from the porch, holding her phone up. "The air is ten degrees, but the wind makes it feel way colder." She wasn't even coming out. She was just there to deliver the news and go back inside to her cocoa.

Noah stomped a path to the fort he'd built from snow and branches back in November, when the yard had still been lush and green at the edges. The fort looked smaller under all the new snow, like something the winter had swallowed. He climbed in through the gap he'd left and sat on his overturned bucket throne. It was actually kind of warm in there, or at least not freezing, which gave him an idea.

If wind made cold air feel colder, then blocking the wind should make it feel warmer. That was testable. He crouched in the still air behind the fort wall for a whole minute, then stepped out into the open where the wind bit at his face, then went back behind the wall. His cheeks told him the answer before his brain did. Behind the wall his face stopped hurting. Out in the open, it stung like needles. Same ten degrees both places, but only one of them felt like two below zero.

He ran inside to nominate Priya as witness number one for his experiment. "Come feel this. Stand behind the fort, then stand in the open. It's the same temperature but your face doesn't believe it." Priya groaned but followed him out, and when she stepped around the wall she actually said "whoa," which from Priya was basically a standing ovation.

They fortified the fort together all morning, packing snow into every gap until the wind couldn't reach them at all. Noah rubbed his red ears, the cold gone from the stiff cartilage of them, and grinned.

"Tomorrow," he said, "we build a roof."

Livia slammed the gym doors open with her shoulder, basketball bouncing against her hip, because tonight was the night she was finally going to beat Marisol in sprints. The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and ambition, and the whole seventh-grade team was already stretching by the bleachers.

But Marisol looked terrible. She was the fastest player Livia had ever seen, the girl who trained every single day, even Sundays, even during a blizzard in February. Tonight, though, she jogged the warm-up lap like her shoes were full of sand, and Coach Delgado's stopwatch caught her at a time so slow that Marisol stared at it and then at the clock on the wall, as if the clock were lying.

"That can't be right," Marisol said. "I never take a day off."

That was exactly the problem, Livia realized, standing there spinning the ball on one finger. She had read a science article for health class about how muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, which meant rest days were actually part of getting better. Marisol was skipping that whole part. Livia had a theory, and theories needed testing.

"Bet you a fruit roll-up," Livia said, "that if you rest tomorrow, completely rest, couch-level rest, you'll be faster on Thursday."

Marisol squinted. "My cousin works at a sports corporation and he says champions train more, not less."

"Your cousin also said glitter would be permanent on your sneakers if you sealed it with hairspray, and it was gone by Tuesday."

Marisol laughed so hard she snorted, which made the whole team turn around, which made her snort again. "Fine. One day. One fruit roll-up."

Thursday night, the gym was loud with squeaking shoes. Marisol lined up, coiled like a spring, and when Coach blew the whistle she flew down the court so fast the stopwatch practically gave up. She turned to Livia, breathless and grinning.

"I owe you a fruit roll-up," she said, "and an apology to my legs."

Ivy wanted the Slate Pro tablet more than she wanted her next birthday, and the poster in the library hallway knew it. It showed five glowing checkmarks: SHARPEST SCREEN, FASTEST CHIP, MOST APPS, LIGHTEST BODY, COOLEST COLORS. Above the checkmarks, a famous singer named Rae Delgado grinned and said, "I never leave home without mine." At the bottom, tiny letters announced that the Tech Store two blocks away would close at 5:00. Ivy checked the clock above the librarian's desk. It was 4:20.

Her best friend Marcus was already at a table, doing homework he should have finished three days ago. "Look at this," Ivy said, spreading the poster flat in front of him. "Rae Delgado uses one. And five great features. Five, Marcus." She tapped each checkmark. "Everyone at school is getting one. Even Priya, and Priya still uses a flip phone."

Marcus squinted at the poster. "Rae Delgado also gets paid to smile at things. That's her whole job." He turned a homework page over. "And 'sharpest' and 'coolest' aren't really facts. They're just loaded words. It's like when my brother calls his sandwich 'legendary' so I'll trade him my chips."

"Okay, but the screen is sharper." Ivy paused. "Sharper than what, though?" She read the poster again, slower this time. Something felt off, like a puzzle with a piece missing. The ad listed everything the tablet was good at and nothing else. "It says lightest body. It doesn't say anything about the battery." That seemed strange to her, because the battery was the first thing her mom asked about any device. It seemed logical that an ad with five checkmarks would add a sixth for battery life if the battery were any good.

She marched to the computer catalog, typed "Slate Pro review," and found a magazine article. The tablet's battery lasted four hours. Four. Her cousin's ancient tablet lasted nine. "Marcus," she whispered. "They stacked the deck. Five great facts, and they left out the bad one." Marcus nodded. "My language arts teacher calls that card stacking. Showing only the facts that support your side, so the message seems stronger than it is." Ivy wrote it on her hand, because some facts deserve ink.

At 4:45 Marcus asked, "Are we still buying it? The store closes in fifteen minutes." Ivy looked at the poster, at Rae Delgado's grin, at the five checkmarks marching in a row like they had somewhere to be. "No. But we can walk past the store on the way home and look through the window. That's free." Marcus zipped his backpack. "Now that's a feature they should advertise."

The snow arrived overnight with no warning at all, so when Marcus woke up and saw the school parking lot buried, the day felt like a spontaneous gift. He suited up and hurried down Maple Street toward the hill behind Mr. Delgado's building, where his friend Theo was already packing snow onto a sled runner. Their favorite run started at the top, but a fallen branch had begun to obstruct the path halfway down, so they took turns steering around it, each pass a little faster than the last.

After an hour of climbing and crashing, Marcus pulled off one glove to shake the snow out and noticed something odd. His fingers were white and stinging, his ears had gone numb enough that he could pinch them without really feeling it, and the tip of his nose had that prickly, half-asleep feeling. Yet his chest and legs, under all those layers, were toasty. He tested the idea on the next run. He kept his gloved hands tucked under his arms, and sure enough his fingers warmed up while his ears stayed cold.

"Why do my hands hurt but my stomach doesn't?" Theo asked, rubbing his own red ears.

"I think fingers, toes, ears and the nose are the parts of the body most likely to get frostbite," Marcus said. "Everything else stays warm longer. My mom's landlord lost a toe that way one winter, so she's always going on about it."

Theo looked down at his boots. "Toes too?"

"Toes too. So we cover all four and we're good."

They dug spare hats and an extra pair of socks out of Marcus's garage, and Mrs. Delgado, watching from her window, waved them in for cocoa when their sled run ended in her hedge. Marcus pressed his warm mug against his cheek and felt his nose wake up, tingling.

"Same time after lunch?" Theo asked, already carrying the sled toward the hill.

The ferry to Owl Lake Campground took forty minutes, and Brielle's little brother Theo turned green ten minutes in. He sat hunched against the rail inside the cabin, staring at the floor, holding a paper bag.

"I'm going to throw up," Theo said.

"Look out the window," Brielle said.

"I did. It made it worse."

That was the strange part, Brielle thought. Watching the water had made him feel sicker, not better. She remembered the museum trip last spring, when the bus had jolted over potholes and she had felt fine the whole ride. What had she done differently? She had sat by the window, but not at the passing trees. She had watched the mountains, far away, which never seemed to move.

"Come on." She took Theo's sleeve and pulled him toward the deck door. He was impulsive about most things, ice cream, puddles, wasps, but moving took persuasion now.

The wind on deck was cold. Brielle steered him to the rail. "Don't watch the water. Watch the shoreline, way out there. The far end, where it doesn't move."

Theo gripped the rail and fixed his eyes on the distant line of pines. A swell rolled under the hull, and another. Slowly his shoulders came down from around his ears. The gray went out of his face.

"It works," he said. "Why?"

Brielle considered lying, then didn't. "I don't know exactly. Something about your eyes and your ears agreeing when you look at the horizon." She pointed anyway. "Keep watching. Dad said the campsite is near that second point."

Their father came out with two granola bars, ready to intervene with crackers and ginger candy, but Theo waved him off and kept his eyes on the far shore.

When the ferry bumped the dock, Theo was the first one down the ramp, running. "Race you to the car," he called.

Brielle jogged after him over the gravel, her knee cartilage aching from a fall off her bike the week before, but not enough to slow her down.

Theo stood in the kitchen with dirt on his shirt and two days until the science fair. On the counter sat four bean seedlings in paper cups, and beside them his project board, which currently said, in giant letters, MUSIC IS GOOD FOR PLANTS. His little sister Maya wandered in, eating a pickle.

"That's your whole project?" she said. "Good for plants how? Also, plants don't have ears, so, nice work."

"Thanks for the exceptional feedback," Theo said. He stared at the board. The trouble was, he couldn't prove music was good for plants, because he couldn't even say what would prove him wrong. He remembered his notebook from class and flipped it open. There it was, in his own handwriting: a useful hypothesis must be testable, meaning an experiment could show it is wrong. Below it, the form it usually takes: If... then...

"So make it testable," Maya said, peering over his arm.

"I'm getting there." He crossed out the giant letters and wrote: If I play music for two seedlings and keep two seedlings in silence, then the music plants will grow taller in one week. He pointed at it. "An experiment could show that's wrong. The quiet plants could win, or it could be a tie. Either way, I'd know something."

"That's less exciting than my idea," Maya said. "My idea is that pickles are good for plants."

"Please don't elaborate."

She elaborated anyway, describing a pickle-watering system, until he handed her a prism from the junk drawer and aimed her at the window. Sunlight split into a stripe of rainbow across her hands, and she went quiet at last.

The next morning Theo measured the cups. The music plants had grown a centimeter. So had the others. He wrote down every number, even the boring ones, then set his ruler beside the cups for tomorrow.

"Tie so far," Maya reported from the window, holding the prism up so a green spot of rainbow landed on the tallest seedling. "Your plants are all winning, basically."

Samantha balanced the mixing bowl on the picnic table and read her grandmother's recipe card again, the one taped inside the camper where the wind couldn't steal it. The card was really a letter Gran had sent last spring, ending with "Save me a slice." Samantha had promised she would, and tonight she intended to bake her first loaf over the campfire.

She remembered the bakery visit from last summer, how Gran had let her poke a squishy lump of dough that seemed to breathe. "It's not magic," Gran had said, winking. "Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles." Samantha had thought that was the strangest thing she'd ever heard, a fungus burping bread into existence.

She mixed flour, sugar, and the packet of yeast, then reached for the kettle. The water had been sitting on the camp stove while Dad ran the generator to charge the lantern, so it was good and hot. She stirred it in, kneaded the dough, and set the bowl near the fire in a sheltered spot, safe from any draft, because Gran's letter said cold air would slow the rising. Then she waited. The dough sat there, round and lazy, as lethargic as her little brother Theo after a swim.

"That's a bread rock," Theo announced twenty minutes later. "You're making bread rocks for dinner."

"It's still waking up," Samantha said, but her stomach twisted. She leaned close and studied the dough. No bubbles. No puff. Nothing. She thought about Gran's letter again, feeding on sugars, releasing gas. The yeast should have been eating and puffing like tiny balloon artists, and it was doing nothing at all. Something had gone wrong before the bowl ever got set down. She touched the side of the mixing bowl where she'd poured the water in. Warm. Very warm. Hot, actually, still hot enough that she pulled her fingers back. The yeast hadn't been sleeping. The yeast had been cooked.

Theo, who had declared the whole project doomed, suddenly changed his mind and became her assistant. "New plan," he said solemnly, holding the fresh packet like it was treasure. They mixed everything again, and this time Samantha tested the cooled water on her wrist, the way you test a bottle for a baby, warm but not hot. They set the bowl by the fire and watched.

Ten minutes later Theo grabbed her sleeve. "Look, look! It's a balloon!" The dough had swelled up round and dome-shaped, and when Samantha pressed one finger gently against it, the surface sprang back like something alive. She grinned and shaped it into a loaf. "Gran," she said, "is getting the biggest slice of all."

"Only if I don't eat it first," said Theo, already reaching for a stick to poke the fire.

Sofia stood in line outside the ticket kiosk in the west wing of the mall, third from the front, her fingers curled around the twenty dollars she had saved from dog walking. The kiosk sold tickets to the Bright Comet concert, and for one day only they were priced at ten dollars. Behind her, the line snaked past the pretzel stand, past the fountain where coins glinted under the water, and out toward the shoe store. She counted at least two hundred people.

At ten o'clock the metal shutter rattled up and the clerk began pulling tickets from a box. Sofia got hers, paper warm from the printer, and stepped aside to look at it. Behind her the box emptied fast. By the time the fiftieth person reached the counter, the clerk raised both hands and called out, "That's it, we're out." The rest of the line broke apart slowly, like ice melting. A girl near the fountain sat down on the rim and put her head in her hands.

"That's so unfair," said Malia, Sofia's neighbor, who had been two spots behind the shutter people. "Ten dollars, and they only had fifty tickets. Look at all these people." She swept her arm at the crowd still drifting, unwilling to leave. Sofia turned the ticket over in her hands. Half the people in that line had wanted a ticket and gotten nothing, because the price had been so low that everyone could afford one, and there weren't enough to go around. She remembered her brother once saying there was a word for that.

A man in a gray jacket moved along the edge of the crowd, speaking quietly. "Bright Comet, forty dollars, I've got two." Malia grabbed Sofia's sleeve. "That's the same ticket," she whispered. "Ten dollars at the kiosk, forty from him." Sofia watched a boy hand over the money and walk away holding the ticket like it was made of glass. Down the corridor, a cart selling phone cases sat stacked with hundreds of them, a sign reading five dollars, two for eight, and barely a customer stopping.

"My brother called it a shortage," Sofia said. "When the price stays low, more people want the thing than there are things to sell." She tested the logic in her head against what she had just watched: low price, long line, empty box. Then the phone case cart: plenty of cases, few buyers, price falling. It wasn't symmetrical, not exactly, but it fit both ways she looked at it.

Malia stared at the man in the gray jacket. "I was going to pay him forty," she said. "I had it in my pocket." She took out the bills, folded twice, and looked at them for a long moment. Then she put the money back in her pocket and straightened her shoulders. "Next time I'm getting here at seven," she said, "and I'm bringing a folding chair."

Megan sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with a notebook open on her knee, staring at a question she had written in big letters: WHEN? Her science fair beans were germinating in a damp paper towel beside her, tiny white roots curling like commas, and she was supposed to be recording their growth for her poster about a jar ecosystem. Instead she kept thinking about something Mrs. Alvarez's health packet had mentioned last week, something that had made half the class giggle and the other half go quiet.

The packet didn't say when anything would happen to her, only that it would, eventually. That was the problem. Megan liked problems with data. So she made a chart on the next page, like her bean chart, and wrote the names of every girl she could think of with an older sister: Priya, Jenna, Bree. At Priya's house on Saturday, she brought it up while they made popcorn. "Do you know how old your sister was when it happened? Her first period, I mean." Priya shrugged and yelled down the hall, and her sister shouted back, "Twelve and a half." Jenna's sister, texting from basketball practice, answered in a message Megan read off Jenna's phone: "i was 11!! still mad about it tbh." Bree's sister, who was in college, sent a note on lined paper she'd scribbled at the bus stop and left in the Mendozas' mailbox: "Almost 14. Everyone's different. Tell Bree to stop worrying." Megan copied each number into her chart.

Back in her bedroom, she laid the numbers out and stared at them. Eleven, twelve and a half, almost fourteen. They didn't match at all, which frustrated her until she remembered her beans. Some had sprouted on day three, some on day five, and one stubborn seed had waited until day eight, but all of them had sprouted. The differences weren't mistakes. They were just the range. She wrote that word in her notebook and underlined it, then added a line underneath: wide range is normal.

On Monday she showed the chart to Priya at lunch. "So there's no exact schedule," Megan said. "It's more like a middle age that lots of girls are near, and a big spread around it. Like my beans." Priya leaned over the chart, and her grin was contagious; by the time the bell rang, half the table was smiling at a page of bean data and sister stories. "You should put this in your poster," Priya said. Megan laughed. "My poster is about ecosystems." But she paper-clipped the chart into her notebook anyway, right next to the beans.

Emma had spread her poster across the picnic table at Grandma's backyard reunion, and that was the problem. For her social studies project she had made a bar graph of the origins of people in Brampton, Ontario, using numbers from a government website. She had checked her addition three times, and the totals still came to far more than one hundred percent. "That's impossible," she muttered, jabbing her pencil at the poster. "A town can't be more than all of itself."

Her cousin Priya leaned over her shoulder, holding a paper plate of samosas. "Maybe the website made a mistake," she said. "Or maybe you did."

"I despise this graph," Emma said, which wasn't true, but it felt true right then. Uncles and aunts drifted past the table, some carrying chairs, some arguing about whose turn it was at the badminton net. Grandma arrived last, drying her hands on a dish towel, and studied the poster the way she studied a chessboard.

"Uncle Ray!" Grandma called across the yard. "Come and settle something." Uncle Ray, whom everyone agreed was the most competent person in the family at anything involving numbers, worked at the town hall. He set down his lemonade and looked at Emma's graph for a long moment. Then he laughed, not at her, but the way people laugh when a puzzle suddenly makes sense. "That's the census," he said. "It's not wrong. Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population."

Emma stared at him. "More than one," she repeated slowly. In her head she tested the idea against her own family, sitting right there in folding chairs. Grandma cooked pierogi every Christmas and told stories about monsoon seasons in Sri Lanka, where she'd taught school for ten years before emigrating. Priya called herself both Guyanese and Canadian and refused to pick. Auntie Joan's family had come from Scotland four generations back, and she still put tartan napkins on the table every reunion. If every one of them could tick more than one box, then of course the bars would stack up past one hundred percent. Nobody had counted twice by accident; everybody had counted all of themselves.

She grabbed a marker and wrote across the top of the poster: "Why the numbers are bigger than 100." Then she drew a small pie chart of her own family, one slice for each thing they claimed, the slices overlapping in the middle like a Venn diagram. "Priya, hold this corner down," she said, reaching for her pencil case. "I'm going to interview everybody before the potato salad runs out."

Brielle sat at the kitchen table with her left arm propped on a stack of cookbooks, the fresh white cast ending just below her elbow. The fall from the dilapidated porch railing had happened three days ago, and she was still turning over what Dr. Okafor had said. "The break missed the growth plate, which is the good news," the doctor had told them, and her mother had exhaled like she'd been holding her breath since the emergency room. Brielle hadn't asked why at the time, because asking felt like admitting she didn't understand something important about her own arm.

Her little brother Theo slid into the chair across from her, holding a jar of bean seeds he'd been trying to germinate on the windowsill all week. "When your cast comes off, we're playing catch," he announced. "Every day. I've been practicing my curveball so I can finally beat you." Theo had wanted to beat her at catch since spring, and now that she was benched, he kept repeating his plan like a promise.

"Growth plate," Brielle said slowly, watching him twist the jar lid. "That's what she called it. She said near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, and that's where bones lengthen while you're still a kid." Theo wrinkled his nose. "Cartilage? Like your ears?" "Sort of, I think. So if a break goes through it, the bone might not grow right. Mine didn't, that's why it's good news."

She went to the hall closet and found the ball of twine. If her arm bone was still lengthening, like a bean seed swelling before it sprouted, she could catch it in the act. She looped the twine from her shoulder to her wrist on the right arm, cut it, and labeled the string with a marker: RIGHT, WEEK ONE. Then she did the same for the cast side, writing LEFT over the plaster instead.

"Do you actually think it's growing right now?" Theo asked, watching her tape both strings into her notebook.

"Seeds don't sprout while you stare at them either," Brielle said. "But the beans on the sill prove things happen slow." She closed the notebook and slid it to the end of the table, where they could both see it. "Six weeks. Then we measure again, and then, curveball or not, you're going down."

Theo grinned and set his jar beside it, fungus speckling the damp cotton inside. "Race you," he said. "Beans versus bone."

James stared at the jumbled tray of foam balls on his workbench and realized, not for the first time, that his whole plan might have been built on a wrong idea. In his garage, with the door half open to let in the afternoon light, he had promised his little sister Maya that he would build her a model of an atom by dinnertime. The trouble was that he had assumed every atom needed the same parts, like every sandwich needed the same two slices of bread.

He had learned this the hard way last summer, and the memory still made him wince. At the science museum he had confidently glued one big ball, one small ball, and a clump in the middle for the neutron, only to have a kid next to him squint at it and say, "That's not hydrogen." James had argued, in a vain attempt to protect his work, until the kid pointed at the chart on the wall. He had walked away without finishing the model, and he still wondered whether he should have just asked someone instead of insisting he was right.

Now he spread out the chart he had copied into his notebook and tested his idea with actual balls instead of glue. He pushed the pieces around on the bench like a puzzle. "Okay," he said to himself, "the most common kind of hydrogen atom has just one proton and one electron and no neutron at all." He set down one large red ball, then one tiny blue ball, and deliberately left the gray clump sitting alone in the tray. It looked unfinished. It looked almost like camouflage, a half-built thing pretending to be complete, but the chart said otherwise, and the chart had been right before.

Maya wandered in, sneakers squeaking on the concrete, and picked up the gray ball. "What's this lonely one for?"

"Nothing," James said. "That's the weird part. Hydrogen doesn't need it." She frowned at the two lonely balls on the wire, so he handed her the glue and the paint. "You do the electron. I'll hold the wire."

She dipped her brush in blue, and the small ball slowly turned from white to bright, spinning between her fingers.

Amelia stood on the porch of Kanya's house holding a box of oranges in both hands, exactly the way her mother had shown her. When Kanya's grandmother opened the door, the old woman pressed her palms together and bowed slightly. Amelia had no idea what to do with her hands, so she just nodded fast and hoped that counted.

Inside, everyone had left their shoes in a row by the door, so Amelia nudged her sneakers into line with the rest. She watched Kanya's little brother, Santi, who was six, dart under the dining table like a fish under a canopy of chairs and tablecloth. He popped out near Amelia and grinned up at her with a gap where his front tooth used to be. Without thinking, Amelia reached down to ruffle his hair.

"Wait," Kanya said, catching her wrist. "Don't touch his head. In Thailand the head is sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude."

Amelia pulled her hand back. Santi didn't look offended, only curious, but she took Kanya seriously. She began testing her theory as the evening went on, watching closely. Kanya's father passed Santi a dish and never once patted him. When Santi fell off a chair, his mother checked his elbow, his knee, and carefully not his head. Nobody touched anybody's head at all.

At dinner, Amelia kept noticing more. The spoon went in the right hand, the fork in the left, and the fork pushed food onto the spoon. She copied Kanya move for move, and when she almost used the fork directly, she caught herself and switched.

"You're learning fast," Kanya said.

"That's because I'm extremely sophisticated," Amelia said, and immediately dropped a grain of rice on her shirt.

Santi laughed so hard he slid off his chair again. This time, when he stood up, Amelia bowed to him, palms together, just like the grandmother at the door. Santi bowed right back.

The snow came down all morning, and by ten o'clock the school district had given up and called a snow day. Charlie yelled so loudly that her upstairs neighbor banged on the ceiling, but she was already pulling on her boots. She texted her friend Maya, and they met at the little park on Maple Street, where the slide was frozen solid and Mrs. Park, who lived nearby, was grumbling that her landlord was negligent and still hadn't fixed the gate, so it hung crooked in the snow.

"We're building a snowman," Charlie announced. "A huge one. Three balls high." Maya knelt down and started packing, but the snow wouldn't cooperate. Every time she pressed a handful together, it sifted back apart like sugar. Charlie tried too, squeezing until her mittens ached. The ball just crumbled in her palms. "This snow is broken," Maya said, kicking at it. The powder flew up in a dry puff and drifted down again without sticking to anything.

Charlie scooped two handfuls and held them side by side, one from the shadow of the bench and one from the sunny patch near the swing set. The sunny one felt heavier, almost damp, and when she squeezed it, it held. "Feel this," she said, and Maya pressed it into a rough little ball. "Snow near freezing has some water in it," Charlie said, turning the ball over. "It's the dry stuff that falls apart." Maya looked around. Half the park sat in shade, where the snow stayed powdery and useless, and half of it was wide open to the morning sun.

"So we wait," Maya said. "It's not even noon yet." They climbed the frozen slide until their mittens froze, then took turns dragging each other on the crooked gate like a sled. Back at home, Charlie's mom made cocoa, and they watched the chocolate dissolve into the milk while the sun climbed higher.

By two o'clock they tested the shady snow again, and this time Charlie could feel the difference before she even squeezed it. The top layer packed, then the next, and the next. Their snowman stood three balls high before the shadows came back, with a stick arm waving at the swing set, and Charlie said, "Same park, same snow. We just had to wait for the sun to do its part."

Liam sat cross-legged on Marcus's bedroom floor with Marcus's phone, because his own phone had died on the bus and Marcus never minded sharing. He was supposed to be looking up cheat codes for Rocket Racers, but when he typed his own name into the search bar just to see what would happen, the first result made his stomach drop. It was a comment he had written two years ago, back when he was eight, under a video of a soccer match. "The goalie is so bad he has an infection of the hands," he had written, misspelling everything, and there it was now, next to his full name, glowing on the screen like it had been waiting for him.

"That's weird," Liam said. "I posted that on my old account. I deleted the whole account last year."

Marcus leaned over, chewing the last of his pretzels. "Try my name," he said. Liam typed it in, and a picture came up that Marcus's mom had posted publicly years ago, of Marcus in a bird costume for the school's migratory animals play. It had spread from one page to another, and now a stranger's blog had it, with a caption underneath that called him "this brave little flamingo."

"Search engines use crawlers," Marcus said, reading from the top of the results page. "Automated programs that copy and index public web pages." He pointed at the small gray text. "So if it's public, it can turn up in search results."

Liam tested it, because it seemed too strange to just believe. He posted a fake comment on a public video, using his first name and a made-up last name, then searched for it. At first nothing came up, but after Marcus made them both quesadillas and they came back with crumbs on their shirts, the comment appeared, sitting there in the results like a photograph pinned to a wall. He deleted the comment immediately, then thought about the flamingo picture, which had already been copied and would not go away just because Marcus asked.

"We should tell your mom about the picture," Liam said. "Before the whole school searches your name." Marcus nodded slowly, and Liam handed him the phone first, letting him decide whether to show her now or after dinner. Down in the kitchen, Marcus's mom was saturating the counter with soapy water, scrubbing a pot and humming. Marcus took a breath and held the screen out to her. "Mom, can you look at something?"

The waiting room clock ticked past 3:40, and Arianna's audition for the spring choir started at 4:15. She twisted a crumpled tissue in her lap, the third one since she'd sat down, each stained the same worrying shade of yellow-green.

"Look," she whispered to her dad, holding it up. "It's getting worse. What if I need antibiotics before I can sing?"

A boy across the aisle, maybe ten, leaned over his own pile of tissues. "Mine's green," he said, his voice brittle with worry. "Green means infection. My sister said so. I bet I need medicine today."

Arianna's name was called before she could answer. In the exam room, Dr. Patel listened to her lungs, looked in her throat, and said, "It's a virus. Rest, fluids, and you can sing tonight if your voice holds."

"But the mucus is yellow," Arianna said. "Practically green."

Dr. Patel smiled. "The color comes from your immune cells and an enzyme they release. Green or yellow doesn't tell us whether it's bacteria or a virus." She tapped the chart. "Your exam does, and this is viral."

Arianna folded the fact into her mind like a note she could pass along. On the way out, she stopped at the pharmacy counter to pick up tissues for the boy's mother, who was juggling a toddler and her purse.

"Hey," Arianna said to the boy, handing him the pack. "I asked the doctor about the green thing. It's just your immune cells and an enzyme they release. My doctor said the color alone can't tell you if it's bacteria or a virus. Mine's green too, and I don't need medicine."

The boy's shoulders dropped an inch. "Really? So I'm not super sick?"

"You're just full of germ fighters," Arianna said. "Same as me."

At 3:58 she and her dad raced for the car. In the parking lot she tested her voice on one soft scale, and the high note came out clean and clear, like a bell through an open window.

Evan stood on the porch of Kenji's house holding a gift bag so tightly the paper crinkled. Inside was a box of chocolate chip cookies, because you can't visit somebody's grandmother with empty hands, that much he'd figured out on his own. Kenji's grandmother opened the door, bowed, and said something quick and musical that Evan didn't understand. He panicked, stuck out his hand, and shook hers. She laughed, a big surprised laugh, and Kenji elbowed him. "You bow, doofus. Like this." Kenji bent from the waist, and Evan copied him so fast he almost head-butted the doorframe.

At dinner there were dumplings, rice, and a huge steaming pot of ramen. Evan was starving. He was also nervous, because Kenji's grandmother had gone quiet and formal, and Evan had a bias that quiet and formal meant "watch your manners or die of embarrassment." He remembered his own family's rule: no noises at the table, ever, or his aunt would raise one eyebrow at you until your appetite diminished on the spot.

Then Kenji picked up his bowl, put his face practically in it, and slurped. Loudly. It sounded like a pool drain. Evan froze with his chopsticks in the air, waiting for the eyebrow. Instead Kenji's father slurped. Then Kenji's little sister, who couldn't have been older than six, produced a slurp so tremendous that Evan's water glass rattled.

Evan studied them, thinking fast. Nobody's face was red. Nobody was apologizing. They were all doing it, even the grandmother, and they were smiling between slurps, which meant it wasn't rude here, it was normal. It had to be. He lifted his bowl, took a breath, and slurped his noodles with everything he had.

"Beautiful!" the grandmother shouted in English, clapping. "More soup for the boy!" She ladled a second helping into his bowl before he could even swallow. Kenji grinned across the table. "Told you this family's frugal," he whispered. "Nobody wastes broth."

"Neither do I," said Evan, and slurped again.

Ella set down her fork when Grandpa Marcus slid his phone across the table, screen up. "Look at this. The river's over the road by the mill. They're saying everyone in the low houses has to evacuate tonight." The photo showed brown water swallowing a stop sign, and it was so sharp it could have been taken that afternoon. Marcus wanted to drive over and help his friend Ruben move furniture before the water came, and he was already reaching for his jacket.

Ella's little brother Theo leaned over her shoulder to mimic the face of the frightened man in the photo, but Ella wasn't laughing. Something about the picture tickled her memory. Last summer, when their cousin had forwarded a shark photo that was "definitely this week," Ella had learned about reverse image search from a video she'd watched on a rainy afternoon. You could show the search engine a picture instead of typing words, and it would show you where that photo had appeared online before. If it had shown up years earlier, then someone was passing an old picture off as new. She took Grandpa's phone, pressed the photo until a menu appeared, and chose the search option.

"Dinner's getting cold," Mom said gently, spooning more rice onto Theo's plate because he always ate more when he was nervous. "Marcus, sit. Five minutes." The search results loaded. There it was, the exact same stop sign, the same tilted mailbox, on a news site from years back. "That flood already happened," Ella said. "This photo's from way before today." Grandpa's hand dropped away from his jacket. He called Ruben, and Ruben's voice came through the speaker, warm with relief, saying the river was low and he'd just been down there fishing.

"Where'd you learn that trick?" Grandpa asked, and there was something distinct in his voice, part embarrassment, part pride. "The internet tried to fool you and you caught it." Theo jabbed his elbow toward Ella, then winced and rubbed it, muttering that he'd bruised the cartilage. "That's not where cartilage is," Ella said, but she passed him the last of the bread anyway. Grandpa raised his glass of sweet tea. "To the fact-checker of the family." Ella tapped her fork against her glass until it rang.

Sadie pressed her nose close to the glass wall of the AgZone barn, where the science center kept three pigs beside its farm exhibits. It was the hottest day of the school year, and the field trip had already included a planetarium show and a room full of Tesla coils, but this was the part she had been waiting for. All three pigs lay in a shallow brown puddle, moving so little they looked like statues.

"They're just dirty," said Marcus, elbowing in beside her. "That's all pigs do. Roll in mud because they like being gross."

Sadie wasn't sure. She crouched down and watched. The smallest pig climbed out, trotted to the water trough, drank, then flopped back into the puddle on its side with a satisfied grunt. It did this twice more in ten minutes.
