The line there had only eleven people in it. As he watched, a boy from the concert queue peeled off and walked toward it. Then a couple followed. Then a family of four. It was contagious, the way the little line began to grow while the big one barely shrank.

Raphael's heart pounded. If he stayed, the man in gray might sell out before he reached the window, and he'd have nothing. If he left, he'd see the songs performed, but not the real band. He made himself wait ten more minutes, watching, testing his idea. The concert line stayed long and hungry. The tribute line kept growing. When the man in gray shouted "Last four tickets, eighty each," four hands shot up at the front, and that settled it.

He walked the three blocks, bought a ticket for fifteen, and still had thirty-seven dollars left. Ahead of him in the new line, the two girls from the concert queue had appeared, and the one who'd talked about chips grinned at him. "You switched too?"

"Substitute," Raphael said, holding up his ticket.

The doors opened, and the line surged forward.

The morning after Tuesday's practice, Simon's legs ached so much that walking down the bleacher steps felt like stepping onto two bricks. Marco, who caught for the team, climbed up beside him rubbing his shoulder.

"It's all that lactic acid," Marco said. "It builds up when we work hard."

Simon thought about that while they took infield drills. Practice had ended at five o'clock yesterday. His legs had felt fine at dinner, fine at bedtime, fine when he brushed his teeth this morning. The soreness had shown up today, more than a day later. If something was building up during practice, it seemed like it should hurt right after practice, not the next morning. He decided to run a test on himself. At the end of warmups he did ten full sprints from foul pole to foul pole, harder than he ever worked in a game, and then he waited.

An hour after the sprints, sitting in the dugout with his glove on his knee, he flexed his calves. Nothing hurt. He could feel his pulse in them, and they were warm, but the soreness was not there yet. The next morning it arrived, right on schedule, in both legs at once. It was the same pattern as Tuesday. Whatever was making his muscles sore, it was not still sitting in his legs from the exercise, because an hour after he stopped, everything felt normal. On Thursday he found Marco by the equipment shed, pumping up a flat football that someone had left in the bin. The pump handle squeaked with every stroke, and the ball grew round and firm with each push of air.

"Marco, I checked," Simon said. "I did sprints yesterday and felt fine an hour later. If lactic acid were the problem, it would have to stick around a whole day to make me sore this morning. It doesn't. It goes back to normal levels within about an hour after you exercise."

Marco stopped pumping and squinted at him. "Then what's making my shoulder hurt?"

"I don't know yet. But it isn't that."

Coach Alvarez walked past and told them practice was starting, and whether Marco's throw to second was late or on time, that was her call, though Marco muttered that the whole strike zone was subjective anyway, so why bother arguing. The football, fat with air now, sat on the bench forgotten. Simon picked it up, tossed it once in his hand, and handed it back to Marco.

"Hold onto this," he said. "We're testing your shoulder next."

The trumpet felt like a brick in Anthony's hands, and Mr. Ruiz had already called his name twice. "Measure sixteen, Anthony. From the top." The music classroom smelled like valve oil and old carpet, and the radiators radiated a dry heat that made his fingers stiff. Anthony lifted the horn, blew, and cracked the same high note he had cracked every Tuesday for three weeks.

Beside him, Priya slid her flute onto her lap and leaned over. "You practice, right?" she whispered. "Sunday night? Because you sound great for the first eight measures and then it all falls apart."

"Two hours," Anthony admitted. "Last night. The whole book." He had meant it as proof. Priya's eyebrows went up, and something about her face made him feel like he'd said the wrong thing even though he'd done more work than she had.

At lunch, Anthony sat with his sandwich untouched and thought it through like a math problem. Priya practiced every single day, he knew that, because she'd told the whole section once. Maybe twenty minutes a day. He did two hours in one night. Two hours was six times twenty minutes, so his total time was way more than hers, and yet she played the solo and he cracked notes. Same amount of practice should mean same result. Unless the total wasn't the thing that mattered. Unless the spreading out was the thing. He turned his milk carton around and around. There was only one way to find out.

He made a chart on the back of his science folder and ruled it into small boxes: fifteen minutes before school, ten at night, every day until the next Tuesday. He didn't tell Priya, in case it didn't work. His little sister, Rosa, pounded the piano keys while he practiced, so he started leaving a bag of pretzels on the bench for her, and she settled into playing her own made-up songs at a gentler volume, which helped them both.

The first few days felt slow. He kept missing the same leap in measure sixteen, and his grandfather's old trumpet, a dented brass alloy that had survived two wars and one fall down a staircase, seemed to laugh at him. But on Thursday something odd happened. He picked up the horn, cold, no warm-up except a few long tones, and his fingers found the fingering for the high note before his brain did. He hadn't drilled it harder. He had just... come back to it, again and again, letting each short session do a little work while he slept, ate, walked to school.

On Tuesday, Mr. Ruiz raised his baton. "Measure sixteen. Anthony." The room went quiet. Priya gave him a tiny nod across the stand. Anthony took a breath, thought of nothing at all, and let his fingers go where they had learned to go. The high note came out round and silver, and the kid on trombone, who had declared trumpets obsolete ever since the school bought the low brass section new instruments, said, "Whoa," into his slide.

After class Priya caught him at the door. "So what changed?"

Anthony held up his folder, the chart with its rows of small checkmarks. "Same twenty minutes every day," he said. "Not two hours the night before. Turns out that's the whole trick." Priya grabbed a marker from her pocket and said, "Draw me one."

The photo went up at 9:02 on a Tuesday night: Willow doing her weird victory dance after finishing her science project, socks half off, face scrunched like a raisin. She had meant to send it only to Priya, but her thumb hit the whole group chat instead. Eighteen people. She deleted it within ten minutes, heart hammering, and then sat very still in her dark bedroom, watching the chat scroll on about weekend plans as if nothing had happened. She let herself breathe. Gone meant gone, she decided, and went to sleep.

At lunch the next day, Priya slid her phone across the table. "Look at this." In a different group chat, one Willow wasn't even in, someone had posted the photo with the caption "found this gem." Beneath it, people she barely knew were typing laughing faces and the word "iconic." Willow's stomach dropped. She had deleted it. How could it be here, in a place she couldn't reach?

"I don't get it," she said. "I took it down."

Priya shrugged. "Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot still has it."

Willow stared at the screen. So that was the rule. It wasn't magic; it was a copy, sitting in someone's camera roll, free to travel anywhere. She scrolled up and found the name of the account that had posted it: a boy named Marcus from her math class. She barely knew him. But the photo hadn't appeared out of nowhere, and somebody had to have passed it along.

That night she ran a test, the way she would for a lab. She posted a harmless picture of her cat to the group chat, waited exactly ten minutes, deleted it, and then texted Priya: "Did you screenshot it before it vanished?" Priya sent back a screenshot, timestamp and all, plus a smug message about how the cat deserved a citation for cuteness. Willow laughed, but her mind was working. The copy survived deletion. That was the whole answer. She couldn't unsend the dance photo, and envying people whose embarrassing moments never surfaced wouldn't help either. What she could do was be objective about the situation, like her science teacher kept saying: state the facts, then act.

The next morning she walked straight to Marcus's table in the cafeteria. "You posted my photo in the other chat," she said, keeping her voice level. "I'm not mad, but I want to know who sent it to you, because I deleted it and it still got around." Marcus looked uncomfortable, then held up his phone. "It was Priya. She thought it was hilarious. She said you'd figure it out eventually." Willow turned around. Priya was standing behind her, grinning, phone raised, and Willow's cat was already on the screen.

Riley pressed three tomato seeds into the dark soil of her aunt's farm and patted them down like she was tucking them into bed. She had claimed the plot behind the barn on day one, and by June the seedlings were knee-high, and by July she had green marbles swelling on every branch. Her plan was simple and enormous: sell her tomatoes at the farm stand by the road, next to her aunt's jam and eggs.

The trouble started at the stand on Saturday. A man in a sun hat picked up one of Riley's ripe red tomatoes, weighed it in his palm, and said, "You've got these in the wrong bin, kid. Tomatoes are fruit. They belong with the peaches."

"They're vegetables," Riley said. "They go in the salad, not the fruit bowl."

"Fruit," the man insisted. "Seeds on the inside. That's a fruit."

Riley's cousin Marisol leaned over the cash box. "Then cucumbers are fruit too. And peppers. And pumpkins."

The man laughed. "Pumpkins? Now you're being ridiculous."

Riley wanted to win this. More than that, she wanted to be right, which she had learned was not always the same thing. That night she borrowed her aunt's laptop and typed one question: is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable. The answer made her sit up straight. Botanically, a tomato was a fruit, full stop. But in 1893, the US Supreme Court had ruled in a case called Nix v. Hedden that for import taxes, tomatoes counted as vegetables. She read it twice, then read it to Marisol over the phone.

"Nix v. Hedden," Marisol repeated slowly, like she was chewing it. "So the Court decided taxes, not lunch."

"So both of us were right," Riley said, "and both of us were wrong. Wait till Sun Hat Man hears this."

Sunday morning, Riley made two signs on cardboard, testing her idea before anyone could argue. One read FRUIT, SCIENTIFICALLY SPEAKING. The other read VEGETABLE, ACCORDING TO THE SUPREME COURT. She set them on either side of the tomato bin with an arrow pointing between them. Her aunt walked by, paused, and said, "Very sophisticated display. Now wash your hands, stand hygiene, customers are watching you handle their food."

The man in the sun hat came back for more tomatoes. He read the signs, read them again, and rubbed his jaw. "Huh. I was scientifically right."

"And I was legally right," Riley said. "The Court said they could enforce the tax that way. So the vegetable side wins for money, and the fruit side wins for science."

He bought two pounds and told two other customers on his way out, loudly, that he had lost an argument to an eleven-year-old and enjoyed it. By noon the tomato bin was empty, and Marisol was drawing a third sign that said SOLD OUT, SCIENTIFICALLY AND LEGALLY. Riley ran back to the garden to count what was still ripening on the vines.

"Ten more turning red," she called. "Tell everyone to come back next Saturday."

The bleachers in the gymnasium smelled like floor wax and popcorn, and Victor sat on the front row of seats going over his word list one last time. He had lost the school bee last year on the word "bite," of all things, because in his head he spelled it the way it sounded and forgot the silent e. Ever since then, English spelling felt like a practical joke someone was playing on him.

Two nights before, he'd almost quit studying. He had thrown his pencil across the kitchen table and told his older sister, Dee, that English made no sense and he was going to postpone the whole thing until a language that made sense came along. Dee, who was frugal with sympathy, slid an old library book across the table instead of a speech. "Look at page forty," she said. So he did, and the page told him something he had never heard before. Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift, and the shift happened after spellings had already started to become fixed. That, the book said, was a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation. Victor read the paragraph three times. The letters hadn't been lying all those years. People had just changed the way they said them, like a town that stays on the map after the frontier moves past it. He didn't suddenly like spelling, but he stopped feeling tricked by it, which turned out to matter more.

Now the principal stood at the microphone on the gym floor. "Contestant twelve, Victor Reyes." Victor walked out, his shoes squeaking on the varnish, and stood beside the judge's table.

"Your word is 'subtle.'"

Of course it was. A word with a silent b, sitting there like a taunt. Victor closed his eyes for a second and ran the pattern through his head: old spelling, shifted sound, the b had probably once done its job before the vowels moved on without it. It wasn't a guess anymore. It was the way the language was built.

"S-U-B-T-L-E," he said. "Subtle."

The judge checked her card and nodded. "Correct."

Victor grinned and walked back to his seat. On his way past the folding chairs he caught Dee's eye in the crowd and mouthed, "Great Vowel Shift." She gave him a thumbs up, and the principal cleared her throat for the next word.

Camille counted her coins twice at the Saturday farmers' market, because the tomato seedlings had to go in the ground before the end of the weekend, and she only had six dollars. "How much for two?" she asked the man at the plant table.

"Three dollars, but I have to warn you," he said. "These are the same variety your mom bought last year, and hers didn't do well."

"My tomatoes got brown spots and fell over," Camille said. "All of them. In the back corner, by the fence."

The man rubbed his chin. "You plant tomatoes in that corner every year?"

"Every year. It's the sunniest spot. What else would I put there?" She waited, but he only shrugged and handed her the seedlings, so she paid and carried them home, frowning.

That evening, she sat on the porch steps and thought about her grandmother's farm, which she visited two summers ago. She remembered walking between the long rows while her grandmother pointed. "Tomatoes here this year, beans here, cabbage there," her grandmother had said. "Next summer, they orbit around, each row takes a turn somewhere new." Camille had thought it sounded tedious, all that moving and mapping. Now she wondered why her grandmother bothered.

On Sunday morning, Camille knocked on Mrs. Petrov's door, because Mrs. Petrov had the best garden on the street. "Can I ask you something?" Camille said. "If somebody plants tomatoes in the same corner every year, and they start getting sick, is it the corner's fault?"

Mrs. Petrov set down her watering can. "It could be. My father rotated crops, always, so the same plant family was never grown in the same spot year after year. He said it keeps the soil from making trouble." She tilted her head. "You know what family tomatoes are in?"

"No."

"Same family as peppers. Not the same as beans, or carrots, or lettuce."

Camille walked home fast, carrying the idea like a full bucket. She dug up the wilted tomato stems from the corner and dropped them in the compost pile, where the decomposers would break them down into dark, crumbly soil over the winter. Then she planted her new seedlings in the middle bed, where the beans had grown last summer. It wasn't the sunniest spot, but she could see it from her window, and she marked the corner with a stick.

All through June she measured the plants with a ruler and drew a map of the yard in her notebook. In the top corner she wrote "tomatoes, last year, sick." In the middle bed she wrote "tomatoes, this year," and every week the number of green dots on her sketch grew. On the last day of school, she counted fourteen little hard green tomatoes hanging from healthy stems.

She ran inside to get her brother. "Come look," she said. "And next spring, the tomatoes move again."

Luca set the last cup on the folding table at the edge of the gymnasium, right under the banner that read Science Fair: Set Up by Noon. In front of him stood nine bean plants in paper cups, each one labeled with a sticky note. Three said Fertilizer A, three said Fertilizer B, and one just said Water. His best friend Marcus leaned over the table and squinted.

"Why does that one only get water?" Marcus asked. "That's like entering a race and not running."

"It's called a control group," Luca said. "It gets no change at all, so I can compare everything else against it."

The trouble was the control group was embarrassing him. Every other plant had grown at least a little, and his plain-water bean sat there with the same two sad leaves it had three weeks ago. Priya from his science class walked past, slowed down, and pointed.

"That one's dead, Luca."

"It's not dead, it's the baseline." He said it with more confidence than he felt. For weeks he had wondered whether his fertilizers were actually working. Fertilizer A plants were tall, B plants were medium, and the control was tiny. If he had no control, he would have nothing to measure against. Now he could see that A had grown twice as much as the plain-water plant, and B about half again as much. The tiny plant was doing its job by doing nothing.

Then Judge Okafor stopped at his table, and Luca's reputation as a kid who glued things together the night before felt suddenly endangered. But the judge picked up the control cup and turned it in his hands.

"Tell me about this one," she said.

"It gets no change at all," Luca said. "Plain water, same light, same everything. The tested groups only make sense if I can compare them against it."

The judge nodded slowly and wrote something on her clipboard. "Most students forget that part," she said, and moved on.

Marcus clapped him on the shoulder. "So the dead-looking plant is actually your best one."

"It's the most important one," Luca said. He watered all nine cups, saving the control for last, and straightened its sticky note so the word Water faced the aisle.

Maeva stood in the kitchen with one sock on the tile and one bare foot in the air, frozen mid-step. The school dance was in three hours, and she had a problem with a name: Daniel Okafor. He'd asked her, she'd said yes, and then he'd texted, "Actually I don't know how to dance with a partner. Sorry." She'd stared at the phone so long her mom asked if the screen was broken.

"It's not broken," Maeva said. "It's just wrong."

Her little brother Theo, who had recently convinced Dad to install a basketball hoop over the garage door, was dribbling a ball against the refrigerator. "Dances are controversial anyway," he said. "Jayden says you have to hold a girl's hand and it's a hygiene hazard."

"You don't know anything."

"I know you're standing on one foot."

She put her foot down. Then she picked up her phone again, not for Daniel's text, but to search. Last summer at the community picnic she'd seen everybody from grandmas to six-year-olds doing the same steps in rows, and nobody had seemed paired up. She found a video from the picnic and watched it twice. Every person faced the same way, toward the picnic table with the lemonade. Every person repeated the same set of steps, over and over, a grapevine to the right, a clap, a stomp, a quarter turn. Nobody touched anybody. She tested her idea right there on the kitchen tile: she followed along, stumbled, tried again, and by the fourth repeat her feet knew the pattern without her watching.

"Whoa," Theo said. "What's that?"

"It's called a line dance," Maeva said. "A whole group does the same steps, facing the same direction, and you don't need a partner at all."

"Prove it."

She held out her hand for the ball, set it on the counter, and started the video from the beginning. "Just copy me." Theo knocked over a chair on the grapevine and laughed so hard he missed the clap, but on the second run he made it all the way to the quarter turn. On the third run they did it without the video, both facing the window, both stomping at the same moment.

At the dance, the gym was hot and loud and half the seventh grade stood along the wall like wallpaper. Daniel was there, arms crossed, alone. Maeva took a breath, walked over, and said, "You don't need a partner. You just need about four steps. Watch my feet."

The DJ started a song with a beat she knew. She stepped out onto the floor, faced the stage, and began.

"Like this?" Daniel said, two beats behind her.

"Just like that."

Elliot stared at the two columns Mr. Ruiz had taped to the whiteboard, and both looked exactly the same to him. By Friday, every sixth grader had to bring in a chart comparing what fifty dollars would become in a savings account after five years, and Mr. Ruiz had made it clear he would call on people at random to explain the difference between simple and compound interest. Elliot's chart showed the simple kind: two dollars fifty each year, added up again and again, until his pencil marks marched across the page in a flat, even line. The compound column was the one that made no sense to him.

"It's like this," said Maya, dropping into the seat beside him. She opened her notebook to a page covered in tiny sketches of paintbrushes. "The compound one goes up faster. Look, here, and here, and here." Her finger tapped the gaps, which grew wider every year. Maya wanted the class prize, a twenty-five-dollar bookstore gift card, because she'd been saving all fall for a real set of watercolors and was still nine dollars short. A gift card would finish it.

"That's what my dilemma is," Elliot said. "If both accounts pay the same percent, why does one end up with more? It's like the money is growing on money that didn't exist yet." He copied both columns onto graph paper, and then, because he wanted to clarify it for himself, he wrote out every single interest payment, year by year, for both accounts. The simple payments never changed: two dollars fifty, two dollars fifty, two dollars fifty. The compound payments did. Three dollars twelve. Three dollars ninety. Each one bigger than the last, even though nobody ever added a penny to the account.

"Wait," Maya said, leaning over his page. "Say that part again."

"The interest payments themselves got bigger," Elliot said slowly, reading his own numbers. "Even though we added nothing." He underlined the column where each new payment was calculated on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself started earning interest. That was the rule. That was the whole difference. The simple account only ever paid on the original fifty, which was why its line lay flat as a ruler while the compound line bent slowly upward.

On Thursday night Maya left a folded note in his locker: "I showed my cousin the chart and she says we're right. She has a savings account and one year her interest payment grew a little even though she added nothing to the account. Want to present together tomorrow? P.S. The art store closes at six on Saturdays." The hallway around the lockers felt almost desolate at that hour, empty and echoing, but Elliot read the note twice and grinned at the ceiling both times.

On Friday they stood at the front with their chart, and when Mr. Ruiz called on Maya to explain the compound column, she pointed at the growing payments and said, "Each one is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest." Mr. Ruiz wrote a big check mark on his clipboard. When the bell rang, Maya held up the gift card they'd split toward the watercolors and said, "Saturday, nine a.m., art store. You're carrying the paint."

The last three gummy bears in the bag dwindled to two, then one, and then just a red smudge on Maya's thumb while she stared out the window of the minivan. Her mom was driving them to Priya's house for a sleepover, and her little brother, Theo, was conducting his own campaign from the back seat. "Can we listen to my dinosaur podcast? Please? I've been waiting all week."

"One episode," Mom said, "after Maya tells me why she's smiling at her phone like that."

Maya wasn't smiling at her phone exactly. She was smiling at a thought. Last weekend at Priya's house, Priya had mentioned that her older sister got her first period at fourteen, which had surprised them both, because Zoe's older sister had gotten hers at eleven. Fourteen and eleven. That was a pretty big spread, and Maya couldn't stop wondering about it. Was there a normal age, or was it all just random? She couldn't see the answer anywhere, but maybe she could find it hiding in the pattern, the way you figure out a rule in math class.

So she had made a survey. She had texted ten friends and asked, "How old was your mom or your sister when she got her first period?" The replies had rolled in all afternoon: eleven, thirteen, twelve, fourteen, ten, twelve, eleven, fifteen, twelve, thirteen. Maya counted them twice on the van's armrest. Four of them were twelve, which was more than any other number, so the middle of the pile sat right there. But the edges stretched all the way from ten to fifteen. There was a center, and there was a range around it, wide as a river.

"Mom," Maya said, leaning between the seats, "when you were a kid, did anyone ever tell you the usual age for getting your first period?"

Mom glanced in the mirror. "My health teacher said something once, but I don't remember it. Why?"

"Priya's sister told her that some big CDC survey found the median age is about twelve," Maya said, "with a wide normal range around it. And guess what my survey says."

"Twelve?" Mom guessed.

"Twelve, with a range from ten to fifteen." Maya held up her phone like evidence in court. "My own data matches a giant government survey. Ten whole people." She felt a little thrill, like she had pulled back a curtain on something invisible. Her own body hadn't started yet, and somehow that felt less like being behind and more like being somewhere inside a wide, ordinary river.

Theo tugged her sleeve. "Enough period talk. Dinosaurs. Now."

"One episode," Mom said, laughing, and pressed play.

Theo leaned back, triumphant, and Maya gave his rebellious, podcast-demanding hand a pat. "Fine," she said, "but when it's over, I'm telling you about medians. It's basically the T. rex of numbers."

Kaylee sat on the crackly paper of the exam chair and stared at the chart across the room, where the third line had gone soft and blurry no matter how hard she squinted. The optometrist swung a heavy metal machine in front of her face and clicked lenses into it, one after another. "Better or worse?" she kept asking, and each time Kaylee answered, the world sharpened a little more. When the chair sank with a hiss, Kaylee glanced down and saw a small brass valve on the side, the kind that let air or fluid in and out. The optometrist must have noticed her looking, because she said, "Handy, right? I can lower it for kids and raise it back for adults."

In the frame room afterward, Kaylee tried on pair after pair while her mom watched from a stool by the window. Everything was too big, too round, or too much like something a grandmother would wear. Finally she found a thin wire pair with purple at the hinges, and the optician said they were titanium, durable enough to survive being dropped, which mattered, because Kaylee dropped things constantly.

"These are the ones," she said, turning her head in the little mirror. Then a thought hit her so hard she said it out loud. "Wait. What did people do before glasses existed? Like, in ancient times? Everyone who couldn't see just... couldn't read?"

The optician hummed and straightened a display of cases. "Well, glasses weren't actually that old an invention, if you think about it. The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy, around 1290."

"Thirteen ninety?" Kaylee said, gripping the mirror's edge.

"Twelve ninety. Central Italy."

Kaylee did the math, and the math made her dizzy. People had been writing things down for thousands of years before that, and for most of that time, anyone with eyes like hers would have had to hold a page practically against her nose, or give up entirely. She began to elaborate her theory out loud: that must be why some old paintings showed scholars holding books at arm's length, or squinting like she did at the whiteboard last Tuesday when she copied the homework wrong and got a zero she didn't deserve. That zero was the reason she was here. She'd spent a month blaming the teacher's handwriting before admitting the real cause was hiding behind her own eyeballs, invisible until she finally tested the idea by sitting in the front row and getting everything right.

"So for thousands of years," she said slowly, "everyone who needed glasses just didn't get any."

Her mom came over and rested a hand on her shoulder. "And now you do. That's something."

The optician slid the purple-hinged pair into a case and wrote the pickup date on a slip. "Next Thursday, after school."

Kaylee folded the slip into her pocket, right next to the crumpled zero she'd kept as evidence.

"Thursday," she said. "I'm going to see everything."

Jacob wanted the good table, the one by the window with the kettle and the plate of samosas, and the problem was that Table One had already claimed it. The community centre's heritage night had split into four tables for the games, and the split had been done by Mr. Okafor pulling names out of a cereal bowl, which felt fair and turned out not to be.

By seven thirty, Table Two, Jacob's table, was chanting "Two, two, two" at Pictionary. Table Three had a secret handshake nobody could have learned in two hours, because two hours was all that had existed of Table Three. Table Four had started calling Table One "the window hogs." Jacob had been dumped into Table Two between Priya, who was telling everyone about her grandmother's Diwali lamps with meticulous, loving detail, and a kid named Marcus who claimed his family invented barbecue, which Jacob doubted but let slide.

"We've known each other since six o'clock," Jacob said to Priya. "Why are we cheering like we're a tribe?"

"Because we're Table Two," she said, as if that explained anything.

It bothered him the way a loose tooth bothers you. He had read something once, in his sister's psychology book, about a man named Tajfel who ran experiments where people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random. Jacob had skipped past it at the time. Now he watched Marcus guard the felt-tip pens from Table Three like they were family heirlooms, and thought: that's us. We're the experiment. So he tested it. He stood on a chair and announced that the tables were random, that Mr. Okafor had drawn every name out of a bowl, that Table Two was not destiny.

It did not help. "So what," Marcus said. "We're still the best random table." Table Two applauded him. Jacob climbed down, the embarrassment warm in his ears, and considered the possibility that knowing about a thing does not switch it off.

But Priya had gone quiet, and when the samosa plate came out, she carried two over to the kids at Table One and asked what was in their dishes, and they turned out to be things their grandmothers made, with stories attached, and Jacob followed her. Mr. Okafor wandered by and tried to incorporate the moment into a speech about community, and Jacob said, "We're just eating, sir." The window table had room after all. Marcus arrived last, plate out, and said, "This doesn't make us friends."
"We're not tables," said Priya. "We're just hungry people near a window."
Marcus bit into a samosa. "Okay," he said. "That one's mine."

The trumpet wasn't working out, so Hailey switched to the flute, and now she had a new problem: reading music. She sat in the corner of the community center music room with a folded sheet of paper, glaring at the five lines and the fancy swirl at the start of every line. Her friend Marisol came over and dropped into the chair beside her.

"You look like the paper insulted you," Marisol said.

"I can find middle C. That's it. Then everything else is guessing." Hailey tapped the swirl. "And this thing just sits there like it's decoration."

Marisol leaned in. "My cousin plays piano. She calls that the G clef."

"The what?"

"G clef. That's the other name for it."

Hailey frowned at the symbol. A clef called G should mean something. She grabbed a pencil and copied the swirl onto her notebook, big and sloppy. Then she laid her flute sheet next to it and traced the curl slowly with her pencil tip, the way you'd trace a maze. The swirl looped around, dipped down, and curled back up, and where it curled it wrapped around the second line from the bottom. She checked her beginner book's note chart. The note on that line was G.

"No way," she whispered. The clef wasn't decoration. It was a marker, curling around the exact line where G lived, like a ring on a finger.

She tested it. G on the line, one space above was A, the line above that was B, and so on up the ladder. She played the little exercise from her book, and the notes came out in the right order for the first time. She played it again, faster, and grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

Marisol pointed at the door. "Little kids are coming for vaccine day. The nurse is setting up in the big room, so we have ten more minutes before they kick us out."

"Ten minutes is plenty," Hailey said. "It's not trivial to me. This was the whole wall in my way."

A small boy in a dinosaur shirt peeked into the music room while waiting for his shot, looking scared. Marisol waved him over. Hailey held up her notebook, showed him the swirl, and traced the curl around the second line. "See the loop? It's holding one spot so you never get lost." The boy forgot to be nervous long enough to trace it with his own finger.

When the nurse called his name, he walked out taller, and Marisol hurried after him with his jacket. Hailey packed up her flute, but she tore the notebook page out first and pressed it flat inside her book, the page she knew she would cherish on every practice day to come.

"Same time Thursday?" Marisol called from the doorway.

"Bring your cousin's number," Hailey said, tucking the flute under her arm. "I have questions."

Lily sat cross-legged on Maya's bedroom floor with Maya's phone balanced on her knees, tapping through photos from Saturday. There was the one of Maya at the ice cream place, grinning with a double scoop. There was the one at the mall fountain. And there was the one Lily had taken of Maya outside Maya's own front door, because Maya had insisted the lighting was perfect.

"Send me the fountain one," Lily said, then stopped. "Wait. How many people can see these?"

"Just us. And my cousins. And probably the group chat." Maya flopped backward onto her pillow. "And that game I play, Frost Fox. It kind of posts stuff sometimes."

"Frost Fox posts your photos?"

"No, no. It posts where I am. Like, 'Maya unlocked the Glacier Zone at Maple Mall!' My aunt commented on it from two states away. She said, weren't you supposed to be at soccer?"

Lily scrolled to the game. A little map pin blinked beside a picture of a fox in a scarf, and next to the fox, Maya's last three locations were listed like trophies. Lily thought about the coyote that had wandered into their neighborhood last winter, how it had seemed to hibernate somewhere unseen all day and appear only at dusk, always knowing exactly which trash cans to visit. Someone had told her the coyote followed patterns, not luck. This felt like that, but backwards: the fox was following Maya.

"Can I check something?" Lily asked. She opened the phone's settings and hunted through screens until she found a list of apps with little arrows beside them. She recognized one arrow right away, because her dad had pointed at his own phone once and said, "That arrow means an app knows where you are." She tapped Frost Fox.

Three choices sat on the screen. Never. While using the app. Always.

"It's on Always," Lily said slowly. "That means it knew where you were even when you weren't playing."

Maya sat up so fast her ponytail whipped around. "You can pick?"

"You can pick for every app, one by one." Lily turned the phone so Maya could see. "My phone asks me the same thing. I always hit Always because I don't read the box. I just want the game to start."

"That's why Frost Fox knew I skipped soccer," Maya said, sounding both horrified and delighted. She jabbed the screen and switched the game to While Using. Then, defiant, she switched it to Never, just to watch the little map pin blink out.

Later, Lily texted her from home: did the fox die? Maya sent back a photo of Frost Fox wearing a blindfold, standing in an empty snowfield, with the caption "he asks where u at and I say none of ur business." Lily laughed out loud, then opened her own phone and went down her list of apps, one by one, arrow by arrow.

The last one, before bed, was a flashlight app. Always.

She stared at it. "You don't even know where I am," she told it, and pressed Never.

Alexis had spent every summer at Abuela's house since she was six, and every summer the streets had felt like a map she carried in her head. This summer Abuela had moved to a new neighborhood, and the map was gone. On the first morning, Abuela handed her a canvas bag. "Take these to the donation bin on Calle Rosa," she said. "And take the phone. In case."

Alexis did not take the phone. She had spent the school year failing Spanish, and she had decided the class was useless, so she left the phone on the table to prove she could manage without it. She walked three blocks carrying the bag of clothes she was meant to donate, and then the streets stopped matching anything Abuela had told her. A man was sweeping in front of a shop with green awnings. She stopped, and the dilemma was simple: ask in English and get nowhere, or try the Spanish she had decided she didn't have.

"¿Dónde está Calle Rosa?" she said.

The man answered fast, too fast, and then slowed down. "Sí. La primera calle a la izquierda." He pointed with his broom, but the street split ahead into two left turns, and she could not tell which one he meant. She knew izquierda meant left, that much had stuck. But which left came first?

She tried the other half of what her teacher had drilled into them, the part she'd thought she'd never use: repeat it back. "¿La primera calle a la izquierda?"

"Sí," the man said. "La primera." He held up one finger.

Alexis looked at the split. One left turn was really just a driveway into a parking area. The other was an actual street with a sign. If the driveway didn't count as a street, then the real street was the first one, the one with the sign. She said "Gracias," walked on, and watched. The driveway went into a lot full of cars. It was not a street. The sign at the second left said Rosa.

The bin stood at the corner, next to a bakery. She pushed the clothes in, and the bakery door swung open behind her. It was the man with the broom, holding a paper bag. "You found it," he said in English. "First street on the left."

"You speak English?" Alexis said.

"All my life." He shrugged. "Your grandmother asked me to keep an eye out. She said you'd refuse the phone." He held up the bag. "Come, she ordered bread. And she says I make the best empanadas in the city, but that is subjective."

Alexis laughed and followed him down Rosa. On Monday, she decided, she would ask Abuela to speak only Spanish at breakfast. She took out her phrase list on the walk home and read it twice.

The group chat lit up at 4:02 on a Saturday: "Dude, why are you at GameStop? I thought you were broke." Brayden stared at his phone. He had told nobody he was going to the mall. He had left the house saying he was "going for a walk," which was technically true if you counted walking to the bus. He typed back, "how do u know where I am," and Marcus answered with a screenshot of a map. There was a little cartoon face on it, standing right on top of the GameStop dot at the Westfield mall. Brayden looked at the ceiling of the store, then at the exit, as if the answer might be floating somewhere between them.

"Bro, that's the Snap Map," Marcus wrote. "It shows your real-time location to your friends on a map." Brayden read it twice. Real-time. He thought about all the times he'd wandered around after school, killing time before his mom got home, and how somebody could have been watching a little cartoon version of him do it the whole while. Weird feeling, like discovering his shoes had been narrating his day out loud.

He decided to test it. It seemed like an inevitable part of figuring things out; you couldn't just panic, you had to run an experiment. His technique was simple: he would walk from GameSpot to the pretzel stand two stores down, and if the cartoon face moved too, then the map was tracking him right now, not showing some old, harmless record. He bought a pretzel he didn't even want, mostly for cover, and stood under the big yellow sign eating it with the concentration of a scientist. Marcus sent a new screenshot. The face was on the pretzel stand. "Enjoy your pretzel," he wrote, adding three crying-laughing faces.

Brayden nearly choked. "This is so creepy," he typed with one thumb, pretzel in the other hand. But another thought itched at him, the curious kind. If it knew where he was, who else could see it? Marcus was his friend, sure. But the settings had layers, he'd heard people mention "friends of friends" like it was nothing. Somewhere out there, maybe strangers were watching the little cartoon face eat its little cartoon pretzel. He wondered how many eyes a dot could collect before the dot's owner even noticed.

Back home, he dug into the app's settings until he found the map options and switched his sharing to Ghost Mode. Then he typed into the group chat, "ok new rule, if anyone knows where I am, it's because I told them." Marcus replied with a single face, the one wearing sunglasses, and a message: "Meet me at the arcade in ten?"

Brayden grabbed his jacket. "Bring quarters," he wrote back, and hit send.

Nora slid her vocabulary list across the desk and sighed. Fifteen word histories by Friday, and the definitions in the back of the book were so tedious that her eyes kept sliding off the page. The last word was "propaganda," and she almost skipped it, except that word had been bothering her all week. Marcus's posters for class president were everywhere, and something about them felt off, like a picture hung slightly crooked.

One poster said EVERYBODY'S CHOOSING MARCUS, with a long line of smiling kids drawn underneath it. Another called his opponent's ideas "dangerous" and "reckless," words that sounded exciting but meant nothing exactly. The biggest poster of all showed TJ, the eighth grader who could dunk, holding a thumbs-up: "TJ says Marcus is the real deal." Nora couldn't point to a single lie in any of them, and that was what made her uneasy. She flipped to the library's dictionary of word origins and ran her finger down the page.

There it was. The word came from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622. Nora read the line twice, then copied it into her notebook. She raised her hand before she could talk herself out of it. "Mr. Reyes, I found where propaganda comes from. The Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622." A boy near the window snickered, and Nora felt her face go hot, but she kept going. "So it just meant spreading an idea around. It didn't start out as a bad word."

That night she tested a theory. If Marcus's posters worked by making people feel like everyone else had already decided, then a poster that pointed at the trick itself might break the spell. She made her own poster, plain and loud: "WHY DOES IT SAY EVERYBODY? ASK SOMEBODY." Underneath she drew a tiny panda chewing bamboo, with the caption "Pandas are herbivores. They eat facts, not hype." It was a strange joke, and she knew it, but she taped it up anyway, right between two of Marcus's.

By lunch, kids were standing in front of it. "What's a fact panda?" someone asked, and Nora said, "It only eats things that are actually true." Priya, who had been on the fence for a week, laughed and said, "Okay, that poster just got my vote for best poster. Marcus's are all sparkle and no sandwich." Marcus himself came down the hall, stopped, and read it twice. He peeled off his EVERYBODY'S CHOOSING MARCUS poster and looked at Nora over the top of it. "So what would a poster look like," he asked, "if I actually told people what I want to do?"

The drive to the coast had taken six hours, and Ethan had spent most of it reading the state park brochure he found in the glove box. His sister Maya said he was biased because he'd already decided the beach would be better than their trip to the mountains last summer. "You only like it because you found that sand dollar," she said. Ethan put the brochure in his back pocket anyway.

That evening a ranger named Ms. Okafor gathered everyone at the fire ring behind the dunes for a talk about national parks. "Whoever answers the final question wins a junior ranger badge," she announced. "The question comes in ten minutes, at sunset, so talk it over now." Ethan's dad immediately claimed he knew everything about parks. Maya said the first one was probably Yosemite. Dad shook his head and said the Grand Canyon, since it was the biggest.

Ethan didn't shout out a guess. Instead he thought about what he'd read in the brochure while the waves hissed in the dark behind them. There had been a whole paragraph about Yellowstone, and he was almost sure he'd seen a date there, and a president's name. It felt like remembering where he'd left his shoes: he couldn't see the page, but he could picture sitting on it. He tested the memory by saying it out loud under his breath. "March 1, 1872. Grant." It sounded like something he'd actually read, not something he'd invented.

The sun touched the water and Ms. Okafor held up her hand. "Final question. Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when which president signed it into law?" Dad whispered "Roosevelt." Maya whispered "Lincoln." Ethan raised his hand so fast he knocked over his cup of cocoa.

"Ulysses S. Grant," he said. Ms. Okafor smiled and pinned the badge to his jacket. Dad threw his hands up. "I was going to say Grant," he said. "You were going to say Roosevelt," said Maya. "I was collecting my thoughts," said Dad, and everyone laughed, even Ethan.

Walking back to the cabin, Maya poked the badge. "Fine, the beach trip is better than the mountains. For now." Ethan crouched by the tideline, where a dead crab was slowly starting to decompose among the kelp, and picked up a spiral shell. "Trade you," he said, holding it out. "Badge for shell." Maya snatched it and ran up the dunes shouting, "No take-backs!"

At dinner Tyler kept glancing at his older sister Priya, who was shoving noodles around her plate with a textbook propped against the milk carton. "Chapter five," she groaned. "There's this test from 1985, the Sally-Anne test, and there's a quiz on it tomorrow."

"Sally Anne is a doll," Priya said. "Sally puts her marble in a basket and leaves. While she's gone, someone moves the marble to a box. Then kids have to say where Sally will look for it." She tapped the page. "Kids from about age four usually say she'll look where she left it, the basket, not where it was moved. Little kids just can't believe Sally could be wrong about something."

Tyler looked down the table at their cousin Marcus, who was four and a half and busy building a tower out of sugar packets. "Wait," Tyler said. "You mean Marcus doesn't know that other people can be wrong?"

"He doesn't know that other people can believe something false," Priya said. "Nobody at this table believes the same thing about the meatloaf, and we all heard Mom's opinion on the school funding census at the last town meeting, so you know we're all capable of opposing each other politely." She grinned at Mom, who had spent two weeks arguing for a recount.

"Marcus," Tyler said, sliding a fork out of the drawer and hiding a sugar packet under it. "I'm putting my treasure under the fork. Watch." Marcus watched with enormous eyes. "Now I'm going to the kitchen. Don't touch it." Tyler walked out, stood against the refrigerator for ten seconds, and listened. When he came back, the fork was in exactly the same place, but Marcus's elbow was suspiciously close and one sugar packet was missing from the tower. Tyler knelt down. "Marcus. Where am I going to look for my treasure?"

Marcus pointed at the drawer. "You're gonna look in the drawer, 'cause you didn't see."

Tyler sat back on his heels. He'd been sure Marcus would point at the fork, because that's where Tyler had put the treasure, and that's what mattered, right? But Marcus had tracked the whole thing: Tyler left, Tyler didn't see the move, so Tyler's mind still held the old picture. Four and a half years old, and he already knew that what you saw wasn't the same as what somebody else knew. Priya was the one who'd gotten it wrong, at least about Marcus.

"Priya," Tyler called. "Wrong kid. He passed." He turned back to Marcus, took the fork, and lifted it slowly. The sugar packet was gone from underneath, and in its place sat a folded napkin with "SORRY" written in wobbling crayon letters.

"You can have this instead," Marcus said, holding out the sugar packet with both hands. "I only borrowed it."

The lights went out while Alicia was watering her grandmother's tomato plants, and the porch swallowed itself into darkness so fast it felt like the evening had decided to accelerate. She stood in the backyard holding the dripping can, listening. No hum from the air conditioner. No glow from the kitchen window.

"Grandma?" she called, and heard shuffling inside. Her grandmother found her at the back door with a flashlight, its beam small and unimpressive next to the extravagant chandelier that hung, useless and dark, in the hallway. Grandma's cordless phone sat in its cradle on the counter, and when she picked it up and pressed talk, nothing happened. Not even static.

"Battery must be dead," Grandma said, tapping it against her palm.

Alicia took the phone and turned it over. "It's plugged into the wall," she said slowly. "The base is, anyway. If the power's out, maybe the phone isn't dead. Maybe the outlet is." Grandma raised an eyebrow, which was her way of saying go on. Alicia set the handset down and stood still, thinking. The phone needed the house's electricity. That part made sense. But something nagged at her, an old memory of phones with curly cords and no plugs at all. How had those ever worked? It seemed like a paradox, a thing with no power cord that still had power. Unless the power came from somewhere else.

"Grandma, did you ever have one of those wall phones? The kind with the cord?"

"Kitchen. Still there, behind the biscuit tin. I keep it because I hate throwing away anything that works."

Alicia pushed the tin aside and found it, a heavy cream-colored phone bolted to the wall with a cord coiled like a spring. No plug, no battery compartment. She lifted the receiver and held it to her ear, half expecting silence. Instead, a dial tone buzzed, steady and alive, as if the power cut had never happened. She nearly dropped it.

"Grandma! It works!" she shouted. "The line gets its power from the phone company, not from our house. That's why it still works."

"Well, I'll be," Grandma said, and then, because she was Grandma, "Call your mother before she worries."

Alicia dialed, and when her mother answered on the first ring, breathless and already reaching for her car keys, Alicia had to talk fast to keep her from driving over in the dark. "We're fine. We have flashlights, the stove is gas, and I found a phone that doesn't need electricity at all." Outside, a neighbor's generator roared to life, and somewhere down the block a dog barked at it. Alicia sat on the kitchen floor, the coiled cord stretching to reach her, and told her mother about the tomato plants she'd been watering when the world went dark. The dial tone hummed softly under her voice the whole time.

Gabriel had babysat exactly nobody before Saturday, which was why Mrs. Yi leaving him alone with eight-month-old Penny felt like being handed a live grenade and a smile. The instructions on the fridge ran to two pages, front and back, in handwriting so small he had to lean in until his nose nearly touched the paper. Behind him, from the playpen, Penny made a sound like a small, judgmental owl.

Everything went fine for an hour. Penny ate her cereal, gravity took its usual cut, and Gabriel learned that a baby could inhale a fistful of banana faster than he would have believed possible. Then Penny stopped eating. She pressed her lips together and turned her face away from the spoon with the determination of a soccer goalie defending a net. Gabriel tried the airplane trick, the choo-choo trick, and the desperate humming trick. Nothing. He looked at the cereal, which was plain oat mush, and thought the problem was obvious: it was boring. He got the honey jar from the pantry and had the lid half off when he noticed a line at the bottom of page two, underlined twice.

No honey, it said. Not until she's over 12 months. Bacteria spores in it can grow in her gut. That last word had sent Mrs. Yi's pen skidding. Gabriel stood there with the jar, rereading it. He'd never once thought of honey as something that could hide trouble. It just sat there looking golden and harmless, like a trap designed by someone with a grudge against toast. He put the lid back on and returned it to the pantry, feeling the embarrassment arrive about one second too late to stop him from having opened it in the first place.

Penny still refused the cereal, so Gabriel got systematic. If the problem wasn't taste, maybe it was temperature. He touched the bowl: cold. The instructions said warm it for twenty seconds, and he'd been so busy with airplanes he'd skipped that step. He tested the idea, microwaved the bowl, stirred it, and offered the spoon again. Penny considered him with the flat stare of an emperor, then opened her mouth like a garage door. The entire bowl vanished in four minutes.

Mrs. Yi came home to find the kitchen clean, the honey jar in its exact spot in the pantry, though it was turned two degrees from where it had been, and Penny asleep in the playpen. "How was she?" she asked.

"Fine," Gabriel said. "Great, actually." He did not mention the honey, or page two, or the fact that his heart had gone briefly extinct in his chest when he'd read it. He took his twenty dollars, and at the door he paused. "Next time could you underline that honey part at the top? Maybe in red."

Tristan discovered the problem at seven o'clock on Tuesday morning, in the driveway, with the car still cold. He had been singing along with the radio, loudly, the way nobody could hear him, when the word "tonight" came out in two pieces. The "to" was high and normal, and the "night" dropped straight down into some gravelly cave he had never visited before. He tried it again. "Tonight." It cracked again, right in the middle, like a stick snapping.

In the car on the way to school, his sister Maya noticed him experimenting. "Why do you keep saying 'ahhh' like a dying robot?" she asked, buckling her seatbelt. Tristan ignored her, which was not easy, because the car was small and Maya was never indifferent to a chance to tease him. He was busy. He hummed a low note, then a high one, then the note in between where the break lived. It was like there were two voices inside him, an old one and a new one, and no bridge between them yet.

By Thursday he had begun to classify the evidence. Low notes worked fine. Talking worked fine, mostly. High notes were the problem, and the break always happened in the same narrow spot. Dad drove them to choir practice that evening, and Tristan spent the whole ride testing his newest idea: if he sang quietly enough, maybe the crack couldn't get enough air to happen. He whispered scales in the back seat. Maya put in her earbuds. "It still cracks," Tristan reported, half thrilled, half annoyed. "Just quieter."

At practice, Marcus got the solo in the new song, and Marcus sailed through the verse and then hit the big high note at the end, and his voice split exactly the way Tristan's had. Mr. Ruiz raised one hand. "Marcus's larynx is growing," he said, "so the vocal folds inside it are getting longer and thicker, and they may crack while that happens." Marcus turned red, but Tristan nearly fell off the riser. Folds. Longer and thicker. That was it. That was the hidden machine.

On the drive home, Tristan leaned forward between the front seats. "Dad, the vocal folds get longer and thicker, and that's why the voice drops. It's like a guitar string, kind of. Except inside." Dad glanced at him in the mirror. "A metaphor," Dad said. "Sure. Every guy in this car went through it." Maya pulled out one earbud. "Even Dad cracked?" "Ask your grandmother," Dad said. "I once scared the dog."

Tristan sat back. The car hummed along the dark road, and he hummed with it, low, in the new voice, the one with no cracks in it at all. He was already planning the choir solo for next year. "Marcus," he said to the window, "your solo is mine in October."

Georgia had measured her bean plants twice, and both times the numbers made her stomach drop. The six pots on the windowsill, the ones she had watered every morning with the special fertilizer her grandmother sent, had grown three inches in two weeks. That was the good part. The bad part was the question her friend Priya had asked at lunch: "Grown three inches compared to what?"

Now, in the kitchen, Georgia laid her science notebook on the counter and stared at her chart. Six plants, all fertilized, all tall. Beside the sink her little brother Theo was gluing popsicle sticks into what he claimed was an authentic Viking longship, though it looked more like a raft with ambitions. "You keep frowning at that notebook," he said. "Is it going to bite you?"

"Priya says my project doesn't prove anything. Maybe the beans would have grown three inches anyway." Georgia tapped her pencil against the page. Her instinct told her the fertilizer worked, but instinct wasn't allowed in the results section. "If I can't compare them to something, I can't tell."

Theo set down his glue. "Compare them to what, the Viking ship?"

"No. Beans." She went quiet, and then the idea landed all at once, so big she actually laughed. "More beans. I'll start six new pots, same soil, same window, same water, everything the same. The only difference is the fertilizer. That way, if the fertilized ones grow more, I know it's the fertilizer doing it, and not the window or the soil or dumb luck."

Theo's eyes lit up. "Can I be in charge of the new ones? I'll water them at the same time you water yours. We can coordinate it, like eight o'clock every morning before the bus." He was already pulling the bag of dried beans from the cupboard, the one Mom used for soup, and lining up six clean yogurt cups on the counter. He filled them with soil from the same bag Georgia had used, patting each one down twice, checking her old pots to match the depth.

"Careful," Georgia said. "The new ones get plain water only. Not one drop of the fertilizer, or it ruins everything." Theo nodded so seriously she believed him. He had wanted his own job for the project ever since she'd started it, and now he had one that actually mattered.

Two weeks later, they knelt side by side at the windowsill with the ruler between them. The fertilized plants had grown three and a half inches. Theo's plain-water beans, the ones nobody had fed anything special, had grown two. Georgia wrote the numbers down twice to be sure, then grinned at him. "Yours are the control group," she said. "The ones treated exactly like mine except for the fertilizer."

Theo straightened up like a soldier receiving a medal. "The control group," he repeated, tasting the words. "Can I put that on the label? In Viking letters?"

Lily slid three dollars across the lunch table and watched Maya count out the last two bracelets from her shoebox. By Tuesday they were gone, and Maya had raised almost enough money to enroll in the Saturday art class she'd been talking about since September.

On Wednesday, four sixth graders walked into homeroom with sandwich bags full of woven bracelets, each one tagged with a price of three dollars. By Friday there were nine sellers, and the hallway outside the science room looked like a tiny market. Nobody was buying much, though, because everyone who wanted a bracelet already had one, or was now making them at home from leftover embroidery thread. Maya sat on the radiator, staring at her empty box and then at the crowded hallway. "Nobody wants mine anymore," she said, "and I still need eight dollars for art class."

Lily couldn't stop watching the sellers, wondering what had changed. Nothing about the bracelets themselves had changed. Was it just that there were so many now? She pulled out her notebook and did something systematic: a column for each seller, the price they asked, and how many bracelets they sold that day. A pattern jumped out by afternoon. The kids charging three dollars sold almost nothing. One boy who had dropped his price to one dollar had sold five. The same bracelets, the same hallway, different numbers. It was like the model wind turbine in Mr. Okafor's room, which spun faster or slower depending on something you couldn't see from across the room, the wind. Lily couldn't see a "price," but she could see what it did.

She shared the notebook with Maya. "When your bracelets were three dollars and there were only a few, everybody wanted them. Then the high price made selling seem worth it, so a bunch of people started making them. Now there are tons." Maya squinted at the columns. "So there's too many for the price they're asking." Lily nodded. "And that boy with the one-dollar sign sold out."

Monday morning, Maya taped a new sign to her shoebox: BRACELETS, ONE DOLLAR, PICK YOUR OWN COLORS. She let buyers choose thread from a box, since everyone else's were the same three patterns. By lunch she had sold eleven, and two of the three-dollar sellers had quietly crossed out their signs and written smaller numbers. After school Maya counted her crumpled bills on the bus, smoothed them flat, and grinned. "Nine to go." Lily looked out the window at the turbines spinning on the ridge past the soccer field, their long white arms turning at different speeds, and started a fresh page in her notebook.

The pharmacy smelled like soap and cough drops, and Kate stood by the shelf of shoe inserts while her mother picked up a prescription. In the basket under her arm sat a box of plasters, a comb, and the money she had saved for the display rack behind the counter. That was the problem: the pharmacy sold arch supports, but it did not sell what she actually needed, which was a reason her brother Tom's shoes had stopped fitting twice since September while his jeans still fit fine.

Kate turned the idea over while her mother talked to the pharmacist about antihistamines. Her premise was simple: if Tom's feet were growing, the rest of him should be growing too, at the same time. That was how she had always assumed growing worked, everything at once, like inflating a balloon. But the evidence did not fit. His trainers were pinching again, and his school trousers still hung the same as they had in autumn. She looked down the aisle as if the shelves could settle it.

She tested her idea on the pharmacist, a woman named Ruth with reading glasses pushed up into her hair. "If someone's feet got bigger twice this year but their legs didn't get longer at all," Kate asked, "would that mean the feet are broken?"

Ruth laughed. "No. Hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms and legs and the rest of the body catch up."

"So the legs will catch up," Kate said. "Later."

"That's the usual order," Ruth said, and rang up a packet of plasters for the woman behind them.

Kate stood there doing the sums. Two new pairs of shoes in one school year was a lot of money, and their family budget was not rich this winter; her mother had called it an impoverished month just last Tuesday, waving the electricity bill. So Kate made a decision she could defend. Instead of buying the sparkly display rack comb, she put her money toward Tom's next pair of shoes, and she wrote a note on the fridge: DO NOT BUY HIM JEANS YET.

When they got home, she found Tom in the hallway trying to jam his heel into the trainer he had outgrown a second time. "Save your trainers," she told him. "And don't ask for new jeans, because your legs are next."

Tom looked at her, then at his feet. "How do you know?"

Kate tapped his shoe with her own. "Your feet told me."

Sawyer refreshed the page for the eleventh time that afternoon. The sneakers he wanted, the white ones with the orange stripe, had been forty dollars two weeks ago. Now the lowest listing read seventy-five, and the little bar under the search filter said only three pairs remained. He had waited because he wanted to spend his lawn-mowing money on a concert ticket instead, and he was still not sure that had been the right call.

"Still checking those shoes?" his dad asked from the kitchen doorway. "Come on, we need gas."

At the station, the sign glowed in the fading light, each number luminous against the dark sky like something from a movie marquee. Sawyer noticed the price first because his dad groaned at it. "It was cheaper last week," his dad muttered, easing the nozzle into the tank.

A kid about Sawyer's age was standing by the next pump, squinting up at the sign. "Why'd it go up since Saturday?" the kid asked nobody in particular. "The gas is the same gas."

Sawyer found himself answering before he thought about it. "My uncle drives tankers, and he says crude oil is usually the biggest single part of what a gallon costs. Like, one chunk, bigger than any other chunk. So when crude gets more expensive, pump prices mostly go up too." He paused. "I think that's how it works, anyway."

The kid shrugged and wandered off, but Sawyer kept turning it over while the numbers climbed on the pump display. It was the same thing happening with his sneakers. Lots of people wanted them, hardly any pairs were left, and the price had shot up. When the warehouse restocked and there were hundreds of listings, the price would sink back down. He couldn't see the wanting or the scarcity itself, only the numbers moving, but the numbers were like footprints. Last month he had tested the idea by watching a different shoe, a pair everyone had said was finished, and he had watched the price fall for nine straight days until it hit nineteen dollars. His technique was simple: check morning and night, write the lowest price in a notebook, and never buy on the first day of a spike.

"Done," his dad said, hanging up the nozzle.

Back home, Sawyer opened his notebook to a clean page and wrote two columns, one labeled shoes and one left blank for now. Seventy-five dollars was too much, and he knew it. But restocks happened, and he could wait. He set an alarm for six in the morning, put the notebook by his pillow, and clicked the refresh button one more time. Two pairs left.

Penelope tapped her pencil against the gym door and counted the seconds until Coach Ruiz stopped talking. He was explaining the wall chart again, the one with every girl's free-throw percentage ranked from best to worst, and Penelope's name was near the bottom. Again. She shot every day at the park, sometimes fifty times, and her ranking never moved. Something was wrong with the chart, or something was wrong with her, and she intended to find out which.

That Saturday, her uncle Marcelo took her to Riley's, the sports bar near his apartment, because her parents were at a conference and somebody had to supervise her while they were gone. Uncle Marcelo wanted the place mostly for the nachos, which he claimed were the best in the county, and he wanted them extra hot. On the big screen, two baseball announcers were arguing about a player. One of them kept saying "on-base percentage" like it was a magic spell.

"That guy's boring," the other announcer said. "Everyone knows home runs win games."

Uncle Marcelo laughed through a mouthful of chips. "There's a book about this. Came out in 2003, written by Michael Lewis. It's called Moneyball. The 2002 Oakland Athletics, the whole team, they didn't have money like the rich teams. So they used statistics like on-base percentage to find players nobody else wanted. Cheap players. Undervalued, that's the word. And they competed anyway."

"You mean the team with the least money won?" Penelope asked.

"Competed," her uncle said, holding up a nacho like a professor's chalk. "That's the important part." Then he ordered a second plate and forgot the whole conversation, but Penelope didn't.

Monday after school, she sat in the library with the chart numbers she had copied into her notebook and a library copy of the book itself, which was thicker than she expected and, she discovered by page thirty, kind of tedious in places. The idea underneath it wasn't tedious at all. Home runs and total points and rankings were just the loud numbers. There were quieter numbers that told you what a player actually did over and over, game after game.

She found a table where her friend Dree was drawing a poster for the pet club, some cartoon herbivore munching leaves. "Dree," Penelope said, "you know the book report you did on dolphins? Where'd you get the database?"

"Library site. Why?"

Penelope borrowed the computer and typed in the coach's practice log, which was posted online every week. She felt like she was doing something slightly against the rules, even though it wasn't. The log had everyone's attempts and makes for three whole weeks. The chart on the gym wall only showed one number per player, and Penelope's number looked bad because she took the most attempts of anyone on the team. Sixty-one attempts. The captain, Roni, had taken twelve and made nine, which put her first on the chart.

Penelope did the division four times to be sure. Over the three weeks, Penelope's percentage was higher than Roni's. Not by much. But higher.

The next morning she asked Coach Ruiz if she could show him something, and she laid her notebook on his desk next to his coffee. He frowned at it for a long moment, the way he frowned at blown plays. "Where'd you get this?"

"The practice log. And a book." She pointed at the column of divisions. "The chart squishes everything into one number."

Coach Ruiz rubbed his jaw. Then he stood, walked to the gym wall, and drew a second column in green marker next to the old one. "Practice attempts logged, three-week average," he announced to the arriving team, and the room went quiet the way it did before a close game's final shot.

Roni stared at the new column, at her name, and then at Penelope's name sitting two lines above it. "How long have you been shooting sixty a day?"

"Since October," Penelope said.

Roni picked up a ball from the rack and bounced it once, hard. "Fine. Then race me to a hundred makes."

The festival filled the park with tents and flags, and Edouard moved through the crowd with a folded card in his back pocket. His grandmother had pressed it into his hand that morning before he left, saying in their family's language, "This is for you, but read it at the lantern table, not before." Edouard understood every word she said. He had been answering her in that language since he was small, at Sunday dinners and on the phone every Thursday. But the card itself was written down, in looping script he could not read at all.

He found the lantern table near the fountain, where volunteers were handing out translucent paper shades for people to decorate and hang on the long strings overhead. Painting a message on a lantern before hanging it was the closing ritual of the festival, and his grandmother had done it every year since they arrived. Edouard unfolded the card, hoping that seeing the whole thing would somehow help. It didn't. The letters sat there like a fence he could walk beside but never get through. He spoke the language, and yet the writing was a stranger to him.

At the next table, a girl about his age was chatting easily with an elderly woman in a language Edouard recognized as the same one. Then the woman handed her a small note, and the girl's face went pink. "Halmoni, I can't read this," she admitted. "I can talk to you fine, but reading it is different." The older woman laughed kindly and read it aloud herself. Edouard drifted closer. "Same thing happens to me," he said. "I chat with my grandmother all the time, but I can't read a word she writes."

The girl, whose name was Naomi, nodded like she'd been waiting for someone to say it. "My cousin calls ours a heritage language," she said. "Because we speak it at home, but out here everyone uses the community's main language." She tapped the note. "So kids like us can speak it and still not read it." Edouard looked back at his card. It wasn't that he was bad at the language. It was that speaking it and reading it were two different skills, and only one of them had ever been needed at his house.

He had an idea. If the grandmother could read the note aloud, maybe he could test whether his ear could do the work his eyes couldn't. He asked Naomi's grandmother, politely, if she would read his card to him. She unfolded it, smiled at the looping script, and spoke the words slowly. As she read, Edouard followed along, and the sentence opened like a door: "Write your wish for the year on your lantern, in our language, any way you can."

His grandmother hadn't asked for perfect spelling. She'd only asked him to try. Edouard picked up a brush, dipped it in the deep blue paint, and, letter by careful letter, copying from the card in front of him, began to write.

The bus smelled like vinyl seats and peanut butter crackers, and Grace ran through her word list for the fourth time even though she knew every entry cold. In thirty minutes the regional spelling bee would start, and only the champion would go to nationals. Second place got a dictionary, which felt to Grace like getting a towel after swimming halfway across a pool. Across the aisle, Marcus leaned his head against the window and watched the fence posts go by.

"You look like you're going to be sick," Grace said.

"I might be," Marcus said. "If I come in second again. Last year I got out on 'rhubarb.' Do you know how it feels to lose to a vegetable?"

Grace opened her mouth to say she didn't care about his rhubarb, then closed it, because the truth was she had thought about little else all week except coming in second herself. She reached into her backpack and pulled out a folded note her older sister had left on her pillow that morning. She smoothed it out on her knee.

"If you get 'presume' in the bee, it's p-r-e-s-u-m-e," her sister had written, "because you presume you're right before you check. Don't presume. Ask for the definition every single time. Also eat something, you spelled better after breakfast at the last one. Love, Tessa." Grace smiled and passed the note across the aisle so Marcus could read it too.

At the bee, the rounds burned down from forty spellers to six, then to three, then to Grace and Marcus alone. He spelled "agile" without a hitch. She spelled "anomaly," asking for the definition first, exactly as the note said, and got it right. Round after round followed, and nobody missed. The pronouncer kept pulling fresh words from the box, and Grace noticed something she had never seen before: there was no rule for ending this. She remembered a fact her sister had mentioned once, and she raised her hand.

"Is it true that the 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right?"

The pronouncer blinked. "That's correct."

"So if we both keep spelling everything right," Grace said, "there doesn't have to be a loser?"

The officials conferred in the corner, and Marcus caught Grace's eye across the microphone. He was grinning now, not green at all. Two rounds later, after Grace sailed through "moratorium" and Marcus handled "vitreous" without a stumble, the pronouncer lifted his hand.

"We are declaring two co-champions," he announced. "Both of you will advance to nationals."

Marcus held up his fist across the stage, and Grace ran over and bumped it with hers. In the back of the hall, her sister was already on her feet, waving the empty note envelope over her head like a flag.

Hannah crouched beside the boardwalk on the Willow Creek trail, her notebook open to a page titled "BIRD EVIDENCE" in fat letters. Her mission for the morning was to watch one bird for ten whole minutes and record what its beak did. Her little brother Marcus wanted only one thing: to reach the frog pond before anyone else in the history of the world. "Slow bird-watchers restrict the pace of fast civilians," he announced, drumming his heels on the boards.

"Shh. I think it's a wren," Hannah whispered, pointing at a stubby gray bird prying something out of a seed head. She drew the beak, small and curved like a bent nail. Then she checked her field guide, and her stomach dropped. The bird on the page had a straight, thick, seed-cracking beak. Her "wren" was a finch, and her whole page of careful notes now belonged to the wrong bird. She flopped back against the railing. "This is hopeless. Even Darwin's birds got mixed up, and I can't even tell a finch from a wren."

Marcus stopped drumming. "Darwin messed up birds? The Darwin?" He sat down, suddenly very interested in the idea of a famous genius being wrong.

Hannah flipped to the back of the guide, where a timeline ran along the bottom of the page. She ran her finger along it and stopped. "Listen to this. In 1837, an ornithologist named John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, some of which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were a new group of closely related finches." She read it twice, and something clicked into place. "So Darwin collected them and labeled them wrong. Gould looked at the beaks and saw what Darwin missed."

"Who's John Gould?" Marcus asked.

"Bird scientist. The one who figured it out." Hannah turned back to her notebook.
