When the Kellers came back at nine, they found their living room arranged like a drum set and Sophie asleep in Chase's arms, one spoon still in her fist. "She cried the whole time, didn't she?" Mrs. Keller asked, wincing. "Only at the start," Chase said. "Turns out she's basically the ambassador of pot music." Mr. Keller laughed and paid him, and at the door Mrs. Keller said, "Same time next Friday?" Chase grinned. "I'll bring my own spoon."

Jade sat in the exam room with her right arm propped on the paper-covered table, the fiberglass cast scratchy against her chin. Six weeks ago she had broken her radius falling off the garage roof while installing a birdhouse with her dad, and today, finally, the doctor would cut the cast off. In the waiting room she had seen a boy about her age leave with his arm out of a sling, and something about it had bothered her. His newly freed arm hung thinner than the other one, the skin pale, like a stick taped to his shoulder. She kept turning the image over in her mind, and by the time the nurse called her name, she had a guess: an arm that stays completely still for weeks loses something.

"So you think you can keep the muscles working from inside the cast?" her little brother Theo asked from the corner chair. He wanted her home by three, because he had plans for the two of them to build a model volcano before dinner, and every extra minute in this office felt like a stolen one.

"That's the idea," Jade said. "I've been squeezing this." She dug a stress ball out of her jacket pocket with her left hand, the one that had done everything for six weeks, and pressed it into her casted palm. Her fingers curled around it, faint and effortful, like they were moving through syrup. "Ten squeezes, four times a day, since week two. If stillness makes an arm shrink, then some movement should keep it from shrinking so much." She had no way to see inside the cast, which was the frustrating part. She could only measure the results today.

The saw whined, the shell split, and the two halves came away. Jade stared at her right arm and her stomach dropped. It was noticeably thinner than her left, the wrist narrow, the muscle of her forearm soft and small where the other one was round and firm. Her experiment had not saved it. "It's so skinny," she said, holding both arms side by side. "Why is it so much smaller?"

The doctor paused on his way out. "Muscles kept still in a cast weaken and shrink," he said. "That's normal." Then he was gone, and Jade turned back to her arm, flexing it, watching a small tremor run through it.

"Theo, grab my notebook," she said. She wanted to write this down while it was fresh: date, arm measurements, squeeze counts. Physical therapy would start next week, and the therapist had warned her that progress would hit a plateau at some point, where the arm would stop improving for a while no matter what she did. She intended to be ready with data, a whole coherent record from cast to recovery. Theo dug the notebook from her backpack and slapped it onto the table.

"Volcano at three," he said. "Deal?"

"Deal," Jade said, and wrote the first number down.

George set the two bean pots side by side on the picnic table, then moved them apart again, because side by side meant the taller one would shade the shorter one, and he wasn't testing shade. His question was simpler: did the plant food he'd bought with three weeks of allowance actually make beans grow faster? Pot A got the food. Pot B got plain water. Everything else, he'd promised himself, would stay exactly the same.

For nine days it worked. Pot A pulled ahead, and George measured both stems every morning with a ruler he kept in his back pocket. Fourteen centimeters versus nine. He wrote the numbers in his lab notebook and tried not to grin, because a real scientist, he figured, would be more like an artisan with data, careful and unhurried, immune to showing off.

Then his little sister Nadia came outside with a popsicle and stopped by the table.

"Why is this one all leaning?"

George looked. Pot B, the plain-water pot, leaned hard toward the fence, its leaves angled sideways like they were trying to escape. Pot A stood straight. He walked around the table twice. Both pots had the same soil from the same bag, the same amount of water from the same cup, the same kind of seeds from the same packet. So why would one lean?

He got down on his knees and scrutinized the yard from pot level, the way a bug would see it. From there he could see it plainly: the picnic table sat half under the big maple, and Pot B was in the shade of the trunk for most of the afternoon, while Pot A caught the window-side sun. Sunlight came from one direction, so Pot B had been bending toward the bright strip along the fence.

He stood up fast. His whole experiment was broken. The fourteen-versus-nine comparison meant nothing, because the pots hadn't been treated the same. One sat in the sun and one didn't, so the difference in the plants could be sun or food or both mixed together, and he couldn't tell which. He pressed his palms flat on the table.

"What?" Nadia said, licking her popsicle.

"Everything was supposed to be the same except the food. That's the whole point. If anything else is different, I can't say the food did anything."

"So make them the same."

He moved both pots to the open middle of the yard, where neither one got shade and neither one leaned anywhere, and turned them so the leaves that had bent all faced the fence. Then he found a scrap of paper and wrote in his notebook: START OVER, DAY 1. FAIR TEST MEANS ONLY ONE THING CHANGES.

The science fair was in eleven days. Not much time, but enough, if nothing else moved. He poured the measured water into each pot, marked the levels with tape, and carried his ruler inside.

"Can I have the plant food for my Venus flytrap?" Nadia asked.

"No." He shut the screen door. "You'll confuse my variables."

The lights went out just as Autumn was reaching for the last slice of pizza, and the whole farmhouse dropped into blackness so complete she couldn't see her own hand. "Grandma!" she called, already grinning, because a power cut at their dilapidated old house felt like the start of an adventure, not a disaster.

She heard her grandmother's chair scrape in the dark, then the sound of a drawer opening. "I'll get the candles," Grandma said. "There's a box on the pantry shelf."

"Wait, don't!" Autumn shot up from the table, arms out in front of her like a sleepwalker, bumping the doorframe before she found the hallway wall. She counted doorways in her head, the way she'd memorized them on a boring afternoon last summer, and felt her way into the kitchen. "We're not using candles. Where are the flashlights?"

"The candles are right here, dear. I've used candles in outages since before your mother was born."

Autumn found the drawer by touch, pulled it open, and her fingers closed around the rubber grip of the big flashlight. She clicked it on and the kitchen blazed back into existence, and she felt absurdly proud, as if she'd personally restored electricity. "In fire safety we learned that safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut," she said, holding it up like a trophy. "A candle can easily start a fire in a dark house."

Grandma paused with the matchbox in her hand. Outside, the wind threw a gust against the shutters, the tail end of the week's storms that had soaked the fields until the ditches ran like little rivers. "Well," Grandma said slowly. She looked at the candle stub, then at the flashlight, and set the matchbox back in the drawer. "I suppose the house has stood two hundred years. I'd like to preserve it a bit longer."

"So it's flashlights?" Autumn was already digging for the second one, the small one with the crank handle that her grandpa kept for camping trips.

"It's flashlights," Grandma agreed, and she laughed. "Look at me, changing my mind at my age."

They carried the lights out to the porch and sat on the swing, watching the stars come out over the dark valley, brighter than Autumn had ever seen them without the porch light washed out. The pizza got cold inside, but Autumn didn't care. She cranked the little flashlight and aimed its beam at the barn roof, then traced it along the fence line toward the road. Somewhere out there the power crews were working, and the lights would come back eventually, but for now the whole dark world belonged to them.

"Want to see how far the beam reaches?" Autumn asked, standing up on the porch rail.

Riley had one goal on Saturday morning: get the library's quiet study room before Marcus did, because Marcus hogged it every weekend. He was halfway across the lobby when he heard voices near the computers, sharp and worried.

"It's the creek," said a girl from his class, Priya, pointing at her screen. "My mom just shared this. Breaking news, it says. The flood is coming tomorrow." A dozen people stood behind her, staring at a photo of brown water swallowing a parking lot. A boy added, "My aunt's packing her car right now. Everybody's saying evacuate."

Riley leaned in. The picture looked terrifying, and everybody's aunts were panicking, but something snagged in his mind. The photo had a strange flatness to it, and he noticed a car in it that looked like a model nobody drove anymore. He couldn't say exactly what was wrong, only that it felt old. That was just his opinion, he realized, the way he felt about roller coasters or cafeteria pizza. But whether the photo was really from yesterday was different. That was a thing somebody could actually check.

"Can I try something?" he asked Priya. He sat down, right-clicked the picture, and saved it. "My cousin showed me this trick last summer," he said, typing. "A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before." The screen filled with rows of results. Priya leaned so close her braid brushed his shoulder. There it was: the same parking lot, the same brown water, on a news site from years ago. The photo had been passed off as new, but it wasn't. It was an old picture, recycled.

"It's not tomorrow," Riley said, and Priya grabbed her phone to call her mom. Around them, people started forwarding the results instead of the photo. The boy with the packing aunt sat down slowly, looking relieved and a little embarrassed. Riley brought him a cup of water from the fountain without being asked, because the kid's hands were shaking.

Then Ms. Adeyemi, the librarian, hurried over, saying the dilemma she faced was whether to post a correction on the community board when the flood rumor felt imminent. Priya held up the search results. "You don't have to take our word for it. Look." Ms. Adeyemi studied the screen, nodded, and said she would need to get the post authorized by the head librarian first, but she would do it within the hour.

By noon the study room was full, so Riley and Marcus ended up sharing the big table by the window. Marcus slid a paper over. "You're the photo detective now, huh?" he said. "Okay. Then tell me if this one's real," and he pointed at a picture of a shark swimming down Main Street.

Mia boarded the school bus on Monday clutching a flyer that read "Bus Radio Coming Friday," with nothing else printed on it but a cartoon speaker and a music note. She had heard rumors all week. Devon, three rows back, swore the school was installing a radio that would play only jazz, because his older brother had said so. Priya insisted it would play pop, because obviously everyone liked pop best. By the time the bus lurched away from the curb, the two of them were arguing so loudly the driver turned up her own dashboard radio to drown them out.

"It's a fact that it'll be pop," Priya said, arms crossed. "Ask literally anyone. Pop is the best."

"That's not a fact," Mia said, turning around in her seat. "That's an opinion. It's just what you like. An opinion is a belief or a feeling, so no evidence can prove it true or false."

Priya rolled her eyes. "Fine, then it's a fact that it'll be jazz, like Devon says."

Devon leaned into the aisle, smug. "My brother heard it from a janitor."

Mia frowned. That part might actually be checkable. A claim like "the radio will play jazz" wasn't a taste; it was a statement about the world that evidence could confirm or knock down. She just needed evidence. The flyer had no contact name, so at lunch she asked the office secretary, who said the radio had been approved by the principal, but she didn't know what it would play. The secretary pointed Mia toward the main office, where a notice on the wall was taped above the mailboxes, half of them labeled with teacher names, the wall around them otherwise sparse and bare. The notice was a permission form, and at the bottom it said the radio system had to be authorized by the district before installation.

That single word, authorized, sent Mia straight to the district website during study hall. She found a monthly facilities report, scanned it until her eyes burned, and finally found the entry: the radio would play one station, chosen by a vote of the bus drivers. The drivers had voted the previous Thursday. The winning station was listed at the bottom of the report, and when Mia read it, she laughed out loud in the middle of the silent library.

On Friday, everyone waited. Priya had already announced the radio would prove her right. Devon had a bet going with a kid from his math class. The bus pulled out, the driver reached over, and the speakers crackled to life with a weather report. Then traffic. Then, at last, music: classical violin, soft and slow.

"Classical?" Devon shouted. "Nobody voted for classical!"

"Wait," Priya said slowly, staring at the driver's head. "Who voted?"

The driver glanced in her mirror and smiled. "Me and my colleagues," she said, turning the volume up.

The cast ran from Vincent's knuckles to above his elbow, and the doctor had said one sentence about it that he kept turning over like a stone in his pocket. "The break missed the growth plate, so that's good news." Vincent had been too dizzy from the X-ray room to ask why. Now he sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field, watching his team run drills without him, and wishing he had asked.

"Six weeks," said Dex, dropping onto the bench beside him, sweaty and loud. "Tryouts for the travel team are in five. That's brutal timing."

"Coach said I can still try out if the cast comes off in time."

"Coach is being polite. Half the kids trying out have never broken anything."

Vincent flexed his fingers out of the cast, the only part of him that still moved freely. He had learned the one thing the doctor disclosed before his mother hurried him out of the exam room: near the ends of long bones there were growth plates made of cartilage, and that was where bones lengthened during childhood. A break through a growth plate could affect how the bone grew. He was still growing. The pitcher's mound had seemed like a reasonable risk in June, when he'd chosen to field that aggressive line drive with his glove hand up and his elbow exposed, but the choice looked different now, sitting on a bench in September.

Here was the part he couldn't see: whether his arm had escaped clean. The doctor said the break missed the plate, but Vincent wanted proof, something he could test himself. So that evening he dug the cloth measuring tape out of his mother's sewing box and marked a spot with a pen, just below his shoulder on each arm. He measured from the mark down to his wrist bone on both sides and wrote the numbers in his notebook: twenty-three centimeters even, left and right. If something invisible had gone wrong inside, he reasoned, the broken arm would fall behind the good one, week by week, and the numbers would disclose it before anyone could see it in a mirror.

Every Sunday he measured again. The first week matched. The second week matched. His mother caught him at the kitchen table with the tape and the notebook and said, "The doctor already told you it missed the growth plate."

"He told me once," Vincent said. "I'm checking."

By the fifth Sunday, the numbers still matched, and the morning the cast came off he carried the notebook to tryouts in his back pocket like a talisman. He stretched his pale, thin arm in the sun, threw ten warm-up pitches, and felt the old snap come back into his shoulder. When Coach waved him toward the mound, Vincent pulled out the notebook and tossed it to Dex on the bench.

"Hold that," he said. "I want it after."

Dex flipped it open. "Twenty-three, twenty-three, twenty-three. What is this, a math project?"

"It's my arm," Vincent said, and toed the rubber.

Austin had played in hotter games than this one. That was the part he couldn't get past. Last July, in a tournament two towns over, the thermometer on the snack shed read ninety-six, and he'd pitched five innings and felt fine. Today the field clock said eighty-eight, and by the third inning he felt like somebody had wrung him out like a rag.

"You're dragging," Marcus said at the fence between innings. He tossed Austin the water bottle. "You accuse me of dogging it every time I strike out, so I'm allowed to say it."

"I'm not dogging it." Austin drank, but the water didn't fix anything. His jersey was soaked through, clinging to his back like a second skin. The sweat just sat there. It didn't dry.

Their opponents were from Fairview, an affluent town with a fancy shaded dugout and matching coolers. Those kids looked fresh. Austin's whole team looked boiled. Devon had already gone to one knee in right field, and even Coach Reyes, who never admitted anything, kept squinting at his players like something about the math was wrong.

Between the fourth and fifth inning, Austin stood by the fence and turned the problem over. It was cooler today than that tournament. Same length of game, roughly the same effort. So why did today feel worse? He kept coming back to his shirt. That day in July, his shirt had been stiff with salt by the second inning, because the sweat had dried. Today nothing dried. The towels on the bench stayed wet. His batting glove stayed wet. His logic told him the difference wasn't the heat. It was the air. The air was already soaked, and it wouldn't take the sweat off his skin.

He grabbed the dugout's damp rag and hung it on the chain-link in the sun. Then he took the dry paper towels from the first aid kit and hung one beside it, after dunking it in his water bottle. Five minutes later, the dry air hadn't come and both towels hung there, dripping and useless, like two little flags of confirmation.

"Fifth inning!" the umpire called.

Austin jogged out to the mound and did the only thing he could think of. He dumped the cooler's ice water over his head, and when Coach shouted at him for wasting it, he waved the empty jug. "It works better out of me than in me," he said. "Trust me on this one. The sweat can't dry in this air, so I've got to get cool some other way."

The twist came after the game. Fairview's shortstop, the freshest kid on the field, collapsed in the handshake line, and Austin was the only one who wasn't surprised. He ran for the ice water first.

Ryder sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table, swinging his feet, waiting for the doctor to come back with his chart. This was his third cold since school started in September, and he had a theory about that. His theory was that something was wrong with him. Nobody else in his class kept getting sick like this. Devonte had caught one cold, back in October, and had talked about it for a week like he'd climbed a mountain.

When Dr. Patel had checked his ears and throat, Ryder had asked the question straight out. "Is my immune system broken? Because this is my third cold since fall." Dr. Patel had said, "Hold that thought," and stepped out to pull his file, which was not the answer Ryder wanted.

While he waited, he looked around the room. There was a poster about washing hands, a diagram of an ear, and a rack of pamphlets by the sink. He slid off the table to verify his count in case he was remembering it wrong. September, the sneezy one. November, the coughing one. Now this one, in February, with the sore throat and the fever his mom had made him stay home for. Three. It was definitely three.

Then a pamphlet caught his eye, a CDC one about colds in kids. He picked it up and read the middle paragraph twice, because the first time he thought he'd misread it. Adults average two to three colds a year, the pamphlet said, and children often catch even more than that. Ryder stood there holding the paper. Three colds in five months wasn't proof of anything broken. Three colds since fall was just... being twelve.

He heard footsteps and climbed back onto the table, keeping the pamphlet in his hand.

"So," Dr. Patel said, coming in with the folder open. "Third cold since fall, and you want to know if your immune system is broken. Here's the thing." He paused. "Actually, you go first. You've got a look on your face."

Ryder held up the pamphlet. "I already figured it out. Adults average two to three colds a year, and kids catch even more. So I'm basically normal." He hesitated. "I thought I was a walking science experiment."

Dr. Patel laughed. "I was going to tell you exactly that. You beat me to it."

"Mom's going to say I'm dramatic," Ryder said. "She has this whole anecdote about how I cried over a splinter when I was five, and she tells it every time I say anything hurts."

"Then here's your homework," Dr. Patel said, tearing a corner off the pamphlet and writing on it. "Show her this number. Three colds is right on schedule." He handed Ryder the scrap of paper, and Ryder folded it carefully and put it in his pocket with his library card, which was where he kept things that mattered.

Emile was sprawled on Denzell's bedroom floor with his phone propped against a stack of comics, waiting for the game to load, when Denzell's little sister Nadia appeared in the doorway holding the family tablet like it had bitten her. "It keeps asking my birthday," she said. "Every time I try to make an account, it asks, and then it says I can't." She was eleven, and she wanted to join the app where everybody in her grade supposedly already was.

Denzell didn't even look up from his controller. "Just put a different year, dummy." Emile watched Nadia's face go stubborn, which he knew from experience was worse than crying. He picked up the tablet mostly to make her stop hovering, typed twelve in the birthday box, and got the same rejection. Then, out of curiosity, he tried thirteen. The screen blinked and moved on, asking for her name and a username. So there was a line, and the line was a number.

He frowned at it. Why thirteen? Not sixteen, not eighteen. He typed the question into his phone and read, scrolling while Nadia bounced on her toes. "Okay," he said slowly. "It's a law. The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998. It says websites need parental consent before they collect personal information from kids under thirteen." He looked up. "So most sites just make you be thirteen instead of dealing with all that." Nadia squinted. "Then why didn't they just say that?" Emile had no answer, because the app had said nothing at all, just rejected her over and over like she'd failed a test she never got to study for.

"You could ask Mom to consent," Denzell said, finally setting down the controller, "if you actually advocate for yourself instead of whining." He made it sound easy, but Emile had heard their mom on the phone with the school, brisk and impatient, and he could picture the consequence already: a whole evening of questions, rules, and maybe a no. Nadia took the tablet back, holding it perpendicular to the light to check her reflection in the dark screen, considering what she might look like with an account.

She sat down on the edge of Denzell's bed with the tablet on her knees, and Emile could see the cursor blinking in the birthday field, waiting. "If I change the year," she said quietly, "nobody ever checks, right?" Emile thought about the line at thirteen, invisible until you crossed it, and about how fast you could cross it with two taps of a thumb.

The game finished loading behind him. Denzell said, "Emile, we starting or what?" Emile picked up his phone but kept his eyes on Nadia's fingers hovering over the numbers.

Sadie had been waiting for this Saturday for two weeks, and now that it was here, she was speeding past the pretzel stand at the mall like the optical shop might vanish if she slowed down. Her mom trailed behind with the paperwork from the eye doctor, while Sadie pushed through the door of Bright Eyes Optical and announced, "I'm here for glasses. My first pair."

The optician, a woman with silver hoops and an eccentric purple vest covered in tiny glasses pins, laughed and pulled a tray from the back. "Let's find you something good." Sadie tried on pair after pair, and each one felt like a different version of herself, a movie star, a scientist, a mysterious spy. Finally she chose slim gray frames, and the whole shop seemed to radiate possibility while the optician slid the new lenses in.

That was when Priya walked in, waving. Priya was already a glasses veteran, and her ambition to become an optometter someday, her word for it, meant she knew all the shop's frames by name. "Ooh, those are so good on you," Priya said, then leaned close to the little mirror on the counter. "Wait. Look at us."

Sadie looked. Priya's lenses made her eyes look noticeably bigger, round and wide behind the glass. Sadie's own reflection showed the opposite: her eyes looked smaller. "Why would they do that?" Sadie asked. "We're both wearing glasses. Mine shrink my eyes and yours blow them up."

Priya shrugged, but Sadie couldn't let it go. She thought about it while the optician adjusted the fit behind her ears. If the lenses did opposite things to how their eyes looked, maybe the lenses themselves were opposite. She pulled her reading homework out of her backpack, held her new glasses up to the page, and read a line easily. Then she asked, "Priya, can I try yours?"

Priya handed them over, grinning like a lab partner. Sadie held Priya's glasses over her homework, and the words swam into blur. When Priya put Sadie's glasses on and tried to read her own magazine, she squinted and said, "Nope, everything close up is a mess."

"Because your lenses are the opposite of mine," Sadie said, snapping her fingers. "Yours make things look bigger. Mine make things look smaller." Priya's whole face lit up. "That's exactly it! The optician told me last year. My problem is farsightedness. The light in my eye focuses behind the retina, so stuff up close looks blurry, and convex lenses fix it." She tapped her frames. "Convex means they bulge out, so they magnify my eyes. Yours must be the opposite kind, because your eyes look smaller through them."

"So near stuff is blurry for me, far stuff is blurry for you," Sadie said, "and opposite lenses fix us." She put her glasses back on, picked up her homework, and read the first line out loud, fast and clear, savoring every crisp letter. Priya grabbed her arm and said, "Come on, we're testing them on the mall directory from way across the food court."

Eleanor stood at the edge of the festival lawn, where the food stalls gave way to a long table draped in blue cloth. Behind the table, a Torah scroll lay open on a wooden stand, its letters small and crowded, and a woman named Rabbi Ora was letting visitors look but not touch. Eleanor's bat mitzvah was in three weeks, and she still could not get through her portion without stumbling at the same verse. She had come here to petition the rabbi for extra practice, though she had rehearsed the asking all morning and now the words felt too big for her mouth.

"My reading keeps breaking in the same place," she finally said. "I thought maybe the scroll itself would help. Seeing it instead of the photocopy."

Rabbi Ora slid the scroll along the stand so the tricky verse faced Eleanor. "Read it here, out loud. The whole festival will hear you, so you might as well practice being nervous."

Eleanor began, and her voice wobbled exactly where it always did. She leaned closer, squinting at the tight rows of letters, and her finger drifted toward the parchment to hold her place.

"Use this instead." Rabbi Ora pressed a slim silver pointer into her hand, shaped like a small hand with one long finger. "It's called a yad."

"What does that mean?"

"Hand. The scroll doesn't get touched, so the reader follows the words with the yad instead of a finger."

Eleanor fit the silver finger beneath the line she was reading, and something unexpected happened. The verses she had been sure she hated, the ones she had grumbled about for a month, went smoothly, because she stopped losing her place. She had been biased against the whole passage, blaming the words themselves, when the real problem was that her eyes kept sliding off the line. Now the pointer held them still. She finished the verse, then the next one, and the crowd noise around the table seemed to fold itself away.

"That was it," she said, almost laughing. "That was the whole problem."

"It usually is," Rabbi Ora said. "Though you'll have to carry the melody alone at your ceremony. No excuses about photocopies then."

Eleanor looked down at the yad lying light in her palm, silver warming to her skin, and thought of the morning she would stand in front of everyone with this same scroll, her grandmother's congregation watching from the third row where her grandmother used to sit. She would get the words right now. That was the gain. The cost she understood only partly: some doors, once opened, showed you exactly how much you still owed.

She handed back the pointer and touched the silver one last time, right at the tip of its long finger.

The field trip was supposed to be about seeds. Aiden had even practiced saying "germinate" on the bus, because the teacher had promised points for using vocabulary words correctly, and he needed those points. But halfway to the nature reserve, the bus coughed, shuddered, and died on the gravel lane. The driver lifted the hood, stared at the engine for a long minute, and announced his diagnosis: "Fuel pump, probably. Or it's haunted." Everyone groaned, which he seemed to enjoy.

They walked the last quarter mile to the reserve's visitor center, which turned out to be an old wooden building with a tower attached to one end. A sign read Engine Company 21, 1878. "Wait," Aiden said. "This is a fire station? On a nature reserve?" A retired firefighter named Mr. Ruiz, who now volunteered leading seed-collecting hikes, let them in out of the drizzle. Priya, whose actual goal for the whole trip was winning the school photo contest with something no one else would have, was already circling the brass pole that ran from a hole in the ceiling to a hole in the floor.

"Go on, guess," Mr. Ruiz said, leaning on the pole. "Why'd stations have poles instead of stairs?" Kids shouted answers. Sliding was fun. Poles were cheaper. Firefighters liked showing off. Priya said, "For the photo op, obviously." Mr. Ruiz just raised an eyebrow and waited.

Aiden stared at the holes. One hole above, one hole below, perfectly symmetrical, like the pole had been dropped straight through the building. Why would anyone cut two holes in two floors? Then it clicked. "Time," he said slowly. "The truck leaves and you're upstairs asleep. If you take the stairs, you're slower. You cut the holes because a pole gets you down faster." He pointed at the sign. "And that's why this one's famous, right? Somebody actually slid down a pole and beat everybody on the stairs, and that's how it started. That's the whole reason poles exist." Mr. Ruiz grinned so wide his mustache moved. "Engine Company 21, Chicago, 1878. Kid gets it."

"Can I slide it?" Priya asked. "Not a chance," said Mr. Ruiz. "But you can hold the old leather helmet while your friend takes your picture next to it." Priya positioned herself under the symmetrical arch of the doorway, helmet on, pole gleaming behind her. Aiden took the shot, and outside a horn honked twice: the bus, alive again. "Told you it was haunted," the driver called from the lane. "Ghost fixed it." Priya checked the photo and whispered, "First prize."

The group chat pinged at 7:42 on a Tuesday night, right while Antoine was gluing a polymer model of a water molecule together for science class. He tapped the phone with one sticky finger. It was Kayla from his basketball team: "Guess who has the BEST shooting percentage on the roster. Go ahead. Guess." Antoine scrolled up. Kayla had posted a screenshot of the league stats page, with her name circled in red at the top of the column marked FG%. It said 100 percent. His name was halfway down the list at 38 percent.

"You take one shot all season and now you're a legend?" typed Marcus, and a row of laughing emojis followed. Antoine frowned at the screen. He remembered the game, back in December, when Kayla had come off the bench for the last forty seconds and taken the only shot of her whole season. It had gone in, a lucky bounce off the back rim, and the whole bench had stormed the floor. One shot. One make. He glanced at the stats page again, then at his own line: 27 attempts, 10 makes.

He opened his notebook, the one he kept for stats, and wrote it out. Kayla: 1 for 1, which the league page turned into 100 percent. Him: 10 for 27, which turned into 38 percent. He tried a test. If Marcus, who was 21 for 50, made his next shot, he'd be 22 for 51, and Antoine worked that out too. Nobody's number stayed put. Every shot nudged the percentage up or down, and the fewer shots you had, the harder each one yanked the number around. Kayla's 100 percent was built on a single attempt, which seemed both hilarious and kind of unfair to everyone grinding through thirty shots.

He typed into the chat: "Can anyone elaborate on how many shots that 100 percent is standing on?" Marcus answered fast: "ONE. She's taken one shot since October." Kayla sent an eye-roll emoji. "Rules are rules, boys. The page doesn't lie." Antoine sent his notebook photo, with her line and his line side by side, and underneath he wrote, "Your percentage is perfect because you only took one shot. One out of one is 100 percent. Take ten more and see what happens."

The chat went quiet for a full minute. Then Kayla typed, "Fine. Challenge accepted. Next practice, I'm shooting ten and posting the math." At Thursday's practice she took exactly ten shots from the elbow, with Marcus rebounding and Antoine calling out each make and miss. She hit four, and afterward she grabbed the phone and typed the new numbers herself: 5 for 11. "Okay," she wrote, "45 percent. Still better than Antoine." He laughed and started typing his reply.

The after-school Heritage Club met in the library on Tuesdays, and Kaitlyn had joined for one reason: she wanted a real answer about her own last name, Novak, which nobody at school could pronounce right. Today's ritual was the display table, where every member put out one object that stood for their family. Kaitlyn had brought a postcard her great-grandmother sent from Budapest in 1949, signed "Novak Anna," and she had written below it, "Great-grandma Anna Novak, who made a mistake signing this." She felt proud of the label until Dani, whose grandfather was Hungarian too, stopped in front of it and frowned.

"That's not a mistake," Dani said. He pulled a card out of his backpack, a birthday card his grandfather had signed for his mother: "Kovacs Peter" in careful blue ink. "My grandpa signs everything backwards like that. Mom says he does it on purpose."

Kaitlyn looked from the card to her postcard and felt something shift. If two people did the same thing, it probably was not a mistake at all. Maybe it was a pattern, and patterns meant a rule was hiding underneath it. She needed more evidence, so she went to find Min, who had brought a calligraphy scroll with her Korean name on it, "Kim Jiwoo," family name first, the way Min always wrote it. Kaitlyn set the card, the postcard, and the scroll side by side on the table.

"Dani's grandfather signs his family name first," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "My great-grandmother did the same thing. And your name is written that way too. Min, is that just a Korean thing, or could Hungarian work like that?"

"Korean, Japanese, Chinese, and Hungarian," Min said, pointing at the three objects in a row. "Same order in all of them. Family name first."

"So in Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name," Kaitlyn said, and as she said it, the whole table of objects rearranged itself in her mind. Her great-grandmother had not been confused. She had been following the custom of her own language, the same order used across the world in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names. Kaitlyn crossed out her label, and the smudge where "mistake" had been did not quite diminish her relief. It made it heavier, somehow.

"That's actually a legitimate reason to fix the sign," said Mr. Okafor from across the room, where he was stapling the banner for Friday's heritage night. Kaitlyn rewrote it: "Novak Anna, my great-grandmother, who wrote her name the Hungarian way." Then she sat back and looked at the corrected card, and a small ache settled in beside the satisfaction. She had solved the puzzle, but the woman who wrote that postcard was gone, and would never know that a great-granddaughter in a library had finally understood her.

"Friday night, you're reading this out loud," Dani said, tapping the postcard. "Both of us. Our grandfathers would like that."

Kaitlyn slid the postcard to the center of the table, next to Min's scroll, and left it there.

Beatrice set the catapult on the kitchen table, loaded a marshmallow, and pulled the release arm. The marshmallow sailed across the room, bounced off the refrigerator, and landed in the fruit bowl.

"That's forty-two inches," said her little brother Oscar, holding the tape measure at arm's length like it might explode. "Can I have the marshmallow?"

"It touched the floor near the bowl. No." Beatrice wrote 42 on her data sheet under Trial 1, then frowned at it. Forty-two was great. Forty-two would probably win the science fair, or at least beat Dwight Yang's volcano, which had won for three years straight mostly because it glowed in the dark.

She reset the arm and launched again. This time the marshmallow went eleven inches and rolled off the table into Oscar's shoe.

"You wrote eleven," Oscar said, reading over her shoulder. "That's terrible. You should erase it and keep the forty-two."

Beatrice didn't erase it. Something about the two numbers bothered her. Same catapult, same marshmallow weight, same angle, and yet one throw went almost four times farther than the other. Either her machine was haunted, or one of those numbers was lying. She thought about the coin-flip unit from math class, how a single flip told you nothing but a hundred flips started showing something true. One launch might be a fluke. A fluke was exactly the kind of illusion that could win you a ribbon on Friday and embarrass you in front of the whole gym on Saturday, if the judges asked you to repeat it.

"I'm going to run it ten times," she announced.

"That's boring," said Oscar.

"Then count."

She launched, and launched, and adjusted the spoon cup a hair after trial six when it started rattling loose, and marked every distance down. The numbers wandered all over the place, 19, 33, 26, 15, 38, and none of them was 42 again, which made 42 look more and more like a freak. When she finished, she added all ten distances, divided by ten, and wrote the average at the bottom of the sheet: 27.4 inches.

"There," she said. "That's my real number."

"That's smaller than forty-two," Oscar pointed out. "You made your project worse on purpose."

"It's not worse, it's true. One lucky throw is just one lucky throw. If I run it ten times, the weird flukes kind of cancel out, and the average is what the catapult actually does." She tapped the 27.4. "That's the fundamental number. That one I can prove."

Oscar ate a marshmallow anyway when she wasn't looking, which she knew, because trial eleven had been sitting on the scale.

The next morning she brought the catapult to school in a shoebox. Dwight Yang was already in the hallway, plugging in his volcano. Beatrice looked at 27.4 on her data sheet, looked at the judges' table, and set up her first launch of the day.

Florence had typed and deleted her message to Marisol three times before her little brother Theo leaned over her shoulder. "You're doing the typing thing again," he said, flopping onto the couch with his tablet. She shooed him away, but gently, because Theo had spent all morning quiet and pale after his recital video had gone up on the school's music page and someone in the comments had called his solo "a crime scene." Florence's plan was to reply to that comment with something clever and cutting. The trouble was that every version she typed sounded either mean or desperate, and she couldn't tell which one it would be until after she posted it.

Instead of sending anything, she opened a new tab and looked up the school's music page itself. There was Theo, mid-note, under the headline "Winter Concert Highlights." An idea nudged her. If the video weren't public anymore, the comment couldn't keep stinging him every time someone Googled his name. The music teacher, Mr. Adeyemi, ran the page, but Florence knew from the contact line that he only checked email on Sundays. She noticed something else while she scrolled: a link at the bottom of the page, small and gray, to an archive site she'd heard kids mention, the Wayback Machine.

"Watch this," she told Theo, pulling him up by the sleeve. She pasted the music page's address into the archive's search box. A whole timeline appeared, row after row of dates going back years, like snapshots taken of the page while nobody was looking. "It says it's saved more than one trillion web pages," Theo read, his voice going up on the last word.

Florence clicked one of the older dates, and there was the page from two autumns ago, before Theo was even in band. It looked almost the same, except the photos showed kids who had graduated. She felt the idea settle into place, cold and clear. Even if the video came down tomorrow, an old copy might still be sitting in that trillion-page pile, waiting for anyone who went looking. Deleting something public didn't mean it vanished. It meant it vanished from one place.

"So my plan doesn't work," Theo said slowly.

"Your plan was to hide. My plan is different." She scrolled back to the current page and found the email link for Mr. Adeyemi. She drafted a message that didn't try to be clever, that didn't invade his inbox with drama, just said: the comments on the Winter Concert video are hurting my brother, and kids at school are sharing screenshots. Could the comment section be turned off? She read it aloud to Theo so he could hear how it sounded, because tone in an email was like tone in a voice, easy to get wrong without a face to check against.

He nodded, then pointed at her screen. "Add that he practices an hour a day. So Mr. Adeyemi knows the crime scene thing is a lie."

Florence typed the sentence in, and Theo, satisfied, went back to the couch and put his tablet face-down on the cushion, which he only did when he was done worrying about something. She hovered over the send button, then clicked it before she could start deleting again.

"Done," she said. "Now we wait until Sunday."

Juliette stood in front of the bathroom mirror with her chin tilted up, counting. Three on her forehead, one beside her nose, and a new one forming on her chin, red and tender. Last year her face had been clear, and this year it wasn't, and she wanted to know why.

At the pharmacy after school, she found the aisle with the face washes and started reading labels. "Oil-free," one said. "For acne-prone skin," said another. She turned a bottle over and squinted at the back. It mentioned unclogging pores. Pores, oil, pimples. Those three words kept coinciding on every label, and she didn't think that was an accident.

Her little brother Marcus appeared beside her, eyeing the candy shelf across the aisle. "Why are you reading shampoo for ten minutes?"

"It's not shampoo." She held up the bottle. "It says it fights pimples by unclogging pores. So pores get clogged with something."

"With dirt," Marcus said.

"Maybe. Or oil." She set the bottle down and picked up another, a scrub with the word "vigorous" splashed across the front, promising a deep clean. On the back, in smaller letters, it mentioned excess oil. She thought about her own face, shiny by lunch even when she washed it in the morning, and about her cousin Leo, who was eleven and whose face was never shiny at all. The difference was that Leo was younger. Something about getting older had changed her skin, and whatever it was, it was making more oil.

"Marcus, if I washed my face five times a day, would that fix it?"

He shrugged. "You'd be very clean."

She felt some skepticism about that plan herself. Washing had never stopped the shine before, so plain dirt didn't seem like the whole story. She took out her phone and typed carefully: why do teenagers get pimples. She scrolled, then stopped at a line that made everything click into place. Puberty hormones made the oil glands in her skin produce more oil, and the extra oil could clog pores, which led to acne.

"It's oil," she said. "There's even a word for it. Sebum."

"Sounds like a potion ingredient."

"It's the stuff clogging my pores." She put the vigorous scrub back, because scrubbing harder wouldn't change how much oil her glands made, and chose instead a gentle wash marked "non-comedogenic," which the label explained meant it wouldn't clog pores. Two weeks, the bottle suggested, before anyone should expect results. That felt long, but at least now she had a real reason for what was happening instead of just blaming herself for being careless.

At home, she set the new bottle on the sink where she would actually see it, morning and night. Her chin still had the tender spot, and her forehead still had its three, but she uncapped the wash, wet her hands, and started anyway. "Twenty-eight washes till the verdict," she told the mirror. "I can wait."

Keira slid her phone across the dinner table before Dad could start on the green beans. "Look at this dress. What color is it?" She kept her voice flat, like it was a quiz with no stakes, but her knee was bouncing under the table.

Dad squinted. "White and gold. Obviously." Mom leaned over, took the phone, tilted it, and frowned. "Blue and black. Dad, your eyes are broken." Dad laughed and pulled the phone back, holding it at arm's length. "White and gold, and I'd bet the house." Keira's little brother Dev grabbed it next and shouted "Blue and black!" before he'd even looked, which meant nothing, because Dev once swore the neighbor's cat had winked at him.

It was a photo from the internet, one her friend Priya had sent with the message "family destroyer, good luck." Keira had looked at it in her room and seen white and gold, plain as milk and honey. Then Mom had seen blue and black on the same screen. Same photo, same screen, same kitchen light. Keira felt a small, itchy suspicion that something invisible was going on, a hidden rule nobody in this family knew. She decided to test it. "Everybody close your eyes. Count to ten. Then look again."

They humored her, even Dev, though he counted wrong. When they opened their eyes, Dad still said white and gold, Mom still said blue and black, and nobody had switched. Keira tried passing the phone around the table, person to person, watching each face. Same split, every time, like the family had been cut down the middle with scissors. "Priya says this photo went everywhere back in February 2015," Keira said. "It went viral because people couldn't agree. Some people see it as blue and black and some see it as white and gold."

"Which is it really?" Dev asked, mouth full. Keira had an answer ready, because she had persevered through fifteen minutes of searching after Priya's text, wading past jokes and arguments and one site that swore the dress was magic, which she refused to be gullible enough to believe. She'd finally found a news story with the actual dress in it. "The real dress is blue and black," she said. "That's a fact. The photo came out in February 2015, and it broke the whole internet."

Mom smugly tapped her own temple. Dad stared at the screen, jaw tight, the suspense dragging out while Dev chanted "blue and black, blue and black." Then Dad set the phone down and exhaled. "Fine. I've been defeated by a picture of a dress. I saw white and gold the whole time, and I'll say it louder: white and gold." He pointed his fork at Keira. "But you saw it that way too, until you didn't. So what color do you see right now?"

Keira looked down at the dress one more time. Gold faded, white turned pale blue, and the dark bands settled into black, like something swimming up through water. She turned the screen toward her father. "I see blue and black now. Same photo you're looking at."

The October sun radiated warm across the empty football field, though the bleachers threw long shadows by the time Jeremy arrived. His right arm hung in a cast that itched in the afternoons, and under his jacket he had hidden something folded twice: the X-ray film from his wrist, taken three weeks ago at the clinic. He wanted Marisol to see it, because Marisol wanted to be a radiologist someday and because she had promised to tell him the truth about how his bones were knitting.

He found her sitting on the bottom row of the bleachers, lacing her cleats. "You brought it," she said, not looking up. Around them the goals stood with their nets sagging, and an ominous bank of gray cloud was stacking up over the far end zone, but the air was still calm.

Jeremy unfolded the film and held it up against the low sun. "Look at this. The bones glow like they're lit from inside. My skin's barely there, just a gray smudge. Why does the picture work like that?"

Marisol took the film and tilted it. "Because of the calcium. Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them. The soft stuff lets the rays pass through, so it hardly shows at all."

Jeremy sat down beside her and studied the white bones again, the two broken edges of his radius angled toward each other like friends about to shake hands. "So the dark gap between them," he said slowly, "that's where the rays went straight through. That's the break."

"Right. No calcium bridge yet, so no white." She pointed to a faint haze already forming at the edges of the gap. "But see that? That's new bone starting to fill in."

Jeremy's dilemma had been simple all week: the coach wanted him at practice throwing left-handed, and Jeremy wanted to sit out entirely until the arm was whole. Now he traced the haze with his finger, thinking. If white meant calcium, and calcium meant bone, then the way to know whether he was healing was to see whether that gap kept getting whiter. He couldn't watch it, not without another X-ray, but he could test the idea a different way. "They took two pictures," he said, pulling the older film from his jacket, the one from the day of the break. He laid them side by side on the metal bench. In the first, the gap yawned wide and black. In the second, it had narrowed, and the haze of white crept further along both broken edges.

"It's working," Jeremy said. "It's actually closing." He looked up, and the first cold drops of rain dotted the films, so they gathered them quickly and ran for the equipment shed, Jeremy holding both X-rays flat against his chest with his good hand, Marisol laughing and pulling her hood up as they ran.

Ryder spent twenty minutes deciding between his conventional blue shirt and the green one nobody had ever seen him wear. He picked green, then changed his mind, then changed it back. His little sister, Nadia, watched from the doorway with a bowl of cereal. "I nominate the green one," she said. "You look like somebody who's about to do something interesting." Ryder frowned at the mirror. "It's just a dance, Nadia." But he kept the green shirt on.

The gym smelled like floor wax and punch, and the music hit him before he even got through the doors. Marcus was waiting near the refreshment table, waving him over. "You came! Okay, the eighth graders are on that side, the seventh graders claim the far wall, and Priya said she might dance with anybody who asks nicely. That's the factor that decides your whole night, basically." Ryder laughed, but his palms were sweating, and not only about Priya.

They drifted toward the stage, where two speakers taller than Mr. Hobbes stood on either side of the DJ booth. The bass thumped in Ryder's chest like a second heartbeat. After one song, his ears felt strange, a tight, fuzzy pressure, and he noticed Marcus rubbing his ear with the heel of his hand. "Yours too?" Ryder asked. Marcus nodded. "It's like they're full of static."

Ryder's phone had an app he'd opened once for a science homework option, a sound meter. He pulled it out and held it up. The number on the screen wobbled around 88 near the speakers. He remembered the chart from that same homework, the one about safe listening: exposure to 85 decibels was okay for eight hours a day, but each 3-decibel increase cut that safe time in half. So 88 wasn't just a little more than 85. It was half the safe time, four hours. And if the meter was reading low, if they were really at 91, that would be two hours. They had been standing there for maybe twenty minutes, and his ears already felt like static. "Let's test something," Ryder said. "We walk toward the far wall and check the number."

They walked. Ten steps, the number dropped to 85. Ten more, and it hovered at 82. By the seventh grade wall, it read 79, and the pressure in Ryder's ears loosened like a fist unclenching. "Whoa," Marcus said, staring at the screen. "So three points is half? That's wild. My brother stands by those speakers all night." Ryder pocketed the phone. "Not me. I plan to hear things when I'm eighty." Marcus grinned. "You're the most careful reckless person I know."

Priya appeared beside them with two cups of punch, holding one out. "You two look like scientists at a concert. What are you studying?" Ryder took the cup, and the fuzzy feeling in his ears was almost gone. "Acoustics," he said. "Want me to tell you about it?" She sipped her punch and shrugged. "Only if you tell me while we dance." Ryder set his cup down on the table and held out his hand.

The car smelled like grandma's house anyway, because the paper lantern Logan held in his lap had been hers, folded flat and tucked in her dresser for years. Outside, huge white wind turbines turned slowly above the hills, each blade sweeping past like a slow hand waving. Dad had the gearshift in neutral at the long red light, his face set and careful, and Mom kept her eyes on the map even though she already knew the way.

"You're sure it's tonight?" Dad asked.

"That's the whole point," Logan said. "It's mid-August. Obon is mid-August. That's when her spirit comes home for a visit, so if we're going to put the lantern out at her house, tonight is when it counts." He had worked this out over three days, checking the calendar twice, deciding he had to prioritize this over the soccer camp he'd already paid for. Coach Ray had not been happy. That was the cost, and Logan had agreed to pay it.

At Grandma's dark house, Dad unlocked the front door and Logan went straight for the kitchen drawer where she kept her old datebooks. He wanted proof, some sign she had done this herself. The summer before she died, in her careful handwriting, was one word: Obon. But it was written in July, not August, and in the datebook from the year before, July again.

"July," he said out loud, feeling the floor tilt under the plan he'd built. "Most places do it in mid-August, but her hometown was one of the places that did it in July. All along, I was a month off. I missed it. I missed it for this year."

Mom crouched beside him. "You didn't miss her," she said. "You just missed the date."

So the lantern went up anyway. Logan unfolded it on the porch steps, and Dad lit the small candle inside, cupping the flame against the breeze coming off the hills. The paper glowed warm orange, and somewhere down the valley one of the turbines caught the last sunlight and flashed. It was the wrong week, maybe even the wrong month, and the house behind them was empty and would be sold by fall.

"Want to say something?" Dad asked.

Logan thought about it, then shook his head. "She'd rather hear the game anyway." So he sat on the steps and told the lantern, quietly, how the team had done without him this week, and how he'd kind of ruined a penalty kick, and how she would have laughed.

The candle fluttered, then steadied.

Eleanor had five dollars and one goal: the box of old comic books on the far table. She had circled the garage sale twice already, pretending to look at lampshades, because the man next to her kept pulling comics out one at a time and reading them. When he finally wandered off toward the record crates, she darted in and grabbed the box, only to hear the seller say, "Those are three dollars each now."

"Each?" Eleanor said. "The sign says a dollar."

The seller shrugged and flipped the cardboard sign over, where a new price was written in fresh marker. "That was before four people asked about them in the last half hour. Only two full boxes left. Somebody just offered to buy a whole box." His prices were volatile, changing whenever the crowd around a table thickened or thinned, and Eleanor had watched a stack of encyclopedias drop from ten dollars to two when nobody touched it for an hour.

She was still holding the box when she noticed a thin old book at the bottom, wedged under the comics. The cover was cracked leather, and inside, in faded ink, someone had copied a passage. It began: "Nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal." Eleanor read it twice. She carried the book to the seller. "What is this?"

"'The Wealth of Nations'," he said. "Published in 1776. My grandfather acquired it at an estate sale, and it's the one thing here I'm not discounting."

Eleanor looked at the sentence again. Water was the most useful thing there was, and it cost almost nothing, while a tiny diamond could buy piles of stuff. She looked at the tables around her: the comics, scarce and fought over, climbing in price; a whole driveway of drinking glasses, dozens of them, marked down to a quarter. She thought of the treaty of comic collectors who had apparently agreed, without ever meeting, that these particular issues mattered. Something invisible was setting every price on this lawn, something she couldn't see but could almost touch now.

"I'll give you my five dollars for this book and two comics," she said, holding her breath.

The seller studied her, then the thinning crowd, and said, "Four dollars, because it's almost noon and you're the only one who asked about that book all morning."

Eleanor counted out the bills, tucked the book under her arm, and walked home reading as she went.

Olivia had been postponing the question all afternoon, but at three o'clock it caught up with her: what do you bring to dinner at a house where you don't know the rules? Her new friend Nadia had invited her over for her birthday, and Nadia's family had moved to town from Malaysia only two months ago. Olivia's own family was eccentric enough that her grandmother kissed strangers on both cheeks and refused to let anyone start eating before a toast, so she knew that every household ran on its own invisible rules. She just couldn't see these ones yet.

She brought a small box of chocolates, wrapped hastily in gold paper, and stood on the porch rehearsing a greeting. When Nadia's father opened the door, he smiled and offered his right hand. Olivia shook it and passed him the gift, also with her right hand, mostly because that was the hand she used for everything. He accepted it the same way, thanked her warmly, and said, "In Malaysia, where we come from, we give and receive with the right hand, as a sign of respect."

In the dining room, Olivia noticed a pattern. Every dish was passed right hand to right hand, and when Nadia's little brother reached across the table with his left, Nadia caught his wrist and switched it for him without a word. Olivia filed that away and watched harder. Nobody said anything about it. The rule was quiet, like her grandmother's toast.

Then the rice arrived, and Olivia realized she had been holding her fork in her left hand all evening, the way her uncle had taught her, scooping with the spoon on the right. Her stomach dropped. Had she been rude for the last twenty minutes without knowing? She considered the probability that no one had noticed and decided it was low, because Nadia's grandmother kept glancing at her plate. Olivia had a simple idea: she would test it. She set the fork down, picked up the spoon with her right hand alone, and took the next bite.

Nadia's grandmother smiled at her, a real smile with crinkled eyes, and pushed the chicken dish toward her side of the table. Olivia reached out with her right hand and served herself. Across the table, Nadia gave her a tiny nod.

After dinner, Nadia pulled her into the kitchen and whispered, "Grandma says you have good manners. She wants to know if you'll come for Hari Raya in the spring."

"Only if you come to my grandmother's house first," Olivia said. "She has rules too. There's a toast, and there's a zero percent chance of escaping it."

"Deal," said Nadia, and handed her the last chocolate from the box, with her right hand.

Nathaniel spread the wires across the kitchen table and counted them twice. Copper, nichrome, and the steel paperclip he had straightened that morning, each one meant to carry current to the same small bulb. The science fair was Thursday, and his data sheet was a mess.

He clipped the copper wire to the battery holder, and the bulb glowed a steady yellow. He wrote down "bright." Then he swapped in the steel wire and a different bulb, because the first one had rolled off the table and he could not find it. The new bulb glowed pale and dim. He wrote "dim" and stared at it. Steel should have been worse than copper, but was the dimness the wire, or the other bulb? He had no way to know. He slammed the notebook shut, and his little sister Maya looked up from her cereal.

"You broke it already?"

"No. I don't know what I measured." He unrolled the crumpled handout from his back pocket and smoothed it flat. Maya leaned over her bowl and read the top line out loud. "Independent variable, the one thing you change on purpose. Dependent variable, what you measure to see the effect."

Nathaniel read it again, lips moving. He had changed two things. The wire and the bulb. That was the problem, sitting there in his own handwriting. "I changed the wire on purpose," he said slowly, "but I also changed the bulb by accident. So the brightness doesn't tell me anything about the wire."

"That's what you get for using my bulbs without asking."

He ignored her. The heater had been running all morning and the air in the kitchen felt arid enough to make the tape crackle when he peeled it off the table, but he kept working. He needed one bulb, the same bulb, every single trial. He searched under the table, found the runaway bulb in the shadow of the chair leg, and taped it down so it could not escape again. Copper went in. Bright. Steel went in, same bulb, same battery. The glow weakened to a dull orange, and this time the difference had to be the wire, because nothing else had moved.

For the last test he used the knife to strip the insulation and expose an inch of the copper, then the steel, then the nichrome, laying the bare metal in a neat row so the clips would touch clean conductor every time. Same battery. Same bulb. Three trials, three honest numbers. Maya slid her empty bowl toward him.

"You still owe me a bulb."

Ryder had watched Mrs. Okafor's apartment exactly twice before, and both times the worst thing that happened was a cat knocking a plant off the sill. Tonight was different. Tonight he was alone with Theo, who was two, and Theo had just produced a smell that no two-year-old should be able to produce.

Ryder laid out the changing mat on the living room rug while Theo's toy trucks continued to orbit the coffee table, as if nothing catastrophic had occurred. The diaper change itself went worse than any video had promised. By the end, Ryder had wipes stuck to his elbow and Theo was laughing like a hyena.

"Okay, buddy," Ryder said, carrying Theo toward the kitchen, which marked the frontier between the disaster zone of the rug and the place where lunch was supposed to happen. He set Theo in the high chair, then looked down at his own hands. He remembered his mother drilling it into him before his little cousin's birthday party: after a diaper change and before touching food, you scrub with soap for at least twenty seconds. Not a rinse. A scrub.

He turned on the tap and started humming the chorus of Theo's favorite song, the one about the shark family. Once through wasn't enough, he decided, so he hummed it twice, working the soap between his fingers and around his thumbs the whole time. Theo kicked his feet and shrieked the melody along with him.

Then Ryder noticed something. Theo had gone quiet, and his small fists were clenched around the tray of the high chair. His face was doing the thing right before crying, the trembling chin. Ryder had been sure the problem was hunger, but Theo wasn't acting hungry. He was staring past Ryder's shoulder, toward the living room.

Ryder followed his gaze. The changing mat still lay open on the rug, and beside it sat the empty wipes container, rocking slightly. The cat from downstairs had slipped in through the balcony door Ryder had left cracked for air, and it was now crouched over the mat like a dragon guarding treasure.

"Ah," Ryder said. "That's your spot, huh."

He dried his hands, shooed the cat out, folded the mat away, and slid it into the diaper bag, zipping it shut. When he turned around, Theo's chin had stopped trembling. Ryder washed up one more time, humming the song through twice again, and then sliced a banana and spread toast with the exact jam Theo pointed to.

Theo ate like a woodchipper. Ryder sank onto a kitchen chair and watched him go.

"You're going to be asleep by seven," Ryder told him.

Theo answered by putting a banana slice on his own nose.

Nicolas stabbed at his broccoli while his older sister Dani scrolled through her phone at the other end of the table. "Mom," she said, "Keisha says Priya's at the shoe store on Maple, the one by the fountain. Can we go after dinner?" Their mom frowned. "How does Keisha know that? Did Priya text her?" Dani shrugged. "She just knows." Nicolas put his fork down. That was the second time this week. Last Saturday, Keisha had known he was at the arcade the moment he walked in, and when he'd asked how, she'd only laughed and said, "Check your map."

He hadn't checked. It had seemed like a joke, and anyway the smell of pizza and the sound of the pinball machines had distracted him before he could think it through. But now the memory plagued him, circling back like a mosquito he kept failing to swat. He looked around the dinner table, at the steam curling off the mashed potatoes and the clink of Dani's fork against her plate, and decided he was done guessing. He had a phone in his pocket, and a test would take thirty seconds.

"Can I be excused for a sec?" he asked. In the hallway he opened the app and found the little map. There was the mall, drawn in simple shapes, and there was a tiny version of Priya's face glowing on the map, right on top of the shoe store by the fountain. It even moved, a small dot drifting toward the corner of the store, as if she were browsing. The map was, in effect, the equivalent of a window that looked directly into everyone's afternoon, except the window worked from anywhere, and it never shut.

He walked back to the table slowly. "Dani, does Keisha see all her friends like that? On a map?" Dani looked up, surprised he'd figured it out. "It's called Snap Map," she said. "Everyone's on it, Nicky. It shows where people are right now." Nicolas sat down, his chair scraping the floor. "Right now, right now? Like, if I went to the park, people would see me at the park?" "Well, your friends would," Dani said, as if this were the most ordinary thing in the world.

Nicolas thought about how many strangers could end up seeing a map like that if one friend shared it with another, and then another, a chain he couldn't see but could now picture clearly. The trouble wasn't one thing he could point to; it was the invisible pattern underneath, and ignoring it would only hinder him from fixing it. He took out his phone again, right there between the potatoes and the broccoli, and opened the settings, his thumb hovering over the map.

"What are you doing?" Dani asked.

"Going ghost," Nicolas said, and tapped the button.

By ten in the morning, Hannah had sold two paperbacks and a single mitten, and the sun on the driveway made her perspire through the back of her shirt. Her card table held everything she owned that she could bear to part with: old sunglasses, a stack of comics, a lava lamp glowing a toxic shade of green, and one volume of poetry with a cracked spine. Across the driveway, at the neighbors' table, a crowd had formed, because Mrs. Delgado had only six pairs of vintage sunglasses left and had just raised the price from three dollars to eight.

"Eight dollars?" a woman muttered, putting a pair down. "It's just sunglasses." One by one, the buyers drifted away from Mrs. Delgado's table, and then, to Hannah's astonishment, they drifted to hers. A man picked up her two-dollar sunglasses and turned them over. "Same job, way cheaper," he said, and bought both pairs. Within twenty minutes, her whole box of sunglasses was gone, and she had eleven more dollars for the telescope she'd been saving toward since March.

She sat back on the warm concrete and thought it through. Nobody had announced anything. The price at one table had gone up, and people had simply walked to the other table and bought the thing that did the same job. She wondered if it would work the other way, so she made a quiet plan. She picked up the poetry book, found her favorite stanza, and read it under her breath to steady herself, then turned her attention to the lava lamp. Two boys had been circling it all morning, but nobody would commit at five dollars, because three other families on the street were selling lamps today.

"Three dollars," she called out, tapping the lamp. One of the boys sprinted back from two houses down, coins already counted into his palm. "My brother wanted one, but the lady up the street is asking ten for hers," he said, handing over the money. "So now he can have this instead." Hannah watched him carry the lamp away like a trophy, and something clicked into place: the other family's high price had sent buyers straight to her table, exactly like the sunglasses, exactly like she'd guessed. The rule was invisible, but she had caught it twice in one morning.

When her mom came out with lemonade, Hannah counted her cash box with careful fingers. "Fourteen dollars toward the telescope," she reported. Her mom raised an eyebrow at the empty space where the lamp had been. "You want to split this lemonade?" Hannah asked, then grinned. "Better hurry, before the neighbor's table raises their price and everyone comes running to ours."

The lights went out at seven, right in the middle of Emilia's homework, and the living room went dark except for the two candles her mother found under the sink. Emilia moved her history notes to the coffee table and tried to keep working by candlelight, but her mind kept drifting to the kitchen. The freezer. She and her brother had eaten through half the frozen food that week because they were too lazy to shop, and now the whole street was black and the fridge wasn't humming anymore.

"Mom, how long is this going to last?" she asked. Her mother, on the couch with her phone held up to the window, shook her head.

"The power company says tomorrow evening at the earliest."

Tomorrow evening. Emilia counted on her fingers. If the outage ended at six tomorrow, that would be almost twenty-three hours from now. She opened her notebook and tried to classify the situation like a math problem: known things, unknown things, things she could test. The known thing was the freezer, sitting in the dark kitchen with its door shut. The unknown thing was how long the food inside could survive.

She remembered a leaflet that had come taped to the freezer years ago, before they owned it, something the previous owners had left in the drawer. She dug through the kitchen junk drawer while her candle dripped onto a saucer, and found the paper folded behind the takeout menus. It said a full freezer holds a safe temperature for about forty-eight hours without power, and a half-full one for about twenty-four hours, if the door stays closed. Twenty-four hours. Her arithmetic from a minute ago had been almost exactly right, and only if nobody opened that door.

Emilia called her family into the kitchen. "We can't open the freezer until tomorrow evening," she said. "Half full, it's only good for about a day. If it were packed full it would be two days, but we ate everything."

Her brother groaned. "The frozen dumplings are in there."

"And they'll still be fine tomorrow at six if you don't stand there with the door open staring at them." She took a roll of masking tape from the drawer and ran a strip across the freezer door and down the side of the cabinet, sealing it shut like crime-scene tape. Then she wrote on the tape with a marker: DO NOT OPEN UNTIL TOMORROW EVENING. Her brother signed his initials under it to make it official, sulking, and their mother wrote hers too.

They went back to the living room, and Emilia read her history notes out loud by candlelight while her brother listened, sprawled on the rug in his synthetic fleece jacket because the house was cooling down. They were supposed to be studying the lives of medieval peasants, who got along without electricity their whole lives, and her brother pointed out that at least the peasants hadn't had a freezer full of dumplings to worry about. Emilia snorted and turned the page, and outside the window the street stayed dark all the way to the corner.

Grandpa's living room smelled like popcorn and radiator dust, and every seat was taken except the piano bench, which nobody wanted because it wobbled. Jeremy dragged it in anyway. On the screen, two teams he didn't recognize were fighting for a ball in the rain, and Uncle Ray was shouting at the referee in two languages.

"Argentina," Uncle Ray announced during a commercial. "First World Cup, Argentina won it. My father told me a hundred times."

"Nope." Grandpa shook his head slowly, the way he did when he was about to enjoy being right. "Uruguay."

"Uruguay?" Aunt Sofia nearly dropped her chip bowl. "Ray, Uruguay hosted it. That doesn't mean they won it. There's a difference."

"Hosts don't win," Uncle Ray said. "It's practically a rule of sports. Ironic, isn't it, the home crowd choking like that."

Jeremy ate his popcorn and thought about that. He didn't know who was right, and nobody in the room seemed able to prove anything. They just got louder. His cousin Marco slid down behind the couch and pretended to be asleep, which was his standard move during family arguments.

Then Jeremy remembered something. Grandpa's den had a shelf of old almanacs and sports annuals, the kind with tiny print and cracked spines. During the next commercial he slipped out of the room. Nobody noticed, which was fine by him. He found a world sports record book from the 1950s and flipped through the soccer section, running his finger down page after page until he hit a table of World Cup results.

There it was. First tournament, 1930, held in Uruguay. Final: Uruguay 4, Argentina 2. He read it three times to make sure he had it straight, then copied it onto the back of an envelope from Grandpa's desk. It felt like holding a card nobody else at the party had seen.

He walked back in and stood in front of the TV. "I have a message from the den," he said, and held up the envelope like a telegram. "To Uncle Ray, from the year 1930. It says: Uruguay hosted, Uruguay won, final score Uruguay 4, Argentina 2. Signed, a book older than everybody in this room."

Marco sat up from behind the couch. "Grandpa wins the argument AND a thirteen-year-old did the research. Ray, that's a double loss."

"Let me see that envelope," Uncle Ray said. He squinted at it, then at the doorway to the den, as if the almanac itself might be lying to protect Grandpa. "Huh."

"Four to two," Grandpa said, holding out his hand. Uncle Ray slapped five coins into it, though Jeremy had never heard a bet announced. On the screen, someone scored, and everyone who had been arguing two minutes ago jumped up and yelled at the same instant.

Avery set the portable grill table at the far end of the backyard, where Dad said the smoke wouldn't drift into the neighbors' windows. Tonight was her turn to cook, and she had promised chicken drumsticks, a green salad, and lemonade for the whole family. Mom was home from work late, so Avery wanted everything ready by the time she walked through the gate, tired and hungry.

She carried out two plastic cutting boards, the knife block, the chicken, and a fat head of lettuce. Her little brother Theo trailed behind her with the salad spinner, which he insisted on operating even though it was mostly empty. The backyard table was sparse, just their supplies and a roll of paper towels, so Avery laid everything out in a line: chicken first, closest to the grill, then the board, then the lettuce at the far end.

She trimmed the drumsticks on the board, salting each one while Theo handed her pieces of lemon peel for the marinade. When the chicken went onto the grill, she washed her hands at the garden spigot and reached for the lettuce. Then she paused. The board still held faint streaks from the raw chicken, even after she wiped it with a paper towel. She couldn't see anything alive on it, but she remembered last summer, when half her class got sick after a class party, and her friend Maya had said the culprit was a virus too small for anyone to perceive, spreading from food to food. Certain things moved invisibly, and wiping a surface didn't mean it was clean.

"We need the other board," Avery said, and she ran inside for the clean one from the dish rack.

"Why?" Theo asked, spinning an empty bowl on his finger.

"Raw chicken and ready-to-eat stuff like salad have to stay on separate boards," she said. "It's called cross-contamination, when bacteria spread from one food to another."

Theo nodded solemnly, as if she had described a dragon, and stationed himself as the board inspector. He brought out only the blue board for vegetables and guarded the chicken board with the tongs.
